Problem & Motivation: The work addresses adaptation of frozen, black-box LLMs on open-ended tasks such as medical consultation, creative writing, and research assistance, where quality has multiple valid dimensions and a fixed natural-language rubric may omit safety, completeness, or other requirements. Existing text-space optimizers can improve a solver only on criteria exposed by the fixed evaluation artifact. Jointly evolving the rubric can expose new dimensions, but accepting rubric changes according to the current solver's aggregate score creates an identification problem: a higher proxy may reflect a better solver or a rubric that is easier for that solver to satisfy. The paper targets this gap by seeking an evaluation-update signal that detects omitted requirements and missed distinctions without using gold rubrics during optimization. Key Idea: The central insight is to treat solver-skill evolution and rubric-generator-skill evolution as different optimization problems and prohibit aggregate solver score from serving as the generator's acceptance objective. Generator revisions instead receive independent evidence from two audits: a structural audit checks whether generated rubrics cover requirements implied by the task, while a rubric-blind near-tie audit first identifies meaningful quality differences between similarly scored responses without seeing the rubric and then asks how the rubric should represent those differences. The generator is therefore revised toward coverage and discrimination rather than toward criteria that maximize the current solver's proxy score. Methodology: DecoEvo maintains a persistent solver skill s and rubric-generator skill g while keeping the underlying LLM frozen. For each question q, the solver produces a response and the generator produces a weighted natural-language rubric; a criterion-level judge returns per-criterion scores and failure rationales, combined into a weighted rubric score S(q,r,R). In the inner loop, batches from a training pool generate solver failures, a rewriter distills reusable fixes into a candidate solver skill, and the candidate is accepted only if its score improves by margin epsilon on a disjoint solver-validation set using cached rubrics. In the outer loop, periodically or after repeated solver-update rejections, a task-conditioned structural auditor evaluates the question, public task description, and generated rubric without seeing the response or solver score; it outputs an adequacy score, evidence-grounded rationale, and repair suggestion. A near-tie contrastive auditor samples L solver rollouts, selects response pairs whose generated-rubric scores differ by at most tau_tie, judges each pair without seeing the rubric, and then diagnoses which criterion or principle fails to distinguish the preferred response. A generator rewriter distills probe-set audit records into a candidate generator skill. The candidate is evaluated on held-out generator-gate data and accepted if at least one available audit objective improves by margin delta while no other objective regresses beyond tolerance eta. Critical design choices are the complete exclusion of aggregate solver score from generator acceptance, rubric-blind preference formation before exposing the rubric, and frozen paired verification sets; the experiments support these choices through ablations, although the audit roles themselves remain LLM-based and their reliability is only indirectly validated. Key Results: On HealthBench, LLMEval-Med, WritingBench, EQ-Bench Creative Writing v3, and ResearchQA, DecoEvo obtains the highest score in all 15 backbone–benchmark combinations. Its five-benchmark averages are 64.8 for GPT-4o, 62.1 for Qwen3-4B, and 65.0 for Qwen3-8B, versus SkillOpt averages of 61.7, 60.4, and 63.2; the corresponding absolute gains are 3.10, 1.74, and 1.78 points, reported as 5.0%, 2.9%, and 2.8% relative. On GPT-4o, individual DecoEvo scores are 45.3 on HealthBench versus 41.7 for SkillOpt, 60.2 versus 57.6 on LLMEval-Med, 66.1 versus 63.9 on WritingBench, 82.7 versus 80.5 on Creative Writing, and 69.7 versus 64.8 on ResearchQA. The two source-to-transfer gains are obtained without updating on the transfer benchmarks: 4.5% relative on LLMEval-Med for GPT-4o and 2.7% on Creative Writing. The matched score-coupled co-evolution baseline performs worse than SkillOpt in 13 of 15 settings and worse than zero-shot in seven, supporting the claimed failure mode, though this baseline is a custom implementation rather than a broad comparison to all adaptive-rubric methods. Five-run GPT-4o, Qwen3-4B, and Qwen3-8B average gains over SkillOpt have 95% confidence intervals of [2.88, 3.32], [1.42, 2.06], and [1.69, 1.87], respectively, and remain significant after Holm correction. On HealthBench, removing structural auditing costs 1.3–1.7 points, removing contrastive auditing costs 1.7–2.1, removing rubric blindness costs 1.0–1.5, removing near-tie sampling costs 1.5–1.7, removing verification costs 2.4–2.9, and removing distillation costs 1.4–1.8 across the three backbones. With GPT-4o, DecoEvo uses 41.7 million optimization tokens, 1.89 times SkillOpt's 22.1 million, and scores 45.3 versus 41.7; budget matching reaches only 42.1 and direct routing of audit records to the solver reaches 43.7. Generated-rubric alignment with held-out gold criteria improves from SkillOpt F1 values of 44.6, 48.1, and 46.4 to DecoEvo values of 56.9, 60.3, and 58.7 on HealthBench, WritingBench, and ResearchQA, using a GPT-5.5 matcher with reported 91.3% balanced accuracy against adjudicated labels. These results measure official benchmark grader scores and criterion overlap, not broad human judgments or real deployment outcomes. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION, NEW METHOD, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, and ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION. The genuinely distinctive contribution is the formulation and implementation of score-decoupled co-evolution for persistent text-space solver and rubric-generator skills, combining structural and rubric-blind near-tie audits with held-out Pareto verification; the individual components—LLM-based rubric generation, textual skill rewriting, contrastive evaluation, and validation-based candidate selection—are largely established ideas recombined for this setting. Rigor & Reproducibility: The study uses disjoint pilot, training, probe, solver-gate, generator-gate, diagnostic, and test partitions, cached paired comparisons for solver updates, frozen audit records for generator verification, five matched end-to-end runs, standard deviations, confidence intervals, and multiple-comparison correction. It includes component ablations, budget-matched and direct-audit controls, proxy-versus-official-grader trajectories, and rubric-alignment analysis. These controls support the mechanism claim more strongly than the headline benchmark table alone. However, the main comparison set is narrow: zero-shot, SkillOpt, and a matched score-coupled variant, with no reported comparisons to several contemporary adaptive-rubric or pairwise-rubric systems cited in related work. All optimization roles use the same frozen backbone within a setting, so the method may benefit from correlated solver, judge, auditor, and rewriter behavior. The official graders and training-time judges are not fully independent in the broader sense of evaluator construction, and the rubric-alignment metric depends on an LLM matcher, albeit one calibrated against 150 criterion pairs with reported human adjudication statistics. The paper is an arXiv preprint dated July 28, 2026; code, data, prompts, skills, model weights, or a repository URL are not stated, limiting independent reproduction. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL. Practical: The method can operate with commercially available hosted or local LLMs because it edits text artifacts and does not require weight access, but optimization requires many calls and 41.7 million tokens in the reported GPT-4o HealthBench setting. Efficient: Deployment retains only the solver skill and adds no stated inference-time model cost, but development consumes 1.89 times the SkillOpt token budget and substantially more calls than solver-only optimization. Effective: The method improves official benchmark scores by 1.74–3.10 absolute points over SkillOpt across three backbones and transfers within medicine and writing, but effectiveness is established mainly against automated benchmark graders rather than downstream user outcomes or broad human judgments. Scalable: The paper tests three backbones and five benchmarks but does not evaluate 10×–100× larger datasets, longer optimization horizons, larger models, many concurrent tasks, or cross-domain transfer, so scalability remains a claim rather than a demonstrated property. The work delivers a text-space optimization procedure and optimized solver/generator natural-language skills; a reusable software artifact, library, CLI, dataset, or trained model release is not stated. Strengths: - It identifies a concrete failure mode in joint solver–evaluator optimization and formalizes it as score coupling, making the distinction between solver improvement and evaluator relaxation explicit. - The rubric-blind-then-rubric-exposed near-tie protocol is a nontrivial mechanism for finding distinctions that the current rubric misses rather than simply adding more permissive criteria. - The experimental design includes strong mechanism-oriented controls: score-coupled co-evolution, budget matching, direct audit routing, leave-one-component-out ablations, and external-grader trajectory analysis. - The gains persist on two within-domain cross-benchmark transfers and coincide with improved criterion-level precision and recall, which is more informative than reporting aggregate scores alone. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state that the evidence is limited to settings where optimization roles share a backbone, that transfer is restricted to medicine or writing, and that broader human evaluation and cross-domain tasks remain future work. They also acknowledge that the generator is discarded after optimization and that validation sets are model-selection sets rather than unbiased final evaluations. These limitations are confronted directly, although the paper does not quantify how much same-backbone role sharing contributes to the results. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The method's central audits are themselves generated and judged by the same frozen backbone, so the paper does not establish that score decoupling protects against correlated evaluator failure or model-specific blind spots. The absence of human evaluation is particularly important because the claimed benefit is better quality coverage, while official graders and the GPT-5.5 criterion matcher may share linguistic or benchmark-specific biases. The comparison omits direct empirical baselines from adaptive-rubric and pairwise-rubric methods cited in the related-work section, making the novelty and practical advantage over the strongest current alternatives uncertain. The evaluation remains restricted to five benchmarks, two domains, and within-domain transfer; there is no cross-domain transfer, cross-backbone assignment of solver versus auditor roles, multilingual test, adversarial rubric-drift test, or robustness analysis under noisy audit judgments. Optimization cost excludes the one-time pilot search, and the paper does not report wall-clock time, monetary cost, acceptance rates, or sensitivity to thresholds such as near-tie margin, audit schedule, and Pareto tolerances. Finally, the alignment matcher is evaluated on only 150 criterion pairs, and rubric overlap does not prove that the generated criteria are causally responsible for improved response quality. Bottom Line: This is a technically coherent and experimentally well-controlled preprint that offers a useful score-decoupling design for black-box text-space LLM optimization, but readers should regard its 2.8–5.0% relative gains as promising rather than conclusive until human, cross-backbone, cross-domain, and stronger adaptive-rubric comparisons are provided.

Problem & Motivation: The work addresses the infrastructure problem of rapidly prototyping online, multi-turn, multimodal, and tool-using RL agents at large model scale. Researchers need to change estimators, reward pipelines, rollout schedules, and environment logic without tracing changes through multi-backend trainers, distributed controllers, and serving adapters. Existing systems trade approachability against scale: lighter frameworks provide simpler experimentation but narrower agentic or frontier-scale support, whereas production-oriented stacks provide distributed breadth at the cost of a larger and less navigable code surface. A second problem concerns silent correctness failures at the rollout–training boundary: retokenization, context compaction, policy staleness, multimodal rendering, and MoE routing can cause the trainer to optimize tokens or model computations that differ from those used during generation. Key Idea: The central insight is to make the generated token trace—not reconstructed text or framework-specific trajectory objects—the canonical interface across an ordinary Python agent, serving engine, asynchronous queue, and policy loss. This token-first contract is paired with a deliberately single-backend architecture and correctness invariants for token identity, policy-version semantics, and rollout–training forward consistency. The paper’s novelty lies primarily in combining these choices into a compact research-oriented system rather than in introducing a new RL objective or scheduler. Methodology: Molt runs an asynchronous Ray-based loop connecting user agents, vLLM rollout engines behind a router, and one trainable PyTorch policy actor built with NVIDIA AutoModel and FSDP2; optional critic and reference workers support PPO and related variants. In the environment interface, Molt owns the model interaction loop; in the ChatAgent interface, an OpenAI- or Anthropic-compatible loopback server captures SDK traffic as token IDs and per-token behavior log-probabilities without requiring agent changes. Prompt groups remain persistently in flight, and completed groups enter training as soon as a batch is available; partial rollouts are paused across weight updates and resumed with stored policy-version log-probabilities plus per-token importance correction and a sequence-level gate. The actor computes advantages through plain functions, including group-mean REINFORCE, RLOO, GRPO, Dr. GRPO, GAE/PPO, REINFORCE++, and on-policy distillation, and normalizes policy-gradient, KL, and entropy terms by one global count of unmasked tokens. Dynamic filtering removes degenerate groups and backfills complete groups. For multimodal MoE models, prompts are rendered once, token and image data remain aligned, weights are refit directly from actor shards to engines over NCCL, and rollout expert choices are replayed during training. The main design decisions—single-backend composition, token-first capture, and persistent asynchronous streaming—are clearly motivated by readability, upstream compatibility, and correctness, although the paper does not isolate their individual effects through controlled ablations. Key Results: The framework-owned RL path is reported as approximately 8.6K Python lines, compared with approximately 62K for verl and 25K for slime under the authors’ import-graph counting method; the paper cautions that LOC measures implementation footprint rather than usability or correctness. On a Qwen3-30B-A3B bf16 workload using 2 nodes × 8 H100 GPUs, 8 training GPUs, 8 rollout GPUs, 2K deduplicated DAPO-Math prompts, 32 prompts × 4 samples per step, and 16,384-token context with an 8,192-token response cap, Molt records 119.4 ± 2.3 seconds per optimizer step and 461 generated tokens/GPU/s, versus 109.5 ± 10.3 seconds and 502 tokens/GPU/s for slime; each configuration uses three independent runs, and the paper reports statistical overlap rather than superiority. Molt’s speculative decoding reduces generation time from 329 seconds to 64 seconds, approximately a 5× reduction, while optimizer CPU offload reduces actor peak GPU memory from 64.7 GB to 46.4 GB, an 18.3 GB or 28.3% reduction, at a reported 18% policy-training time increase from 213 to 251 seconds. Prefix-cache re-prefill takes 0.05 seconds on a cache hit, but no cache-miss or end-to-end speedup baseline is provided. The full asynchronous loop, including rollout, refit, and optimizer steps, is reported to run on a 700B MoE at expert parallelism 256, but no throughput, convergence, or quality numbers are given at that scale. Most importantly, the head-to-head benchmark is throughput-only: an approximately one-nat actor/reference MoE forward mismatch causes the [0.99, 1.01] sequence gate to reject every batch, so the comparison does not establish learning equivalence. Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION, and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely new contribution is a compact, open implementation that unifies token-exact SDK-compatible agent capture, asynchronous prompt-group streaming, policy-version correction, and native FSDP2/MoE scaling in one research-oriented path; the underlying RL estimators, importance correction, routing replay, Ray/vLLM composition, and distributed training mechanisms are largely adopted from prior work. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper provides a public Apache-2.0 repository at https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/labs-molt, reference agents, one-command recipes, and prebuilt containers, and states that the reported configurations are shipped. The head-to-head benchmark specifies hardware, model, precision, topology, batch, context, sampling, optimizer, commits, and three independent runs, and it discloses residual asymmetries between Molt and slime. However, no component ablations quantify the effects of token capture, streaming, routing replay, direct NCCL refit, or sequence-level correction; no learning curves, reward/pass-rate results, convergence comparisons, or statistical tests for policy quality are reported; and the three-run sample is small. The baseline is a relevant contemporary Megatron-based stack, but the comparison changes both training backend and rollout engine—Molt uses AutoModel plus vLLM, while slime uses Megatron-Core plus SGLang—and the benchmark’s rejected updates prevent it from testing the complete training system. The code and recipes improve reproducibility, but the paper does not provide an independent usability study validating its human- or AI-assistant-readability claims. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS, because the paper delivers and benchmarks a software framework rather than only a method or formal result. Practical: Molt runs on commercially available NVIDIA H100 hardware and uses standard PyTorch, Ray, vLLM, FSDP2, and NCCL components, but it is intentionally limited to NVIDIA AutoModel and vLLM rather than supporting multiple training or serving backends. Efficient: It matches slime within the reported high-variance benchmark while speculative decoding provides a 5× generation-time reduction and CPU optimizer offload saves 18.3 GB of GPU memory at an 18% policy-training penalty; full framework overhead relative to alternatives is not separately measured. Effective: The system demonstrates token transport, asynchronous execution, refit, memory optimizations, and a 700B end-to-end execution path, but the central benchmark does not demonstrate effective policy learning because all updates are rejected by a MoE consistency gate. Scalable: The same loop is reported to execute a 700B MoE at expert parallelism 256 and exposes configuration knobs for 1T-class models, but the paper supplies no 10×–100× throughput, memory, fault-tolerance, or convergence evaluation and explicitly leaves end-to-end convergence measurement for future work. The work delivers a reusable open-source framework, recipes, containers, and reference agents rather than stopping at a paper-only design. Strengths: (1) The token-first contract addresses a concrete and consequential failure mode: it preserves generated token IDs and behavior log-probabilities across ordinary SDK agents, multi-turn interaction, context compaction, asynchronous updates, and multimodal inputs. (2) The system makes several correctness checks explicit, including policy-version correction, sequence-level mismatch gating, and MoE routing replay, and it fails fast on unsupported combinations instead of silently producing suspect updates. (3) The implementation demonstrates meaningful systems integration: FSDP2 tensor/expert/context parallelism, vLLM serving features, direct NCCL refit, CPU optimizer offload, speculative decoding, and a reported 700B MoE execution all use the same visible loop. (4) The authors disclose the decisive limitation in their main benchmark—the MoE mismatch that invalidates policy updates—instead of presenting throughput as evidence of training quality. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The paper explicitly limits itself to one training backend, NVIDIA AutoModel, and one serving engine, vLLM, accepting narrower deployment coverage for reduced indirection. It states that multi-version serving, skew prediction, elastic environment services, optimal resource planning, enterprise data conversion, and unified production control planes are outside scope. It also acknowledges unsupported combinations such as packed batches under context parallelism, the absence of cache-miss measurements for prefix caching, and the upstream MoE forward mismatch that prevents convergence-parity validation. The authors identify end-to-end convergence measurement at 700B and beyond, plus usability and quality studies, as future work; these limitations are confronted directly rather than hidden. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The paper does not measure whether Molt’s central research benefit—faster or more reliable algorithm iteration—actually improves researcher productivity, code-modification time, defect rates, or AI coding-assistant performance. It lacks ablations showing whether the compact architecture causes any throughput, reliability, or correctness trade-offs, and it does not compare against all closely related asynchronous systems under equivalent hardware and workloads. The principal benchmark uses a DAPO-Math prompt set and a single Qwen3 MoE configuration, with no task-quality evaluation on real multi-turn tool use, multimodal environments, long-horizon agents, or context-compaction scenarios. The 700B claim reports successful execution but not resource utilization, throughput, stability, recovery behavior, or learning. Finally, the authors extrapolate that backend differences diminish at longer generation lengths without measuring the stated 32K–128K regime, and the LOC comparison may favor Molt’s narrower feature scope rather than establish superior usability. Bottom Line: Practitioners building NVIDIA-centered agentic RL infrastructure should read Molt for its token-exact interface and unusually explicit correctness design, but its current evidence supports a promising open systems substrate—not a demonstrated improvement in RL training quality or a definitive replacement for broader production frameworks.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Metis, a causal language model with a persistent, fixed-size native memory state and learned memory procedures for storing, using, updating, and forgetting information across interaction steps. - Why it's important: Native memory could reduce the latency, storage growth, and pipeline fragmentation of retrieval-based or test-time-adaptation memory systems for long-running AI agents. - How it does it: Metis adds local fast-memory matrices and hyper-memory networks to Transformer layers, using learned token aggregation, memory attention, and gradient-free recurrent updates trained through memory-specific mid-training. - The good: In no-context evaluation, Metis-27B reaches 73.77 average on the authors' test set and 26.74 on LoCoMo (Gold), while at 128K tokens it is 1.50–1.60× faster than full-context inference and uses constant per-session state. - The missing: The central scalability claim remains limited by severe fixed-state capacity degradation, with accuracy falling as a single update grows beyond several hundred words or as trajectories extend to 40 updates, and no evaluation demonstrates reliable deployment-scale long-term memory. - Read it or not: Researchers working on latent memory, fast weights, test-time training, or stateful agents should read it for the architecture and extensive failure analysis, while practitioners seeking reliable long-term memory should treat it as an early prototype rather than a replacement for external memory.

Problem & Motivation: AI agents must retain information from prior interactions and apply it later, but most current systems implement memory externally through retrieval, text concatenation, explicit storage rules, or test-time adaptation. These approaches separate memory construction from backbone inference, make end-to-end optimization difficult through discrete retrieval and storage operations, add preparation or adaptation latency, and often require storage that grows with history. The paper targets stateful language-model agents that need to remember, update, forget, and combine interaction-specific information without replaying the original context. Its claimed gap is the absence of a foundation-model architecture in which both the memory state and the procedures that transform and read it are integrated into the backbone's forward computation; however, this gap overlaps substantially with prior fast-weight, recurrent-state, latent-memory, and parametric-memory work. Key Idea: Treat online memory as dynamic parameters inside the language model rather than as text or a separate memory module. Metis compresses selected intermediate hidden states into a fixed-size key-value-like matrix and normalization vector, reads that state through a separately learned memory query, and trains the update and readout mechanisms so that semantic operations such as remembering, updating, forgetting, and reflecting emerge from ordinary forward computation. Methodology: Metis inserts a memory block into each Transformer layer. The local memory block maintains a dynamic matrix M^(l) in R^(d_k × d_v) and normalization vector S^(l), initialized to zero and updated across interaction steps. The hyper-memory block contains learned aggregation, key, value, and query projections. During storage, hidden states from the current interaction are normalized, scored by a learned importance vector, and selected using a top-ρ cumulative-probability rule with a straight-through estimator; selected states are projected to keys and values and written into M and S using a discounted recurrent update, ultimately implemented with a Gated Delta Network update rather than the basic linear rule. During utilization, the current hidden states are projected into a separate memory query, which reads M using normalized linear attention; this readout is combined with ordinary causal attention using a fixed mixing coefficient γ. Memory updates occur after an interaction using the current input and generated output, while model weights remain frozen online. Mid-training uses token-averaged autoregressive negative log-likelihood on sequential trajectories, with a curriculum over reconstruction data, explicit/implicit operation data, distractor data, multi-fact data, and memory-irrelevant dialogue. The reconstruction objective encourages lossless recall, the operation objective supervises remember/forget/update/reflect behavior, and the regularization objective targets cross-fact interference and memory pollution. The most consequential design decisions—adaptive aggregation, a separate memory query, query-key normalization, and GDU updates—are empirically ablated; the paper's theoretical analysis explains how the dense state approximates virtual prefix attention and decomposes retrieval error into irrelevant-information and normalization terms, but it does not establish a formal performance guarantee. Key Results: On MemOps (Gold), Metis-27B obtains 28.27 remember, 31.02 update, 10.91 forget, 26.55 reflect, and 24.76 average in the no-context setting; on the authors' Metis test set it obtains 61.08, 68.13, 77.50, 93.44, and 73.77, respectively. On LoCoMo (Gold), Metis-27B scores 31.01 single-hop, 27.97 multi-hop, 13.83 temporal, 28.93 open-domain, and 26.74 average; on NextMem it scores 43.42 on SQuAD, 66.54 on HotpotQA, 39.71 on LongMemEval, 60.41 on LoCoMo, and 50.82 average. These results outperform the reported no-context Temp-LoRA and δ-Mem baselines, but remain far below full-context Qwen3.5-27B, which scores 65.03 on LoCoMo (Gold) and 78.80 on NextMem. On OOD ATM-Bench, Metis-27B reaches 18.56 average versus 2.86 for Temp-LoRA-9B and 2.57 for Temp-LoRA-27B; on MemDaily it reaches 59.04, below Temp-LoRA-27B's 59.45. The strongest ablation effect is removing selective adaptive aggregation, reducing the overall 4B score by 60.98%; removing query-key normalization reduces it by 28.44%, and removing the separate memory query by 12.23%. Low-rank memory with rank 64 retains 99.9% of full-state average performance while reducing the 4B state from 16.79 MB to 2.11 MB. On a single A800 with controlled histories, Metis becomes faster than full context at 64K tokens: 5.390 versus 5.909 seconds for 32 generated tokens and 9.522 versus 10.228 seconds for 128; at 128K, the speedups are 1.497× and 1.595×. At 32K, full-context state is 1,118.86 MB compared with 16.79 MB for full Metis and 2.11 MB for rank-64 Metis. Active irrelevant memory also harms general capability: Metis-4B loses 22.18 points on IFEval, 5.61 on GSM8K, 5.10 on MMLU-Pro, and 3.30 on MMMLU relative to the backbone. The capacity study is counter-intuitive relative to the efficiency claims: compression makes storage constant, but recall accuracy declines sharply with longer individual updates and repeated trajectories. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION, NEW METHOD, NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, and ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION. The genuinely new element is the explicit formulation of “memory foundation models” as models with persistent dynamic parameters plus learned native memory procedures, instantiated by Metis's hyper/local memory architecture; the underlying ingredients—fast weights, recurrent state compression, linear attention, learned key-value memories, and test-time adaptation—are established and are combined in a new agent-memory setting rather than replaced by a wholly new learning principle. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper provides broad ablations, OOD tests, backbone transfer to Llama-3.1-8B, capacity studies, general-capability checks, latency measurements, storage measurements, and explicit training and prompting details. It reports one training seed (42), but does not report error bars, multiple training seeds, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests; several comparisons therefore rely on single checkpoints and LLM-as-a-judge scores. The evaluation uses GPT-4.1-mini at temperature zero with three repeated judgments and median aggregation, but much of the evidence is still judge-dependent. Training data are synthesized from 27 public benchmarks into 357,137 primary samples and 609,443 auxiliary samples; although the paper evaluates OOD ATM-Bench and MemDaily, several central results use the authors' Metis test set, MemOps, and NextMem, and the training sources overlap semantically with some evaluation domains. The authors state that exact QA behaviors are not leaked, but provide limited independent verification of this claim. Baselines include full-context, top-5 dense RAG, Temp-LoRA, and δ-Mem, yet comparisons are not uniformly matched: δ-Mem uses a different Qwen3 backbone/configuration, and full-context and partial-context systems have different information interfaces. Code is released at https://github.com/MemTensor/Metis, and model checkpoints are released at https://huggingface.co/collections/IAAR-Shanghai/metis. The paper does not establish that the reported parallelism is realized in the released implementation; it explicitly does not enable asynchronous CUDA overlap. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS, because the paper builds and evaluates a runnable model architecture and releases code and checkpoints, while also providing empirical experiments. Practical: Metis runs on commercially available NVIDIA H100/A800 GPUs and is built on 4B, 9B, and 27B causal language models, but practical deployment still requires storing a substantial per-session state for the full-rank version and processing the entire history during memory ingestion. Efficient: The method has constant per-session state and lower query latency than Temp-LoRA and δ-Mem; at 32K tokens it uses 16.79 MB full-rank or 2.11 MB at rank 64, and at 128K it is 1.50–1.60× faster than full-context inference, although it is not faster than partial-context retrieval in the reported cold-start LoCoMo test and still pays the cost of encoding history. Effective: Evidence shows meaningful no-context recall and operation performance above the baselines, but the method remains well below full-context performance, performs poorly on some forget and open-domain cases, and can contaminate unrelated tasks when irrelevant memory is present. Scalable: Storage scales favorably because the state size is fixed, but semantic capacity does not: accuracy degrades with longer single updates and repeated updates, the longest reported trajectory contains only 40 facts, and no experiment validates reliable behavior at 10×–100× beyond the tested interaction horizon. The work delivers a software repository, downloadable trained model checkpoints, a reusable Metis architecture, synthesized memory-training data procedures, and evaluation code or configurations described in the paper; it does not deliver a production-grade memory service, interpretable memory representation, or guarantee of durable information retention. Strengths: - It articulates a clear architectural distinction between external memory, latent memory, parametric memory, and native memory, and connects that distinction to statefulness, optimization, and inference efficiency. - The Metis design couples a fixed-size dynamic state with learned storage and readout procedures rather than relying only on a recurrent state or a manually specified retrieval policy. - The empirical study does more than report benchmark averages: it measures OOD transfer, long-horizon capacity, interference, memory pollution, general-capability degradation, low-rank compression, latency, and per-session storage. - The component ablations identify adaptive aggregation and query-key normalization as materially important, while the GDU ablation honestly shows that the more sophisticated update rule is not uniformly better than a linear update. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state that fixed-size compression causes information loss on long-term tasks and that semantically blended latent representations can cause information confusion. They also acknowledge that Metis cannot yet replace external memory and present hybrid memory, improved capacity, controllability, interpretability, and longer interactions as future work. Case studies show that the forgetting instruction may still repeat the old fact in the immediate response even when the subsequent memory query correctly reports that the fact is unavailable. The general-capability study acknowledges degradation after irrelevant memory is accumulated, particularly on instruction following. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The paper does not sufficiently separate the benefit of native memory from the benefit of extensive task-specific supervision and a fixed “commit to memory” interface. The main comparison omits strong hybrid systems that combine retrieval with latent or parametric memory, and the RAG baseline is restricted to top-5 dense retrieval rather than a tuned production-grade memory pipeline. The evaluation is dominated by synthetic fact-level interactions and short-answer judging, which may not represent noisy, adversarial, multimodal, privacy-sensitive, or continuously changing user histories. The claimed end-to-end and parallel-efficiency advantages are measured mainly on one GPU and a Qwen3.5 configuration whose 24 of 32 layers already use linear attention; batch-serving behavior, memory-update concurrency, multi-session throughput, and hardware diversity are not evaluated. The method's fixed global mixing coefficient γ, discount factor, and fixed-size state raise unresolved issues about per-user isolation, rollback, provenance, exact deletion, security, and catastrophic interference. Theoretical error analysis is an approximation under a high-similarity assumption, not a bound that predicts the observed capacity limits. Finally, one seed and no uncertainty estimates make it difficult to determine whether some benchmark and ablation differences are robust. Bottom Line: This is a significant and unusually well-instrumented prototype for native parametric memory in language models, worth reading for researchers in fast weights and agent memory, but its evidence supports a promising complementary memory mechanism—not the paper's broader vision of reliable long-term memory foundation models.

Problem & Motivation: Robot-learning practitioners need demonstrations that are both scalable and sufficiently action-aligned for deployment. Real-robot teleoperation captures embodiment-correct trajectories but requires the target robot, specialized hardware, operator time, resets, and safety supervision for every demonstration. Conventional UMI-style robot-free capture reduces collection cost but commonly suffers from visual-SLAM drift, reconstructed rather than native inter-gripper pose, software-level time alignment, narrow camera coverage, and weak contact correspondence. These limitations have led prior work to use robot-free data primarily for pre-training while retaining real-robot data for deployment-specific post-training. The paper targets the gap between scalable robot-free supervision and deployment-grade embodied supervision, asking whether improving capture fidelity can remove the real-robot post-training anchor. Key Idea: The central insight is to make robot-free demonstrations sufficiently faithful to the target robot’s action interface at capture and curation time, rather than relying on downstream adaptation to correct noisy trajectories. HiFi-UMI observes both grippers from a head-mounted stereo rig, composes offline head SLAM with fiducial hand-to-head poses, synchronizes all sensors with one hardware trigger, provides wide wrist views, and rejects trajectories that cannot be reconstructed or replayed by the target robot. The paper’s main conceptual contribution is therefore an end-to-end fidelity-and-validation design, not a new policy-learning objective. Methodology: The capture device uses a head-mounted stereo camera pair with IMU for offline stereo-inertial SLAM; fiducial marker cubes on the hands provide native bimanual relative pose in the head-camera frame; each hand carries two non-parallel fisheye cameras with approximately 200° coverage; encoders measure gripper opening; and a shared GPIO trigger provides measured cross-sensor offsets below 40 microseconds. A full-palm asymmetric two-finger gripper is intended to preserve natural contact and force distribution. During collection, online checks flag exposure, blur, excessive speed, and hand visibility failures, while operators mark temporal boundaries. Offline processing then performs local-consistency SLAM reconstruction, automatic anomaly detection, target-robot whole-body-control retargeting, simulation replay validation, AI-assisted segmentation and labeling, human verification, and distribution-aware export. Approximately 98% of captures pass trajectory reconstruction and 98% of reconstructed trajectories pass replay validation, yielding an approximately 96% cumulative validity rate. Policies consume the four wrist views rather than the head views and predict bimanual relative pose increments plus absolute gripper opening. StarVLA-QwenPI uses a conditional flow-matching action head with 20-step chunks and executes 10 steps receding-horizon; OpenPI-π0.5 uses its released continuous flow-matching interface; LingBot-VA jointly predicts future visual latents and actions with equal video and action losses. The main design decisions—head-relative tracking, hardware synchronization, and simulation replay filtering—are motivated plausibly, but their individual contributions are not experimentally separated. Key Results: The processed corpus reportedly contains more than 20,000 hours, 4.32 million episodes, and 480+ scenes; the released HiFi-UMI-2K subset contains 2,000 hours, more than 482,100 episodes, 110+ scenes, and six camera views per episode. Against base-station ground truth over an approximately 2 m workspace, the system reports 3 mm mean local translational end-effector error, less than 40 microseconds cross-sensor timing offset, fewer than one dropped frame per 270,000 frames, 98% trajectory reconstruction success, and less than 0.1° gripper-state error. On four bimanual tabletop tasks—stain wiping, shirt folding, remote insertion, and produce sorting—StarVLA-QwenPI obtains 51.3% success with UMI post-training versus 53.8% with teleoperation, OpenPI-π0.5 obtains 77.5% versus 74.4%, and LingBot-VA obtains 56.9% versus 57.5%; each task–policy pair has 40 real-robot trials. The strongest reported task result is 85% on remote insertion for UMI-post-trained OpenPI-π0.5. These comparisons favor teleoperation in scene familiarity but favor UMI in demonstration count: UMI uses 3,200 trajectories per task from multiple non-evaluation environments, whereas teleoperation uses approximately 300 trajectories collected on the evaluation robot and in the evaluation scene. For OpenPI-π0.5 remote insertion, scaling UMI post-training from 400 to 800, 1,600, 3,200, and 6,400 episodes produces 37.5%, 65%, 70%, 85%, and 82.5% success, respectively. On LingBot-VA with ground-truth future-video conditioning, UMI-to-real action decoding has 24.33 mm full-chunk XYZ RMSE and 0.65° frame-to-frame SO(3) error, versus 21.64 mm and 0.46° for teleoperation-to-real. StarVLA-QwenPI pre-training on 4,000 hours reduces held-out action error by 61%, reduces error on ten unseen tasks by 41%, follows a pre-decay exposure fit with exponent α = 0.268 and R² = 0.993, and improves aggregate real-robot success after matched UMI post-training by 18.1 percentage points, from 51.3% to 69.4%. The pre-training scaling law measures repeated exposure to a fixed corpus, not scaling with independently added dataset size. Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, and ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION; the genuinely new result is the controlled, cross-backbone demonstration that high-fidelity handheld robot-free data can replace task-specific real-robot teleoperation under the tested setup, while the underlying components—stereo SLAM, fiducial tracking, flow matching, imitation learning, and simulation filtering—are established techniques co-designed into a new capture and curation system. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper holds the backbone, action convention, normalization, training recipe, deployment controller, and evaluation protocol fixed within each UMI-versus-teleoperation comparison, separates scene construction from policy execution, randomizes policy order, freezes checkpoints and benchmark definitions before evaluation, records termination causes, and evaluates a total of 960 real-robot rollouts across the main comparisons. It also uses episode-level bootstrap intervals for the WAM offline diagnostic. However, the success-rate comparisons report only 40 rollouts per task–policy pair and do not provide confidence intervals or formal significance tests for the main binary outcomes; one trial changes a task rate by 2.5 percentage points. The teleoperation and UMI datasets are intentionally not sample matched, so parity conflates source fidelity with a roughly tenfold difference in task-specific trajectory count. The paper explicitly lacks fidelity-component ablations, cost-normalized comparisons, broader robot or task evaluations, and pre-training experiments on the other two backbones. The dataset is released at https://huggingface.co/datasets/simple-world-lab/HiFi-UMI-2K under CC BY 4.0, and the project website is https://cloud.simpleai.tech/simple-world-lab/hifi-umi/; no code repository, capture-device designs, trained model weights, or complete processing implementation is stated as publicly released. The dataset and evaluation are largely produced by the authors’ own pipeline, and reported capture-scale figures for the full 20,000-hour corpus are not independently audited in the paper. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS/EMPIRICAL, because the paper delivers a capture and data-processing system and evaluates policies on physical robots. * Practical: The method uses wearable cameras, IMUs, fiducial markers, encoders, a custom glove gripper, and a target-specific whole-body controller; these components appear implementable with commercially available sensors, but the paper does not report full hardware cost, setup time, operator burden, or whether the complete capture stack is reproducible outside the authors’ infrastructure. * Efficient: UMI collection is claimed to require substantially less wall-clock time than teleoperation, and the pipeline retains approximately 96% of raw captures, but no quantified dollars-per-hour, operator-hours-per-trajectory, throughput, compute cost, storage cost, or end-to-end latency comparison is provided. * Effective: On the tested bimanual platform and four tabletop tasks, UMI-only post-training reaches aggregate success within 3.1 percentage points of teleoperation across the three backbones, including scene-level visual shift; this demonstrates effectiveness for the measured benchmark but not for general manipulation reliability. * Scalable: The corpus scales to more than 20,000 internally processed hours and the released subset to 2,000 hours, but policy deployment is evaluated on only one robot platform, four tasks, and task-specific datasets up to 6,400 episodes; behavior at 10×–100× the evaluated deployment scale and across substantially different embodiments is not tested. The work delivers a released dataset and a publicly described capture/data-engine pipeline; it does not state that the capture hardware, full processing software, policy checkpoints, or trained models are released. Strengths: - It tests a consequential systems hypothesis directly on real hardware: whether robot-free demonstrations can replace, rather than merely supplement, real-robot post-training. - The hardware and software choices address distinct sources of label error—long-horizon pose drift, bimanual relative pose, temporal synchronization, visual occlusion, and retargetability—rather than improving only one sensor modality. - The within-backbone comparisons are reasonably controlled, span two VLA architectures and one WAM, and use an evaluation scene unavailable during UMI collection, making the evidence stronger than comparisons against baselines trained on the same handheld data. - The pre-training analysis connects offline action error, unseen-task transfer, data composition, and downstream real-robot success; the finding that interaction-dynamics coverage matters more than object identity is useful for dataset design. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly note that the zero-robot evidence covers only four tabletop bimanual tasks and three backbones, that pre-training benefits are measured only on StarVLA-QwenPI, that each task–policy pair has only 40 rollouts, that fidelity is evaluated jointly rather than through controlled degradation, and that UMI-versus-teleoperation comparisons are not sample matched. They also identify the need to test larger scales, additional embodiments and backbones, the transfer of UMI pre-training to teleoperation post-training, and whether fidelity benefits persist or saturate. These limitations are confronted directly rather than hidden, although their implications for cost and causal attribution remain substantial. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The strongest unresolved issue is causal attribution: because the system changes tracking, synchronization, camera coverage, gripper morphology, online filtering, simulation replay, and dataset composition simultaneously, the experiments show that the complete package works but do not establish that the claimed fidelity properties are necessary or sufficient. The main parity claim also compares 3,200 UMI trajectories with approximately 300 teleoperation trajectories, so it does not show that UMI is more sample efficient or that fidelity alone closes the gap. The 3 mm pose number is workspace-local and the paper separately acknowledges centimeter-level long-horizon drift; the relationship between this measurement and policy-relevant action-label error is not fully established. The teleoperation baseline is collected in the evaluation scene, while UMI data are collected across other sites, but there is no scene-matched UMI control or a teleoperation baseline collected under comparable scene diversity. The benchmark uses one custom bimanual platform with matching grippers and wrist cameras, which narrows the embodiment gap and may favor transfer from UMI. The paper does not report hardware cost, collection throughput, training compute, storage burden, operator demographics or consistency, calibration failures, performance under severe occlusion or low texture, safety incidents, or long-horizon recovery metrics. Finally, the released dataset’s filtering, annotation, and validation procedures could create selection bias toward trajectories already easy to retarget to the authors’ robot, and the paper does not quantify how performance changes when retained and rejected data are sampled from different tasks or collection sites. Bottom Line: This is a valuable systems paper and dataset release with credible evidence that carefully engineered UMI data can replace real-robot post-training for a narrow but meaningful bimanual setting, but its claims should be read as evidence for the complete HiFi-UMI pipeline—not as proof that any particular fidelity component or robot-free data generally removes the need for embodied data.

Rethinking Classifier-Free Guidance in On-Policy Diffusion Distillation (63 ▲ )

Bingnan Li, Haozhe Wang, Haozhong Xiong, Fangtai Wu, Jinpeng Yu, Yang Shi, Jiaming Liu, Ruihua Huang · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 28 Jul 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Positive–Direction Matching (PDM), a branch-aware on-policy diffusion distillation objective that separately matches the teacher and student positive predictions and classifier-free-guidance conditional directions. - Why it's important: Matching only the CFG-composed prediction can hide incompatible positive and negative branch errors, causing distilled models to fail when deployed at guidance scales different from the training scale, especially when the teacher has privileged conditioning. - How it does it: It replaces guided-velocity matching with the loss \(\|e^+\|_2^2 + \lambda\|d_T-d_S\|_2^2\), where \(d=v^+-v^-\), thereby eliminating cross-branch error cancellation while retaining a separate CFG interface. - The good: On dense-to-sparse video control, PDM improves control metrics over naive OPD at the training scale and remains stable under guidance changes, whereas naive OPD's pose FVD rises from 67.44 at \(\gamma=5\) to 507.70 at \(\gamma=1\). - The missing: The paper does not provide statistical variation across seeds or a theoretical explanation for why PDM outperforms the equally identifiable Independent Branch Matching objective (IBM), and its strongest privileged-conditioning evidence is concentrated in one video task. - Read it or not: Researchers working on CFG, diffusion distillation, or privileged-information transfer should read it for the branch-identifiability diagnosis; readers seeking broad evidence across architectures, datasets, and teacher-student configurations can defer judgment until such evaluations appear.
Why this rank
Scored using the Empirical profile. Rigor (74), Completeness (80), and Resilience (75) benefit from controlled shared-versus-privileged conditioning comparisons, IBM and other ablations, guidance-scale stress tests, and explicit limitation acknowledgment, but are reduced by the preprint status, lack of repeated seeds, narrow privileged-conditioning evidence, and missing broader branch-matching baselines. Impact (70) reflects a simple potentially useful objective and measured training-cost savings, but no clearly released artifact or broad-scale validation. empirical Novelty 80 Rigor 74 Non-Obv 84 Completeness 80 Resilience 75 Impact 70

Problem & Motivation: On-policy diffusion distillation trains a student on states from its own denoising trajectories while matching local teacher predictions. In branch-retaining CFG systems, both teacher and student produce positive and negative predictions that are combined as \(v^{cfg}=\gamma v^+ +(1-\gamma)v^-\). Matching only this composition constrains the weighted error \(\gamma e^+ +(1-\gamma)e^-\), not either branch individually. The paper studies when this ambiguity matters: it appears benign when teacher and student share negative conditioning, but can become harmful when the teacher's negative branch retains reference or control information unavailable to the student. The practical problem is therefore robust transfer of teacher behavior across inference guidance scales under conditioning asymmetry, with dense-to-sparse video control as the main application. Key Idea: The core insight is that CFG-composed supervision is non-identifying at the branch level, and the resulting compensation freedom becomes an optimization failure when privileged negative conditioning prevents joint reduction of branch errors. PDM resolves the ambiguity by anchoring the positive prediction and matching the difference between positive and negative predictions—the CFG conditional direction—instead of directly matching only their weighted sum. This preserves the branch interface and constrains both errors to zero at the loss minimum. Methodology: The method samples noisy states from the student's evolving denoising trajectory, evaluates teacher and student positive and negative velocity predictions at each state, and applies a weighted pointwise OPD loss. The naive baseline minimizes \(\|\gamma e^+ +(1-\gamma)e^-\|_2^2\). PDM minimizes \(\|e^+\|_2^2+\lambda\|d_T-d_S\|_2^2=\|e^+\|_2^2+\lambda\|e^+-e^-\|_2^2\), with \(\lambda=1\) in the main video experiments; IBM separately matches both branches with the expanded naive weights, \(\gamma^2\|e^+\|_2^2+(\gamma-1)^2\|e^-\|_2^2\). The experiments use LoRA adapters over frozen diffusion backbones, AdamW optimization, on-policy rollouts, and teacher evaluation at student-visited states. In the video setting, the teacher receives dense per-frame controls and the student receives only keyframes; the student rollout still uses 50 denoising steps, but supervision is applied to the first \(K=8\) states to reduce teacher-query cost. The positive-prediction anchor is motivated by identifiability, the direction term is motivated by preserving CFG behavior, and the early-trajectory horizon is justified empirically rather than by a formal analysis. Key Results: In text-rendering distillation using SD3.5-Medium, training at \(\gamma=4.5\) and evaluating 1,018 held-out prompts, teacher OCR reward is 75.24 at \(\gamma=1\), 92.91 at 2, 94.16 at 3, 94.43 at 4, and 94.09 at 4.5; naive OPD obtains 73.87, 92.72, 94.52, 94.43, and 94.11, while PDM obtains 74.48, 93.73, 93.99, 94.02, and 94.38. Thus, in the shared-negative-conditioning regime, naive matching does not show substantial excess guidance sensitivity. In the reference-conditioned image case, the teacher receives reference images on both branches while the text-only student does not; the paper reports branch-error trajectories and qualitative outputs over 12 held-out prompts, but no aggregate quantitative metric. In dense-to-sparse video control, the benchmark contains 600 OpenHumanVid clips, 81 frames at 832x480, and pose, depth, and scribble modalities. At \(\gamma=5\), PDM versus naive OPD gives pose MPJPE 4.13 versus 4.43, all-frame PCK@0.1 82.48 versus 80.28, and FVD 62.77 versus 65.12; depth SI-RMSE 10.31 versus 10.69 and correlation 91.24 versus 90.58; and scribble F1 76.22 versus 75.00 with FVD 50.53 versus 59.95. Against the unadapted student, PDM reduces pose MPJPE from 5.92 to 4.13 and depth SI-RMSE from 14.36 to 10.31. Under guidance-scale generalization for pose, naive OPD's MPJPE/FVD change from 4.62/67.44 at \(\gamma=5\) to 8.98/507.70 at \(\gamma=1\), whereas PDM changes from 4.27/58.65 to 4.48/60.97. The supervision-horizon ablation reports approximately 23, 38, 69, 132, and 790 seconds per step for \(K=1,2,4,8,50\), respectively; \(K=8\) gives the strongest reported control metrics among the tested settings, but is not uniformly best on distributional metrics. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION, NEW METHOD, and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING: the paper formulates CFG-based OPD as a branch-identifiability problem, names the privileged-negative-conditioning failure mode Negative Branch Asymmetry (NBA), and proposes PDM, although the underlying ingredients—CFG, prediction matching, on-policy distillation, and branchwise squared losses—are established techniques combined in a new analysis and conditioning-asymmetry setting. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper includes useful controlled comparisons: naive matching, PDM, IBM, positive-only matching for optimization diagnosis, SFT, off-policy distillation, and the unadapted student. It evaluates shared versus privileged negative conditioning, guidance-scale shifts, the PDM weight \(\lambda\), and the supervision horizon \(K\), and keeps architecture, budget, rollout states, and optimization settings aligned for the main video comparison. However, no error bars, multiple random seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported; the text-rendering experiment uses seed 42, and the reference-conditioned study is explicitly qualitative with only 24 demonstrations and 12 held-out prompts. The authors provide implementation details and a project page at https://rethinking-cfg-opd.github.io, but the paper does not explicitly state that code, data, checkpoints, or model weights are released. The main video benchmark is derived from the authors' processing of OpenHumanVid and uses automatically re-extracted control metrics, which may inherit annotator bias. The baselines are relevant OPD and fine-tuning baselines, but the paper does not compare against a broader set of CFG-transfer objectives or alternative branch parameterizations. The claimed mechanism is supported by branch-error trajectories and off-scale evaluations, but the optimization dynamics are observed empirically rather than derived. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL, with a method that could be integrated into a diffusion-training system but no released software artifact explicitly established. * Practical: The experiments run on commercially available H100 GPUs and use LoRA adapters over frozen SD3.5, FLUX.2-klein, and Wan2.1-VACE backbones, although training requires multi-GPU infrastructure and teacher evaluations. * Efficient: Early-horizon supervision reduces reported video training time from approximately 790 seconds per step at \(K=50\) to 132 seconds at \(K=8\), but PDM still requires separate teacher and student positive/negative evaluations and the paper does not report inference-cost changes relative to naive branch-retaining OPD. * Effective: The evidence shows improved proxy control fidelity, distributional quality, and guidance robustness on dense-to-sparse pose, depth, and scribble control; it does not establish improvement in human-rated video quality, downstream editing utility, or performance beyond the tested benchmark. * Scalable: The method is tested on a 1.3B-parameter video backbone at 81 frames and 600 test clips, plus image models, but there is no 10x–100x scale experiment, larger-resolution study, longer-video study, or evidence that the observed NBA dynamics persist across substantially larger models and datasets. The paper delivers a proposed training objective and an empirical diagnostic framework, not a clearly documented reusable library, CLI, dataset release, or trained-model release. Strengths: - It identifies a concrete failure mode in a commonly used objective: the equation \(\gamma e^+ +(1-\gamma)e^-=0\) makes the branch-level non-identifiability explicit rather than treating CFG sensitivity as an unexplained empirical artifact. - It separates benign ambiguity from harmful NBA and tests this distinction in contrasting shared- and privileged-negative-conditioning settings, avoiding the stronger but unsupported claim that all CFG-composed matching is defective. - PDM is simple, compatible with branch-retaining CFG interfaces, and empirically improves both matched-scale control fidelity and off-scale robustness; IBM's gains provide evidence that removing cross-branch cancellation matters independently of the exact PDM parameterization. - The video study measures three distinct control modalities and reports both fidelity and quality metrics, while the horizon ablation quantifies a concrete teacher-computation tradeoff. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that the relative behavior of PDM and IBM is incompletely understood because both share the same branch-level zero-loss solution under non-degenerate weights. They explicitly note that PDM's advantage is empirical rather than theoretical and call for analysis of their optimization behavior and extension to other guidance mechanisms and conditioning asymmetries. The reference-conditioned experiment is also described as an illustrative qualitative case study rather than an aggregate performance estimate. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The paper does not report repeated runs, variance, or statistical tests, so several small improvements—for example PDM versus IBM on some video quality metrics—cannot be judged for reliability. - The privileged-conditioning evidence is narrow: the reference experiment uses six styles, 24 demonstrations, and 12 qualitative test prompts, while the quantitative video study uses one backbone, one sparse-keyframe layout, one benchmark construction, and three related control modalities. - The paper does not compare PDM with alternative ways to expose or regularize CFG branches, such as direct branch matching with independently tuned weights, randomized training guidance scales, multi-scale supervision, or distilling a single composed teacher field. - The claim that privileged information in the negative branch is the causal source of NBA is plausible but not isolated through a systematic sweep over information overlap, guidance scale, teacher-student capacity gap, or conditioning placement; branch-error plots alone do not establish a general causal law. - The early-horizon result is reported only for pose-only ablations and lacks teacher-query counts, memory measurements, wall-clock breakdowns, and tests at longer trajectories or larger video resolutions. - Automatic pose, depth, and scribble re-extraction evaluates proxies that may favor the same annotators used to construct the controls; perceptual quality and temporal consistency are reported, but human judgments and downstream task success are absent. - The manuscript is a preprint dated 30 July 2026, and the cited 2026 OPD baselines are themselves preprints or recent technical reports, so independent replication and peer-reviewed comparison are not yet available. Bottom Line: This is a technically useful and plausibly important diagnosis for CFG-retaining OPD, with convincing initial video evidence for PDM, but its innovation and generality remain moderate until the optimization explanation, statistical reliability, alternative baselines, and cross-model evaluation are strengthened.

#11 — Highly Innovative (77)

Novel Claim or Déjà Vu? Rethinking "Contamination-Free'' Dynamic Evaluation for Multimodal Automated Fact-Checking (12 ▲ )

Haorui He, Xinwen Chen, Dacheng Wen, Reynold Cheng, Francis C. M. Lau, Yupeng Li · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 29 Jul 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces an evidence-sufficiency pipeline for detecting potential benchmark contamination in multimodal automated fact-checking and uses it to reassess static and dynamic MAFC evaluation. - Why it's important: Timestamp-based benchmarks can overestimate systems' ability to retrieve and reason over external evidence, leading to misleading model comparisons and deployment decisions. - How it does it: It generates fact-checking articles from LLM parametric knowledge, extracts evidence from those articles and human oracle articles, and matches the evidence with lexical and embedding-based Hungarian similarity scores. - The good: Across six LLMs, contamination-controlled comparisons show performance drops of up to 11.34 Macro-F1 points and change the apparent model ranking, providing direct evidence that contamination affects evaluation rather than merely correlating with publication date. - The missing: The contamination detector measures similarity to oracle evidence rather than proving that the model memorized the evidence or that it would avoid web retrieval, so its contamination labels remain an imperfect proxy. - Read it or not: MAFC benchmark designers and researchers evaluating browsing or retrieval-augmented LLMs should read it; readers seeking a new fact-checking algorithm can largely skip it.
Why this rank
Profile: empirical. Novelty (78) and non-obviousness (82) are the main strengths: the paper identifies evidence-level contamination as a distinct failure of timestamp-based evaluation and demonstrates ranking reversals. Rigor (78) is solid due to six models, multiple similarity metrics, threshold calibration, controlled subsets, significance testing, and released code, but the proxy is not proof of memorization and depends on proprietary components. Completeness (75) and resilience (70) are reduced by the contestable contamination definition, unknown model cutoffs, selection bias in the unified set, and reliance on one English benchmark and agent framework. Impact (78) reflects a reusable benchmark and decontamination pipeline; weighted composite: 0.20*78 + 0.25*78 + 0.15*82 + 0.15*75 + 0.15*70 + 0.10*78 = 77.

Problem & Motivation: Multimodal automated fact-checking systems are intended to retrieve and reason over external textual and visual evidence for emerging claims, but commonly used static benchmarks contain claims from older fact-checking articles that may overlap with LLM pretraining data. Dynamic benchmarks attempt to avoid this problem by collecting claims published after a model's nominal knowledge cutoff, yet publication time does not guarantee novelty: a newly written claim may concern old events, established policies, or combinations of facts already publicly available. The resulting gap is a lack of empirical measurement of whether static and dynamic benchmarks actually test evidence retrieval and generalization to unseen claims, rather than verification from parametric knowledge. Key Idea: A claim should be treated as potentially contaminated when an LLM, prompted to write a fact-checking article without external retrieval, produces evidence sufficiently similar to the human fact-checking article's oracle evidence. The central insight is that benchmark novelty must be assessed at the level of verifiable evidence and compositional knowledge, not only by comparing claim or article publication dates with an LLM's stated cutoff. Methodology: The study first crawls human-written oracle fact-checking articles for 491 unique AVeriTeC development claims and 901 English claims published in Q4 2025 from IFCN-signatory agencies, forming the ClaimReview2025Q4 dynamic benchmark. For each claim and target LLM, it prompts the LLM to generate a fact-checking article without web access. GPT-4o-Mini extracts claim-relevant evidence statements from both the generated and oracle articles; the authors also test GPT-5-Nano as an extractor. A Hungarian one-to-one matching procedure maximizes pairwise evidence similarity, with the score normalized by the number of oracle evidence items. The study uses METEOR with the AVeriTeC threshold of 25%, plus cosine similarity from Gemma-Emb-0.3B and Qwen3-Emb-0.6B with a threshold of 0.6. The semantic threshold is selected using 180 human-labeled claims, on which the two annotators agreed on 97.8% before adjudication, but the resulting threshold-label agreement is only 75.6% for Gemma-Emb and 82.2% for Qwen3-Emb. Six LLMs are evaluated: GPT-5.2, GPT-4o-Mini, Gemini-3.0-Pro, Gemini-3.0-Flash, DeepSeek-V3.2, and Qwen3.5-122B-A10B. To measure downstream impact, the authors place each model inside the DEFAME ReAct-style MAFC agent, which uses Serper-backed web and image search, and compare Accuracy and Macro-F1 on model-specific contaminated and remaining subsets drawn from the same dynamic benchmark. They additionally classify adjacent query reformulations as specialization, generalization, exploration, or repetition using GPT-5-Nano, and construct a unified evaluation set containing claims uncontaminated for all six models under all three metrics. The major design choices—using oracle-evidence similarity as a contamination proxy, intersecting all three metrics for conservative subset construction, and holding source and time period constant between subsets—are motivated, but their validity is not fully established. Key Results: On AVeriTeC, average contamination scores reach 23.78%–26.80% with METEOR, 63.70%–67.00% with Gemma-Emb, and 61.67%–65.78% with Qwen3-Emb across the six models. ClaimReview2025Q4 reduces these averages by 2.92–4.95 percentage points for METEOR and 6.20–11.16 points for the semantic metrics, but the dynamic benchmark still contains 17.09%–29.30% potentially contaminated claims when requiring an intersection across all three metrics; Qwen3.5-122B-A10B has the highest intersection rate at 29.30%. Semantic metrics identify substantially more potentially contaminated claims than lexical matching, indicating that paraphrased or semantically equivalent evidence is common. Four qualitative cases show how post-cutoff claims can be answered from old facts directly or by composing multiple old facts, such as combining Barron Trump's birth year with the constitutional Senate age requirement. In DEFAME, moving from contaminated to uncontaminated claims reduces Accuracy for all models: the largest drops are 10.88 points for Qwen3.5-122B-A10B, 10.50 for Gemini-3.0-Pro, and 9.60 for GPT-4o-Mini; statistically significant drops are reported for those three models and Gemini-3.0-Flash. Macro-F1 falls by 4.87 points for GPT-5.2, 9.59 for GPT-4o-Mini, 8.57 for Gemini-3.0-Pro, 11.34 for Gemini-3.0-Flash, 2.22 for DeepSeek-V3.2, and 10.31 for Qwen3.5-122B-A10B, with significance reported for GPT-4o-Mini, Gemini-3.0-Pro, Gemini-3.0-Flash, and Qwen3.5-122B-A10B. Gemini-3.0-Flash ranks first on the contaminated subset at 61.22 Macro-F1, whereas GPT-5.2 ranks first on the uncontaminated subset at 52.81, demonstrating a ranking reversal. Contaminated trajectories for Qwen3.5-122B-A10B and Gemini-3.0-Pro use significantly fewer exploration transitions, while specialization, generalization, and repetition are not significantly different. On the unified 154-claim contamination-controlled set, DeepSeek-V3.2 obtains the highest Macro-F1 at 55.93%; all six models remain below 56% Macro-F1. This set is heavily imbalanced, with 68.18% Refuted, 12.34% Supported, and 19.48% Not Enough Evidence claims. Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING and NEW EVALUATION FORMULATION, with a supporting DATA PROCESSING TOOL; the work's main novelty is the empirical demonstration that timestamp-based dynamic MAFC benchmarks retain substantial evidence-level contamination and can change model rankings, while the generation, extraction, embedding, and Hungarian-matching components are adapted from established evaluation techniques rather than constituting a fundamentally new algorithm. Rigor & Reproducibility: The study evaluates six contemporary proprietary and open-source LLMs, averages contamination scores over at least three trials, uses three similarity metrics, calibrates semantic thresholds against human judgments, tests an alternative evidence extractor, controls the contaminated/uncontaminated comparison for source and publication period, and reports bootstrap significance tests for performance drops. Code and the appendix are stated to be available at https://trustworthycomp.github.io/Rethink-MAFC-Eval/. The evaluation is nevertheless dependent on proprietary models, search APIs, and GPT-based evidence extraction, and the knowledge cutoffs of DeepSeek-V3.2 and Qwen3.5-122B-A10B are unknown. The human threshold-validation sample contains only 180 dynamic claims, and the best semantic threshold agrees with human labels at 75.6% or 82.2%, leaving substantial label noise. The detector does not establish actual memorization, does not test whether the generated evidence was retrieved from model weights, and may conflate general world knowledge, reasoning from first principles, and contamination. The use of the same oracle articles for detection and similarity matching creates a reference-dependent proxy, while the downstream analysis relies on one MAFC framework, one search configuration, and one Q4 2025 English benchmark. The authors do not report detailed compute/API costs, confidence intervals for all headline comparisons, per-class metrics, or comparisons with stronger contamination-detection alternatives such as training-corpus audits, temporal leave-one-event-out protocols, or retrieval-disabled versus retrieval-enabled counterfactual evaluations. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL. Practical: The DEFAME experiments can run using commercially available hardware and hosted model/search APIs, although reproducing the largest open model and six-model pipeline requires substantial infrastructure and paid services. Efficient: The paper reports no end-to-end latency, token, API, GPU-memory, or monetary cost, so its efficiency relative to ordinary dynamic evaluation is not established. Effective: The evidence supports the narrower claim that evidence-similarity-defined contamination correlates with inflated MAFC scores and ranking changes, but it does not fully establish real-world fact-checking accuracy or prove that contamination caused every observed performance difference. Scalable: The study tests 491 static and 901 dynamic claims and six models, but it does not test 10×–100× larger benchmarks, more languages, longer time horizons, additional modalities, or changing model cutoffs; scalability is therefore not demonstrated. The work delivers code and an appendix, and it produces a reusable decontamination pipeline and a 901-claim ClaimReview2025Q4 benchmark for analysis, but it does not introduce a deployable MAFC system or trained model. Strengths: - It isolates contamination from simple temporal distribution shift by comparing contaminated and uncontaminated subsets from the same sources and quarter, rather than merely comparing pre-cutoff and post-cutoff claims. - It combines lexical and semantic evidence matching, showing that lexical overlap alone misses many semantically similar reformulations; the three-metric intersection provides a conservative operational filter. - It connects benchmark contamination to practical evaluation consequences, including up to an 11.34-point Macro-F1 inflation and a reversal in the top-ranked model. - The qualitative analysis identifies a non-obvious failure mode of timestamp filtering: claims can be newly phrased yet answerable through direct retrieval from old knowledge or composition of multiple pre-cutoff facts. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state that similarity-based contamination estimates may be conservative because they detect observable evidence overlap rather than subtle latent contamination. They acknowledge that the controlled set is English-only and that its label distribution is imbalanced, particularly toward Refuted claims. They also frame ClaimReview2025Q4 as an analysis-enabling benchmark rather than the primary contribution, and call for improved novelty controls, detection of latent contamination, and evaluation beyond English. These limitations are confronted directly in the conclusion, although their quantitative implications are not fully analyzed. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The central contamination definition is contestable: an LLM can generate evidence matching an oracle article because the claim follows from common knowledge or reasoning, without having seen the oracle article or bypassing external retrieval in an operational MAFC run. The study therefore supports “potential evidence-level contamination” more strongly than actual pretraining contamination. The four-case causal explanation is qualitative and too small to establish prevalence or distinguish memorization from ordinary reasoning. Unknown knowledge cutoffs for the open models undermine the post-cutoff interpretation, and Qwen3.5's high score could reflect a broader or more recent training corpus, online data access, or model behavior rather than contamination in the benchmark. The unified 154-claim set may induce selection bias and has severe label imbalance, yet the headline model ranking is based on this small, filtered subset without uncertainty intervals or significance tests between models. The analysis also does not evaluate other dynamic benchmarks such as VERITAS directly, does not include multimodal-specific ablations showing whether images or videos drive contamination, and does not compare against a no-parametric-knowledge or retrieval-only control. The t-SNE and centroid-similarity analysis provides limited evidence against confounding and does not rule out differences in claim difficulty, verifiability, label noise, source quality, or entity familiarity. Finally, the paper's conclusions about real-world MAFC capability are broader than the evidence from one English quarter, one agent framework, and one search backend supports. Bottom Line: This is a valuable evaluation study for MAFC and LLM benchmark researchers because it demonstrates that post-cutoff collection is not sufficient for contamination control and quantifies consequential ranking distortions, but its contamination labels should be treated as conservative similarity-based risk indicators rather than definitive measurements of memorization or real-world generalization.
