Position: Current Benchmarking Hinders Real Progress in Deep Learning for Time Series Forecasting

V Moretti, I Marisca, C Alippi, A Cini · openreview.net · 10 new citations to your articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper presents an empirical analysis of four overlooked forecasting-design dimensions—global/local model configuration, preprocessing and exogenous variables, temporal processing, and spatial processing—and proposes a forecasting-specific model-card template. - Why it's important: Misaligned design choices can make benchmark comparisons attribute gains to sequence-modeling innovations that actually arise from data access, parameter sharing, normalization, or other implementation decisions, thereby misdirecting research progress. - How it does it: The authors reimplement and standardize representative forecasting architectures, construct modular reference models that vary one design dimension at a time, and compare accuracy, ablations, and GPU cost across four common datasets. - The good: Across the controlled experiments, simple MLP, TCN, Transformer, and pyramidal-attention references often match complex baselines, while removing iTransformer's spatial-attention module improves or preserves performance on all four datasets in the main ablation. - The missing: The evidence remains concentrated on four widely used long-horizon benchmarks and does not establish that the proposed benchmarking protocol generalizes to broader datasets, probabilistic forecasting, short-horizon tasks, foundation models, or real deployment workloads. - Read it or not: Read it if you design or evaluate deep forecasting models and need a concrete taxonomy for fair component-level comparisons; skip it if you want a new forecasting architecture or a broad, current benchmark leaderboard.

Problem & Motivation The work addresses the methodological problem of determining which architectural components actually improve deep-learning forecasts for collections of time series. Researchers and practitioners in electricity, weather, transportation, solar-energy, and related domains commonly compare architectures that differ simultaneously in parameter sharing, normalization, covariate usage, temporal operators, and inter-series processing. This makes accuracy differences difficult to interpret and can confuse global, local, hybrid, univariate, and multivariate forecasting settings. The paper argues that existing benchmark practice focuses on whole-model scores while failing to factor out these design dimensions, extending known concerns about dataset selection, hyperparameter tuning, and benchmark quality rather than merely repeating them. Key Idea The central insight is that many supposedly architectural comparisons are confounded comparisons between different forecasting problems. In particular, global versus local or hybrid parameterization, access to exogenous variables, and treatment of inter-series dependencies can have effects as large as or larger than the choice of temporal sequence operator. Therefore, a benchmark should represent forecasting models as explicit combinations of design dimensions and isolate the effect of a proposed component while holding the remaining dimensions fixed. The forecasting model card operationalizes this insight by requiring authors to document the relevant choices. Methodology The paper first formalizes point, multi-step forecasting for a collection of time series, distinguishing global models with shared parameters, local models with series-specific parameters, and hybrid models with both shared and local parameters. It then evaluates seven established models—PatchTST, DLinear, TimeMixer, Linear, iTransformer, ModernTCN, and Crossformer—using open-source implementations adapted to a unified setup. The experiments use four datasets: Electricity (321 series), Weather (21), Traffic (862), and Solar (137), with 70%/10%/20% train/validation/test splits, mostly 96-step windows and horizons, and additional horizons of 192, 336, and 720. The authors construct modular reference architectures consisting of RevIN-style normalization, feature/covariate encoding, a temporal module, an optional spatial module, a linear decoder, and de-normalization. Temporal alternatives include an MLP, causal dilated TCN, gated RNN, Transformer, and pyramidal attention; spatial processing uses standard spatial attention. The four analyses are: adding or removing local embeddings to test global versus hybrid configuration; adding or removing sinusoidal calendar covariates; comparing temporal operators under standardized inputs and hybrid embeddings; and comparing spatial models with an iTransformer ablation in which spatial attention is replaced by a feed-forward layer. Models are tuned over hidden sizes from 32 to 256, with additional settings for Weather, and results use MSE and MAE on scaled data. The paper does not state a single explicit training objective in the main text beyond describing point forecasting and reporting MSE/MAE, although the implementations appear to use standard supervised regression losses. The choices to standardize inputs and covariates, use modular references, and report compute are well aligned with the stated causal-comparison goal; the decision to rely on four conventional benchmarks and to reduce input windows for spatial models limits the scope of the conclusions. Key Results At horizon 96 without spatial processing, PatchTST obtains the lowest MSE on Electricity (0.125), Traffic (0.345), and the lowest MAE on Electricity (0.218) and Traffic (0.234), while simple reference models are close: the reference MLP gives MSE 0.129/0.148/0.376/0.194 on Electricity/Weather/Traffic/Solar, and the reference Transformer gives 0.129/0.149/0.362/0.203. Across horizons 96–720, no temporal operator consistently dominates; at horizon 720, PatchTST reaches MSE 0.197 on Electricity, 0.322 on Weather, 0.435 on Traffic, and 0.247 on Solar, while reference TCN/MLP/Transformer models remain competitive. Local or hybrid configuration materially changes results: for example, the reference Transformer on Electricity changes from MSE 0.136 with local parameters to 0.151 without them, while on Traffic the global version improves from 0.417 to 0.392. Calendar covariates also change scores substantially: PatchTST on Traffic improves from MSE 0.383 without covariates to 0.355 with them, whereas DLinear on Weather slightly worsens from 0.196 to 0.199. With spatial processing at horizon 96, Crossformer is best on Electricity (MSE 0.136) and Solar (0.184), but performs poorly on Traffic (0.527); the reference pyramidal-attention-plus-spatial-attention model is best on Traffic (0.389). The iTransformer spatial ablation removes spatial attention and changes MSE from 0.148 to 0.149 on Electricity, 0.171 to 0.171 on Weather, 0.393 to 0.390 on Traffic, and 0.208 to 0.194 on Solar; extended experiments across windows and horizons generally show similar or better results without spatial attention. Compute measurements on Electricity show large cost differences: at horizon 96, DLinear uses 615.5 MB and 18.9 ms per batch, reference MLP 628.0 MB and 27.6 ms, iTransformer 1,729 MB and 50.8 ms, Crossformer 5,702.8 MB and 138.0 ms, and ModernTCN 10,620.3 MB and 145.4 ms. The additional Chronos-2 experiment shows covariates can hurt substantially in zero-shot settings, including Solar MSE 0.771 without versus 1.029 with covariates at window 96 and ETTm1 MSE 0.919 without versus 5.667 with them, but this is a limited probe rather than a full foundation-model study. Novelty Classification NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, NEW FORMULATION, and NEW SYSTEM/TOOL: The paper's main novelty is an empirical and conceptual framework that treats forecasting benchmarks as comparisons across explicit design dimensions, supported by controlled re-evaluations and a forecasting model-card template; the individual architectures, operators, datasets, normalization methods, and ablation techniques are standard, so the contribution is not a new forecasting algorithm. Rigor & Reproducibility The study includes controlled component ablations, multiple temporal and spatial reference architectures, four datasets, four forecasting horizons, three random seeds for most learned-model results, MSE and MAE, and explicit batch-time/GPU-memory measurements on a specified NVIDIA A100 40 GB system. Code is reported at https://github.com/valentina-moretti/deep-forecasting-benchmarking-issues, and the forecasting model-card resource is reported at https://valentina-moretti.github.io/forecasting_model_cards. The use of open-source baselines and a common input/covariate setup improves reproducibility, but several results have extremely small reported standard deviations and the Chronos-2 table reports zero deviations, so uncertainty across data splits, tuning procedures, and model checkpoints is not characterized. The paper does not report significance tests despite calling for them, and three seeds are insufficient to establish robust differences when MSE gaps are small. Hyperparameter tuning is described but the exact search protocol, budgets, and per-model tuning fairness are not fully visible in the parsed main text. The evaluation relies heavily on the same four saturated benchmarks criticized in the paper and on author-modified implementations, which creates a risk that implementation choices in the standardized setup influence the findings. Comparisons with published numbers are appropriately questioned, but the paper does not provide a broad independent replication across newer realistic benchmarks. Deployability (4-property check) Profile: EMPIRICAL. Practical: The evaluated models can run on commercially available GPUs; the reported experiments use a single NVIDIA A100, although the paper does not report CPU-only or low-memory deployment behavior. Efficient: Efficiency varies substantially, from 615.5 MB and 18.9 ms per batch for DLinear to 10,620.3 MB and 145.4 ms for ModernTCN in the reported spatial setup, so complex spatial models can impose large resource costs without consistent accuracy gains. Effective: The experiments support the narrower claim that controlled design choices materially affect benchmark accuracy and that simple models can be competitive; they do not demonstrate improved forecasting outcomes in an operational application or under decision-relevant costs. Scalable: The paper tests horizons up to 720 and series counts up to 862, but not 10×–100× larger collections, substantially longer histories, streaming inference, distributed training, or foundation-model-scale workloads; the scalability claims therefore remain limited. The work delivers reusable code and a forecasting model-card template, but not a new forecasting library, trained model, or benchmark dataset. Strengths - It identifies a concrete confounding structure—global/local/hybrid configuration, covariate access, temporal processing, and spatial processing—instead of treating benchmark unfairness as only a matter of tuning or dataset selection. - The modular reference architecture makes component-level comparisons more interpretable than direct leaderboard comparisons among monolithic models. - The empirical results are actionable: for example, removing iTransformer spatial attention improves Solar MSE from 0.208 to 0.194 at horizon 96, and simple reference models achieve performance close to PatchTST while using substantially less memory and time. - The model-card template translates the conceptual critique into a documentation practice that can expose inductive/transductive assumptions, parameter sharing, covariate handling, and complexity. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors explicitly limit the analysis to selected design dimensions, recent long-range point-forecasting architectures, four common datasets, MSE/MAE-style evaluation, and models that can be retrained under controlled configurations. They state that the analysis should be extended to additional baselines, probabilistic and short-term forecasting, alternative metrics, and foundation models. They acknowledge that foundation models require a different experimental setup and provide only a covariate ablation for Chronos-2. These limitations are confronted directly and framed as scope boundaries rather than being minimized. Analyst-Identified Gaps - The central evidence does not test newer realistic or distribution-shift benchmarks, so the conclusion that current benchmarking broadly hinders progress may be stronger than the four-dataset evidence supports. - The study standardizes and modifies public implementations, but it does not fully quantify how its choices of normalization, covariate injection, batch size, tuning budget, local embeddings, or input-window restrictions affect each baseline; this is especially important because the paper's thesis is that such details drive results. - The spatial comparisons are not perfectly controlled: spatial models use a reduced input window for computational reasons, and the reference spatial models, iTransformer, Crossformer, and ModernTCN differ in more than the spatial operator, weakening causal attribution across the full comparison even though the iTransformer ablation is more controlled. - Three seeds and no statistical tests are inadequate for claims about small performance differences, particularly when several reported standard deviations round to zero. - The paper does not evaluate missing observations, cold-start or unseen-series generalization empirically, probabilistic calibration, forecast intervals, operational latency, or downstream decision utility, despite discussing some of these settings conceptually. - The claim that simpler architectures can match the current SOTA is benchmark-relative and does not establish robustness under changing regimes, larger collections, heterogeneous multivariate series, or genuinely inductive deployment. Bottom Line This is a useful methodological critique with credible controlled evidence and a practical documentation artifact, but its strongest contribution is to improve how forecasting experiments are designed—not to establish a universally valid ranking of architectures or a new forecasting method.

Problem & Motivation The work addresses the deployment problem of selecting a retrieval architecture for growing enterprise knowledge bases containing hundreds of thousands of heterogeneous documents, including wikis, chats, tickets, email, meetings, CRM records, and code reviews. Lexical and dense retrievers pay relatively little construction cost but may miss semantic or relational evidence; graph-based RAG shifts cost into corpus-wide entity and relation extraction; agentic file-system search shifts cost into sequential query-time exploration. Prior comparisons generally evaluate these paradigms on different datasets and at one corpus size, making accuracy–cost scaling and the point at which one paradigm overtakes another unclear. The study targets the specific gap between isolated benchmark comparisons and controlled measurements of behavior as irrelevant background documents increase while the question workload and relevant evidence remain fixed. Key Idea The core insight is that corpus growth makes global candidate discovery more important than local sequential exploration: BM25 performs corpus-wide lexical ranking once and keeps query cost nearly invariant, whereas a file-system agent must increasingly explore a larger tree. The Agent+BM25 control supports this causal interpretation by replacing only the raw-file search primitive while preserving the agent model, prompt structure, budget, question subset, and judging protocol; at full scale, the combined score rises from 36.9 for the raw-file agent to 69.4 for Agent+BM25. Methodology The benchmark contains 511,959 documents and 600.8M tokens with 500 questions: 470 source-grounded, 10 high-level scaffold-supported, and 20 not-found questions. The smallest tier contains 722 annotated gold documents, 326 hard traps, 99 not-found lures, and two organizational scaffold pages, yielding 1,144 documents after deduplication. A seeded, source- and noise-stratified order appends the remaining documents in approximately 1.25-fold increments, producing 28 exactly nested tiers from 1,144 to 511,959 documents. Seven native pipelines are evaluated: BM25; DenseRAG using chunk embeddings; HippoRAG 2; MS-GraphRAG; LightRAG; LinearRAG using local NER and embeddings; and a File-System Agent using list_dir, grep, and read_doc over raw files with an 80-call budget. Qwen3.6-27B at temperature zero serves as the shared reader, and the same model also serves as the file-search policy; Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B supplies embeddings. Most systems retrieve top-five chunks, and token metering separates construction from query costs. The official score gates atomic-fact completeness by holistic answer alignment; document recall is computed separately. The main design decisions are the fixed bedrock, which isolates added background scale; the common reader and judge, which reduce model and evaluator confounding; and the Agent+BM25 intervention, which isolates retrieval substrate from agentic reasoning. These decisions are well motivated, although the fixed corpus-growth order, 80-call budget, and native configurations are only partially justified as representative deployment choices. Graph systems are evaluated only at tiers whose indexes complete; unsupported tiers remain missing in the main accuracy curves and are converted to zero only in a coverage-adjusted summary. Key Results On the 1,144-document bedrock, the File-System Agent scores 77.4% and BM25 74.7%, with overlapping 95% intervals of 73.9–80.8 and 71.4–77.9. BM25 scores 71.4%, 70.1%, 64.9%, 61.2%, 55.2%, and 50.5% at selected tiers from 2,254 through 511,959 documents; the File-System Agent scores 75.4%, 69.9%, 62.6%, 58.9%, 50.9%, and 30.7% at those comparable tiers. The point-estimate crossover occurs around 10M corpus tokens, after which BM25 leads at every larger shared tier; the paper presents this as a rounded regime marker rather than a fitted or significance-tested threshold. DenseRAG falls from 58.1% to 29.9% across the reported scale range. HippoRAG 2 reaches 66.2% at the bedrock and 41.0% at 131,876 documents, but does not complete the full corpus. LinearRAG reaches 46.2% at the bedrock and 29.8% at 131,876 documents. MS-GraphRAG reaches 45.9% at the bedrock and 38.4% at 6,980 documents; LightRAG reaches 48.0% at the bedrock and 42.5% at 2,254 documents. Build costs extrapolated from power-law fits to the full corpus are 2.9B generative tokens for HippoRAG 2, 7.9B for MS-GraphRAG, and approximately 102B for LightRAG; these are projections, not full-scale measurements. DenseRAG completes construction with 659.4M embedding tokens, while LinearRAG uses no generative construction tokens but still performs local NER and embedding work. Query costs are 5.8K tokens per question for BM25, 4.9K for DenseRAG, and 6.5K for HippoRAG 2; the File-System Agent uses 226K tokens at the bedrock and reaches 343K at 21,614 documents, with a separate full-scale control report giving 895K tokens per question including failed attempts. Its median calls rise from 5 to 8, budget exhaustion reaches 31% at full scale, and accuracy also declines among within-budget questions. In the 150-question Agent+BM25 control, full-scale score is 69.4% versus 36.9% for raw-file agency, document recall is 72.4% versus 36.8%, calls are 5.79 versus 36.12, and tokens per question are 101K versus 895K. On question types at 42,587 documents, the File-System Agent leads BM25 on completeness, scoring 56 versus 27, and also leads on intra-document, project-related, and conflicting-information questions; BM25 is best or tied on the other five types. The strongest counter-intuitive finding is that an agent with many more LLM calls loses to a simple lexical index as the search space grows, while agency becomes useful again when applied after ranked candidate discovery. Novelty Classification NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, NEW BENCHMARK/EVALUATION PROTOCOL, and NEW SYSTEM/TOOL ARTIFACT: the genuinely novel contribution is the controlled, nested corpus-scaling comparison and the measured crossover between raw-file agency and BM25, together with the Agent+BM25 mechanism control; the individual retrieval systems, graph methods, reader model, and agent loop are standard or adapted combinations rather than newly invented algorithms. Rigor & Reproducibility The study uses a fixed 500-question workload, exact tier nesting verified by manifests, common reader and judge prompts, separate construction/query token ledgers, 10,000-question-bootstrap confidence intervals, paired bootstrap intervals for matched controls, and independent judging checks. A binary rescoring protocol preserves all nine shared family rankings, and an independent judge agrees with 96.2% of pooled alignment decisions, with per-cell agreement from 94.4% to 98.0%. The paper does not report multiple stochastic seeds for model execution because the main systems run once per question at temperature zero; uncertainty therefore captures question sampling rather than run-to-run variance. Ablations and controls cover retrieval depth, question paraphrasing, agent harness choice, retrieval-substrate replacement, and graph access layers, but do not provide broad hyperparameter tuning or systematic ablations of chunking, prompts, agent budgets, BM25 parameters, embedding models, or graph construction settings. The benchmark labels were refined using candidate evidence from BM25, dense retrieval, and file-agent search, which reduces direct BM25-only label bias but still makes the benchmark and adversarial set dependent on retrieval-generated proposals; a direct dense audit addresses only part of this concern. The supplement lists scripts, aggregate CSV/JSON ledgers, figure inputs, schemas, and a README, but no public URL, repository, dataset mirror, or model-weight release is stated in the paper text. Deployability (4-property check) Profile: EMPIRICAL and SYSTEMS, because the paper runs multiple retrieval systems and supplies a reproducibility-oriented code/data supplement, although it is not a deployed production system. Practical: BM25, dense retrieval, and the agent pipelines can run on commercially available hardware, while the reported graph construction costs range from roughly three single-instance days for HippoRAG 2 to an extrapolated four instance-years for LightRAG at the full corpus. Efficient: BM25 uses 5.8K query tokens and no generative construction, compared with 226K–895K agent query tokens and projected graph construction costs of 2.9B–102B tokens; actual CPU, memory, storage, monetary, and multi-GPU costs are not fully reported. Effective: Within this benchmark and fixed reader protocol, BM25 has the strongest large-scale measured score and retrieval recall, but Agent+BM25 performs better on the 150-question full-scale control, showing that the result favors ranked discovery plus agency rather than BM25-only answering for all question types. Scalable: The paper measures scaling through 600.8M tokens and 511,959 documents for BM25, dense retrieval, and the raw-file agent, but graph behavior beyond completed tiers is extrapolated or treated as unavailable; performance at 10×–100× larger corpora is not evaluated. The work delivers a reusable nested-corpus evaluation harness, scripts, aggregate result ledgers, figure inputs, data schemas, and a command-line interface for graph access according to the supplement; it does not state a public repository URL or provide a general-purpose packaged library or trained model. Strengths - The 28 strictly nested tiers hold questions, gold evidence, and adversarial documents fixed while varying only background corpus size, directly addressing a confound that affects most cross-paradigm RAG comparisons. - The study measures both accuracy and where cost is paid: offline construction tokens, online query tokens, calls, and latency. This exposes graph construction walls and agentic query costs that accuracy-only evaluations would miss. - The Agent+BM25 intervention is a useful mechanism control rather than merely another leaderboard point: it changes the retrieval primitive while preserving the agent model and budget, and the 32.52-point full-scale improvement supports the candidate-discovery explanation. - Robustness checks are unusually concrete for an LLM-evaluated comparison: paired bootstrap intervals, an independent judge, binary scoring, paraphrased questions, top-10 controls, and a direct dense-retrieval proposal audit all test whether the broad ranking is an artifact of one scoring choice. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The paper explicitly distinguishes measured accuracy from extrapolated graph construction cost, reports graph systems only at completed tiers, and warns that unavailable tiers should not be interpreted as observed answer failures except in the separately labeled coverage-adjusted summary. It also notes that the roughly 10M-token crossover is a rounded interval marker rather than a fitted threshold or significance boundary, that LinearRAG's construction accounting excludes non-generative CPU and embedding work, and that the benchmark is an enterprise-style corpus with lexical anchors and adversarial factual traps. The paper does not provide a dedicated limitations section, and broader external-validity boundaries are discussed only indirectly. Analyst-Identified Gaps - The primary conclusion rests on one public synthetic enterprise benchmark, one question set, one fixed relevant-document bedrock, and one stratified document-addition order; different domains, query distributions, document deduplication levels, or growth orders could change the crossover. - BM25 is not compared against several strong modern alternatives, including learned sparse retrieval, hybrid sparse+dense retrieval, late interaction, reranking, query expansion, or tuned commercial search stacks; the result therefore supports BM25 over the selected representatives, not over retrieval methods generally. - The common Qwen3.6-27B reader and Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B encoder may favor or disadvantage particular evidence forms, and the paper does not test smaller, larger, proprietary, or non-Qwen readers and embeddings. - Agent conclusions depend on a fixed prompt, raw file hierarchy, tool return limits, 80-call budget, and one policy model. The study does not sweep budgets, compare stronger search policies, or evaluate agents with parallel or learned retrieval strategies. - Graph comparisons are confounded by incomplete coverage and native implementations with different chunking, extraction, and tuning procedures; extrapolated construction fits use short measured ranges and should not be treated as reliable long-range laws. - The evaluation uses LLM judging for answer alignment and fact completeness, and although judge robustness is measured, human validation, calibration against difficult factual cases, and per-question statistical tests for all headline differences are not reported. - Latency is measured on a single idle-server, single-stream setup, with hardware and concurrency details insufficient for production capacity planning; storage, indexing memory, monetary cost, and update/delete costs are also missing. Bottom Line This is worth reading for its unusually controlled evidence that global ranked discovery scales better than raw-file exploration on the tested enterprise benchmark and for its Agent+BM25 design lesson, but practitioners should validate the conclusion with hybrid and learned-sparse baselines on their own workloads before adopting BM25 as a general default.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Mage-VL, a 4B-parameter multimodal model with a codec-native visual encoder that selectively processes motion- and entropy-rich video patches and supports event-triggered streaming interaction. - Why it's important: Continuous video understanding is computationally expensive under dense frame sampling, limiting real-time applications such as monitoring, robotics, interactive assistants, and live commentary. - How it does it: Mage-ViT uses HEVC-derived motion/residual importance maps or neural-codec entropy maps to retain dense anchor-frame patches and sparse predicted-frame patches, while a lightweight gate activates a frozen causal language decoder only at response-worthy events. - The good: Under matched visual budgets, Mage-VL improves substantially over Qwen3-VL-4B on temporal grounding and spatial video tasks, reaches 3.5x lower measured wall-clock time on NExT-QA, and scores 64.00% on OVO-Bench. - The missing: The paper lacks strong component-level ablations and reproducible end-to-end latency accounting at realistic single-stream rates; most timing results use an 8xB200 evaluation node and compare against baselines with different video-loading accounting. - Read it or not: Video-LLM and streaming-perception researchers should read it for the codec-native token-allocation design and empirical efficiency results, while readers seeking rigorous causal evidence for the seven broader training claims should treat the conclusions as provisional.

systems Novelty 82 Rigor 68 Non-Obv 78 Completeness 70 Resilience 65 Impact 87

Problem & Motivation: Standard vision-language models process video as uniformly sampled, densely encoded frames, repeatedly recomputing largely unchanged background regions and scaling computation with duration. This creates a mismatch between continuous, event-driven visual input and image-centric visual encoders, particularly for real-time perception, proactive interaction, long-video understanding, temporal localization, and spatial reasoning. The paper targets users building streaming assistants, live video analysis systems, robotic or embodied agents, and interactive commentary systems. The specific prior-art gap is not simply token compression after encoding: most existing approaches either sample complete frames, compress features after dense visual encoding, or add streaming memory and gating to conventional frame-based front ends. The authors seek to move redundancy reduction before expensive visual encoding by using video-codec signals as a proxy for local temporal information. Key Idea: Allocate visual tokens according to local temporal unpredictability measured by video codecs rather than according to a fixed frame grid. Mage-VL fully encodes sparse anchor I-frames, selects only top-ranked 16x16 patches from predicted P-frames using motion-vector magnitude and residual energy, and preserves their original 3D positions. The same representation feeds a lightweight event gate and a causal language decoder, separating continuous low-cost monitoring from expensive response generation. The codec-native representation builds directly on the cited OneVision-Encoder direction, so the main conceptual advance is a systems-level integration of codec-guided patch selection, video-native pre-training, and proactive gating rather than an entirely new sparsification principle. Methodology: Mage-ViT consists of a codec-driven patchifier, a 24-layer pre-norm ViT with hidden size 1024 and 16 attention heads, FlashAttention-2, and shared 3D rotary positional encoding over the unpruned spatio-temporal grid. For HEVC/H.265, patch importance combines motion-vector magnitude and P-frame residual energy; for DCVC-RT, it uses per-patch negative log-likelihood from the neural codec. All I-frame patches are retained, while P-frame patches are ranked and selected under a token budget; a stated 64-frame, 4096-token configuration reduces tokens by approximately 75%. The encoder is trained from scratch in two stages using cluster-discrimination against K-means prototypes derived from MetaCLIP features: variable-resolution image pre-training at 224–448 pixels, followed by joint image/video training with 64-frame clips, 4096 tokens, and a 50% codec, 40% chunk-wise, 10% collage mixture. Mage-VL then uses a two-layer MLP projector and a Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 causal decoder. Its five-stage curriculum progresses from 350M dense image captions and short-video captions, through image/video instruction tuning and long-video training, to codec-native adaptation and streaming alignment. The streaming gate consumes an event-preserving recurrent perception state, predicts silent or speak with a class-weighted token cross-entropy loss, and triggers the frozen decoder on a local recent-segment window when the speak probability exceeds a fixed threshold. The critical design decisions—codec-based importance, variable-resolution training, and frozen-decoder gate tuning—are plausible and supported by targeted studies, but the paper does not isolate their interactions sufficiently to establish which decisions are necessary. Key Results: Mage-ViT trained on approximately 560M unlabeled images and 100M unlabeled video frames reaches 85.69% ImageNet top-1, 95.60% Food-101, 99.33% CIFAR-10, 85.17% HMDB-51, and 84.66% Kinetics-400 under the reported probe protocols. With codec selection over 64 frames at the same 4096-token budget, Diving-48 improves from 60.45% to 64.14% relative to its chunk-wise mode. On image understanding, Mage-VL-4B scores 95.14 DocVQA, 80.33 InfoVQA, 84.88 ChartQA, 81.80 OCRBench, 87.79 CV-Bench, and 94.75 CV-Bench-3D; it is competitive with Qwen3-VL-4B but loses on several OCR/document benchmarks, including CC-OCR Doc (32.25 vs. 39.69), DUDE (46.44 vs. 50.98), WebSRC (92.80 vs. 95.40), and TextVQA (77.28 vs. 80.55). On video, it exceeds Qwen3-VL-4B on NExT-QA (83.1 vs. 79.8), VideoMME (64.0 vs. 59.7), LongVideoBench (61.3 vs. 57.7), LVBench (41.8 vs. 39.2), MLVU-dev (68.7 vs. 61.5), VideoEval-Pro (45.2 vs. 20.7), Timelens-ActivityNet (45.4 vs. 28.4), Timelens-QVHighlight (57.4 vs. 34.9), VSI-Bench (64.3 vs. 53.3), and several referring-video tracking benchmarks, but loses on MV-Bench, TempCompass, VideoMME with subtitles, VideoMME-V2, and MMOU-Test-Mini. On one 8xB200 node, the tc8 setting reduces NExT-QA evaluation time from 1460 seconds for Qwen3-VL to 415 seconds while scoring 80.8 versus 79.8; on VideoMME it takes 270 seconds at 57.9, compared with 463 seconds at 59.7 for Qwen3-VL. Streaming evaluation reports 79.21% TriggerAcc, 55.54% TimVal, 83.14% ROC-AUC, and 9.30% PR-AUC on SoccerNet-Caption, and 64.00% overall on OVO-Bench, including 79.84% real-time perception and 48.15% backward tracing. The OVO-Bench score exceeds the listed Qwen3-VL-4B score of 63.00%, but the streaming timing comparison is not fully controlled because cited baselines use different training distributions and temporal tolerances. The seven additional findings—data efficiency, monotonic resolution scaling, codec robustness, redundancy of long-VideoQA SFT, motion-to-spatial transfer, AI4AI caption optimization, and Zero-Vision SFT for multimodal RL—are supported by selected experiments but vary substantially in causal strength. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD, NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The paper delivers a codec-native visual tokenization and streaming architecture, open Mage-ViT and Mage-VL artifacts, and several empirical observations; the patch-selection principle extends prior codec-aligned sparsity and combines it with known ViT, instruction-tuning, event-gating, and causal-decoder components rather than introducing a wholly new learning formalism. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper reports many controlled comparisons, including a matched 4B Qwen3-VL baseline, three Mage-VL token budgets, HEVC versus DCVC-RT selection without retraining, variable-token-budget plots, and an image-captioning pipeline ablation. It provides code at https://github.com/microsoft/Mage, project materials at https://microsoft.github.io/Mage, and model links at https://huggingface.co/collections/microsoft/mage. However, it reports no random-seed variance, error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests. The central five-stage curriculum is not decomposed through a full factorial ablation, and the authors explicitly acknowledge that the motion-spatial synergy lacks rigorous single-variable ablations. Dataset composition, filtering, exact training compute, optimizer schedules for the full multimodal stages, codec extraction cost, gate latency, and memory usage are incompletely specified. The AI4AI caption study relies on captions produced by a frozen Qwen3-VL-32B and rubric scores from GPT-5, making the ablation dependent on proprietary teacher and evaluator behavior; the 1,000-image optimization set and 200-image validation batches are small relative to the 350M-caption corpus. Some comparisons are also difficult to interpret because Mage-VL uses codec processing over 8x denser source frames, while timing baselines exclude estimated video-loading costs and run on different model architectures. The paper is a July 2026 arXiv v1 preprint, not a peer-reviewed publication according to the supplied document. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS, with substantial empirical evaluation. Practical: The model is intended to run on commercially available accelerators, and the authors release code and weights, but the reported efficiency measurements require a single node with eight B200 GPUs and do not establish real-time operation on edge or commodity hardware. Efficient: The method reduces visual tokens by approximately 75% and reports up to 3.5x wall-clock speedup over a dense-frame baseline, but codec parsing, patch-selection overhead, recurrent gate processing, decoder generation, and end-to-end per-stream throughput are not separately measured. Effective: The benchmark evidence supports improved long-video temporal localization, spatial reasoning, tracking, and streaming perception, while static performance remains mixed and the qualitative live-sports example does not establish robustness across domains or event types. Scalable: The paper evaluates clips and codec streams up to 384 or 768 frames and long-video benchmarks, but it does not test 10x–100x longer continuous streams, sustained multi-hour operation, concurrent streams, memory growth, or degradation under changing camera, codec, bitrate, and event-density conditions. The work delivers a reusable software repository, released model artifacts, and model collections; it does not release the full large-scale training corpus, and the exact availability and licensing of all generated captions and source data are not stated. Strengths: - The codec-native front end attacks redundancy before visual encoding, which is more structurally appropriate for streaming than post-encoder token merging and yields a clear accuracy-efficiency trade-off. - The matched-Qwen3-VL comparison isolates the visual front end reasonably well and shows especially large gains on temporal grounding, long-video evaluation, spatial reasoning, and referring-video tracking. - The model unifies offline image/video QA and proactive event-triggered interaction, rather than treating streaming as a separate inference wrapper. - The release of code and model artifacts, together with cross-codec evaluation and explicit token-budget operating points, improves practical usefulness and enables independent reproduction. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that Mage-VL underperforms on complex agentic workflows and mathematical reasoning because of limited high-quality text data and the omission of RL post-training. They propose Zero-Vision SFT plus RL as future work and identify native audio-visual fusion and embodied edge deployment as future directions. They also acknowledge that the motion-spatial synergy claim lacks rigorous single-variable ablations. These limitations are stated directly, but the conclusion does not discuss the missing end-to-end latency breakdown, hardware dependence, or limitations of synthetic and AI-generated supervision. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The strongest concern is that the paper presents a large composite training recipe and then attributes broad gains to codec-native processing without sufficiently separating codec selection, variable-resolution training, data scale, caption quality, curriculum stages, and changes inherited from OneVision-Encoder or LLaVA-OneVision-2. The matched-budget comparison controls nominal visual tokens but not the cost of reading 8x more source frames or running the codec, so the reported end-to-end advantage may be hardware- and implementation-dependent. Wall-clock measurements on eight B200 GPUs are not representative of deployment latency, and baseline loading-time exclusions make the speedup claim difficult to reproduce fairly. Streaming evaluation uses a heavily imbalanced SoccerNet setting, zero temporal tolerance for Mage-VL, and baselines with different training and tolerance protocols; OVO-Bench uses a recent-four-frame protocol that does not fully evaluate the claimed persistent continuous-stream memory. The use of codec bit allocation as visual importance may miss semantically important but temporally predictable content, yet the paper lacks targeted failure analysis for static objects, text, small objects, sudden illumination changes, camera cuts, and adversarial or codec-dependent artifacts. The AI4AI pipeline evaluates captions with another language model and reports downstream gains from a single optimized-data configuration without human caption-quality measurements, teacher diversity, or multiple independent optimization runs. The work also does not report energy consumption, cost per processed hour, throughput at 1 fps or full frame rate, gate false-trigger rates by event class, response latency distributions, or long-duration memory stability. Bottom Line: This is a practically relevant and technically coherent preprint for researchers building efficient video-language systems, with credible evidence that codec-guided patch selection improves temporal coverage per token, but its broad training conclusions and real-time deployment claims require stronger ablations, fairer systems accounting, and evaluation beyond large B200 clusters.

MPIE-Bench: Benchmarking Anatomically Plausible Multi-Person Interaction Editing (34 ▲ )

Jiajia Lin, Mingxuan Du, Tuowen Zhou, Benfeng Xu, Hongtao Xie · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 31 Jul 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces MPIE-Bench, a 2,500-sample benchmark, and MPIE-Eval, a mesh-based protocol for measuring anatomical completeness and contact geometry in multi-person personalized image editing. - Why it's important: Existing interaction benchmarks can rate images above 0.95–0.99 despite fused limbs, invented extremities, and body interpenetration that humans can readily see. - How it does it: It mines separated-reference/contact-target pairs from video and scores generated images with a frozen Multi-HMR reconstruction using leftover-mass, mesh-penetration, and surface-distance proxies conditioned on contact intent. - The good: On ten editors, mesh scores preserve meaningful separation—Anatomy ranges from 0.54 to 0.65 and Interaction from 0.45 to 0.72—while the VLM interaction baseline remains near 0.93–0.99; the Seedream–Gemini Interaction gap is 0.042 with a scene-clustered 95% CI of [0.019, 0.064]. - The missing: The principal Interaction metric evaluates whole-body proximity rather than the requested contact locus, and the human-consistency study is limited to 170 hard items with moderate inter-rater reliability (mean Krippendorff’s α=0.53). - Read it or not: Researchers developing or evaluating multi-person image editors should read it for the benchmark and metric design, but practitioners should treat its rankings as frontend-dependent diagnostic signals rather than definitive physical-validity measurements.
Why this rank
Scored using the Empirical profile. Novelty (78) and Non-Obviousness (75) are strong because the paper identifies a concrete failure mode in interaction editing and introduces a contact-aware benchmark rather than another generation model. Rigor (78) is supported by scene-level splitting, controlled corruptions, sensitivity analyses, bootstrap comparisons, released evaluation code, and audit dumps, though the preprint status, single frozen reconstruction frontend, limited multi-seed coverage, and small human study prevent a higher score. Completeness (82) is strong because the authors directly acknowledge contact-locus failure, frontend dependence, moderate human agreement, and proxy limitations. Resilience (70) remains limited by poor standalone HMR2 agreement and the possibility that fixed weights and whole-body proximity distort rankings, while Impact (72) reflects a useful released benchmark artifact with clear diagnostic value but incomplete validation.

Problem & Motivation: Multi-person personalized image editing must preserve multiple identities while rendering physically contacting actions such as hugs, handshakes, carrying, dancing, and grappling. Existing benchmarks measure person count, identity, semantic instruction following, and aesthetic quality, but generally do not test whether the bodies remain anatomically complete or geometrically non-interpenetrating at contact. VLM-based interaction judgments often saturate because they recognize that an action occurs without detecting fused limbs, redundant body parts, or pathological overlap. The paper targets this evaluation gap rather than proposing a new image-generation model. Key Idea: The central insight is to separate semantic interaction success from contact-time body coherence and measure the latter through a frozen multi-person 3D mesh reconstruction. Anatomy measures whether human-like image mass is explained by a complete set of reconstructed bodies; Interaction measures whether reconstructed pairwise penetration and surface distance agree with whether contact is required, forbidden, or unspecified. This is a nontrivial reframing of interaction evaluation, although the underlying reconstruction and geometric quantities are existing components adapted into a benchmark protocol. Methodology: MPIE-Bench first collects interaction videos from Pexels, Harmony4D, and CHI3D, computes a contact-density signal from person-box IoU, pose proximity, optical flow, and occlusion, and selects separated valley frames as identity references and dense-contact peak frames as held-out targets. A VLM reverse-captions each reference-target pair into an instruction, after which human reviewers filter approximately 20,000 candidates into 2,500 samples across 405 scenes, 14 interaction categories, four density levels (C0–C3), and mostly two-person cases; 399 samples contain three or more expected people. For each editor output, the protocol keeps the top k=expected-person-count Multi-HMR detections and computes six axes: Count, Identity, Instruction, Quality, Anatomy, and Interaction. Anatomy constructs a classical human-foreground mask and compares it with rasterized mesh coverage, using leftover fraction, detached blobs, enclosure, ownership, scale, part-structure, over-detection, and residual-mass diagnostics; its fixed mixture weights are 0.40 attached/fused, 0.20 orphan, 0.25 structural, and 0.15 residual. Interaction computes a hull-normalized penetration proxy Vp, an in-hull vertex fraction, and minimum surface distance ds, then combines penetration, proximity, and mesh-quality terms with fixed weights of 0.45/0.35/0.20 for required contact, 0.55/0.45 for forbidden contact, and 0.85/0.15 for unspecified contact. The worst pair governs multi-person interaction, and missing detections halve the Interaction score while reconstruction failure sets mesh scores to zero. The use of scene-level splits, frozen prompts and embeddings, held-out calibration reconstructions, fixed thresholds, two resolution tracks, and separate VLM paths for instruction QA and checklist baselines is generally well specified. However, the choice of whole-body proximity for contact locus is only weakly justified, and several weights and thresholds remain hand-designed or percentile-calibrated rather than learned from a large human-labeled set. Key Results: On the 2,500-sample Track A benchmark at vendor-native resolution, Gemini-3-Pro-Image has the highest Anatomy score at 0.65, Seedream-5-Pro has the highest Interaction score at 0.72, and no editor leads both axes. Other closed editors score 0.58/0.61 for GPT-Image-2 and 0.62/0.72 for Seedream on Anatomy/Interaction; open editors range from 0.54 to 0.63 in Anatomy and 0.45 to 0.60 in Interaction, with FireRed-Image-Edit reaching 0.63 Anatomy and 0.60 Interaction. VLM checklist scores for Anatomy and Interaction are much higher, ranging from 0.56–0.96 and 0.88–0.99 respectively, including 0.98–0.99 Interaction for closed systems. Identity is substantially weaker for open systems, ranging from 0.02 to 0.21 versus 0.49–0.58 for closed systems; instruction scores range from 0.54 to 0.93. On the letterboxed 1024² track, absolute mesh scores rise by approximately 0.06–0.14, but Anatomy rank correlation with Track A is 0.89 for open models and 0.83 across all ten editors, with the top three largely unchanged. High-contact C3 Interaction scores are approximately 0.51–0.69. Controlled corruption of 200 reconstructed ground-truth examples lowers Interaction by 0.15 for forced penetration, 0.04 for excessive separation, 0.35 for dropping a person, and 0.14 for duplication. On 170 hard contact units, the mesh-to-human Spearman correlation exceeds the VLM correlation on 9 of 10 items, with statistically significant improvements on two interaction items, but absolute agreement remains moderate. The metric is therefore stronger evidence for model-level ranking than for per-image correctness. A notable counter-finding is that contact-density trends are not uniformly monotonic: some editors remain nearly flat from C2 to C3, while Anatomy degrades for several stronger systems. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK, NEW METHOD, NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING; the genuine contribution is a contact-rich, scene-split editing benchmark paired with mesh-derived Anatomy and prompt-conditioned Interaction axes, while Multi-HMR, foreground mismatch, penetration, distance, VLM judging, and standard identity/quality metrics are existing ingredients combined for this evaluation setting. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper provides extensive protocol freezing, controlled mesh corruptions, weight/gate/threshold sensitivity tests, scene-clustered bootstrap analysis, a small multi-seed study, and released per-sample Multi-HMR dumps for audit and recomposition. Anatomy editor rankings remain highly stable under stated ablations (rank Spearman at least 0.98), and the Seedream–Gemini Interaction difference is statistically separated under scene-level bootstrap. Code, evaluation scripts, the redistributable test subset, frozen reference embeddings, calibration recipe, human checklist, agreement scripts, and diagnostic JSON dumps are reported at https://github.com/AnnLin0628/mpie-bench; restricted source pixels are not fully redistributed. Important concerns remain: the primary leaderboard freezes one Multi-HMR frontend, and an alternate HMR2 frontend agrees poorly with it on a 150-sample subset when used alone (ten-editor rank Spearman 0.10 for Anatomy and 0.25 for Interaction), although a two-frontend mean reaches 0.92/0.68. The human validation uses only 170 hard units and five raters, with mean α=0.53; only two of the mesh advantages over VLM judging are significant. Main results use one generation per sample and open models use seed 0, while the multi-seed analysis covers only 150 samples and three open editors. The benchmark is partly authored by reverse-captioning target frames with a VLM, creating possible prompt-selection and language-mediated bias, although the authors freeze prompts before evaluation and report 85.3% intent agreement on a 170-unit consistency pool. The paper is an arXiv preprint (v1, dated July 30, 2026), so the reported vendor-model comparisons and closed-source settings should not be treated as independently verified. Deployability (4-property check): EMPIRICAL profile, because the paper evaluates an implemented benchmark and scoring pipeline rather than a theorem or deployed production system. Practical: The evaluator can run on commercially available hardware in principle, but reconstruction latency, GPU memory, total evaluation cost, and API expense are not reported. Efficient: The paper gives no runtime or memory comparison against alternative mesh frontends, and the top-k Multi-HMR reconstruction plus per-pair geometry may be costly for large evaluation suites. Effective: Evidence supports improved model-level sensitivity to contact-related failures relative to a saturated VLM checklist, but the metric remains a proxy and does not reliably verify contact locus or physical correctness per image. Scalable: The benchmark tests 2,500 samples and up to nine expected people, with 16% of samples containing at least three people, but it does not evaluate 10×–100× larger datasets, substantially more people, video sequences, or higher-resolution outputs. The work delivers a research software artifact, redistributable benchmark subset, evaluation scripts, calibration recipe, frozen embeddings, and audit dumps; it does not release a trained generator or a new reconstruction model. Strengths: (1) It identifies a concrete and consequential blind spot—semantic interaction scores can remain near ceiling while contact anatomy is visibly broken—and operationalizes it with separate Anatomy and Interaction axes rather than hiding failures in a blended score. (2) The valley-to-peak video mining procedure creates references and targets from the same real interaction, producing a more realistic reference-conditioned editing task than random multi-person image collages, while scene-level splitting addresses leakage. (3) The protocol is unusually auditable for a benchmark: constants, weights, thresholds, reconstruction dumps, calibration recipes, and failure handling are exposed before leaderboard scoring. (4) The paper does not rely only on headline scores; it includes controlled corruptions, density stratification, resolution sensitivity, alternate-frontend analysis, prompt-intent checks, human comparisons, and seed variance, revealing both the usefulness and limits of the metric. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state that Interaction uses whole-body proximity and does not enforce the requested contact locus; hand–hand distance is only a supplementary probe and part-conditioned contact remains future work. They acknowledge that the hull penetration quantity is a ranking proxy rather than a physical volume, that hulls can be inflated by outstretched limbs, and that the frozen Multi-HMR frontend can be replaced by stronger alternate tracks. They report moderate human agreement, frame the human study as a ranking check rather than a per-image oracle, note that ground-truth numeric anchors are pending in the release, and disclose that valley-to-peak pairs can change camera or background. They also acknowledge one-generation-per-sample evaluation, limited multi-seed coverage, detection-confidence dependence, incomplete identity-aware mesh selection, and the possibility that higher-than-ground-truth Interaction can occur when a generation under-penetrates relative to real contact. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The strongest remaining concern is validity across reconstructors: the poor standalone HMR2 agreement on the 150-sample audit indicates that leaderboard conclusions may depend materially on Multi-HMR’s detection and topology biases, despite the proposed optional ensemble. The human study is small relative to the 2,500-sample benchmark, has only moderate reliability, and does not establish calibration or per-image validity for the continuous scores; the reported editor-level correlations also use a small number of editors. Whole-body minimum surface distance can reward the wrong body region, and the reported 1.3% gaming proxy is VLM-dependent and therefore likely underestimates this failure mode. Dataset diversity is also narrower than the sample count suggests: approximately 2,135 targets come from stock footage, targets are selected by contact heuristics and reviewer filtering, and the benchmark contains no video-generation or temporal-consistency evaluation. The comparison does not include all potentially relevant recent contact-aware editors or human-produced editing baselines, and closed-source outputs, default settings, and single samples limit reproducibility. Finally, the metric’s fixed weights and thresholds are calibrated on related CHI3D reconstructions and may encode source- and frontend-specific notions of plausible contact; robustness to body shape, clothing, extreme occlusion, unusual camera views, children, and non-Western interaction styles is not evaluated. Bottom Line: MPIE-Bench is a useful and technically careful benchmark contribution that exposes a real failure mode missed by current VLM-heavy evaluations, but its mesh scores should be adopted as auditable diagnostic ranking signals—not as validated measures of anatomical or physical correctness—until multi-frontend, larger human-validation, contact-locus, and runtime studies are provided.

Pass the Baton: Trajectory-Relayed On-Policy Distillation (23 ▲ )

Haolei Xu, Xiaowen Xu, Haiwen Hong, Zixuan Ni, Hongxing Li, Yiwen Qiu, Weiming Lu, Yongliang Shen · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 29 Jul 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Relay On-Policy Distillation (Relay-OPD), a distillation procedure that detects likely reasoning-direction failures in student trajectories and inserts short teacher-generated correction segments before resuming student generation. - Why it's important: Prefix failures in long-chain reasoning cause on-policy distillation to spend compute and learn from increasingly misdirected continuations, while fixed truncation removes supervision without teaching recovery. - How it does it: It triggers a teacher handoff when the teacher’s top token is a reflection word but none of the student’s top-5 tokens is, then limits intervention with a takeover-count and paragraph-length budget and trains on the resulting relay trajectory. - The good: With a Qwen3-4B teacher and Qwen3-1.7B student, Relay-OPD reaches 46.96 average accuracy across eight math benchmarks versus 41.23 for OPD and 45.47 for FastOPD, while reducing average training trajectory length by 50.7% versus OPD. - The missing: The evaluation does not establish robustness beyond two Qwen3 student sizes and mathematical reasoning, and it reports no multiple-seed variation, error bars, significance tests, or direct wall-clock/cost accounting for the additional teacher-side intervention. - Read it or not: Researchers working on on-policy distillation and reasoning-model post-training should read it for the state-triggered intervention design and ablations; readers seeking evidence for general-purpose deployment can defer until cross-domain and broader-model evaluations appear.
Why this rank
Scored using the Empirical profile. Novelty (80) and Non-Obviousness (82) are strong because Relay-OPD turns a concrete prefix-direction failure signal into a bounded teacher handoff rather than relying on fixed truncation or generic token mixing. Rigor (70), Completeness (78), and Resilience (72) are supported by broad math-benchmark coverage and detailed intervention, budget, and objective ablations, but are materially reduced by the lexical trigger heuristic, checkpoint-tuning concerns, absent training-seed uncertainty, and missing end-to-end teacher-cost accounting. Impact (70) is credible due to the released implementation and sizable reported gains plus shorter trajectories, though deployment beyond Qwen3 mathematical reasoning is unverified. Weighted composite: 0.20*80 + 0.25*70 + 0.15*82 + 0.15*78 + 0.15*72 + 0.10*70 = 75.3, rounded to 75.

Problem & Motivation: On-policy distillation obtains supervision on prefixes generated by the student, reducing train–inference distribution shift but also exposing the training process to student prefix failures. In long mathematical reasoning, an early incorrect direction can produce long, repetitive, or self-consistent but invalid continuations whose later token-level supervision is less useful and whose generation consumes substantial compute. Prior remedies considered in the paper—fixed-length truncation, offline teacher rewriting, and generic token-level teacher–student mixing—either intervene at positions unrelated to the actual failure, repair trajectories only after the fact, or lack an explicit signal that the reasoning direction has diverged. The target users are practitioners transferring reasoning capabilities from a stronger language model to a weaker one, particularly in strong-to-weak mathematical post-training. Key Idea: The central insight is to treat a disagreement about reflection versus continuation as an online failure signal: if the teacher’s most probable next token is a member of a manually specified reflection-token set such as “Wait,” “But,” or “However,” while no reflection token appears in the student’s top-K support, the prefix is considered a handoff trigger. The method then gives the teacher a short, local “relay leg” to redirect the context rather than replacing the entire trajectory or truncating it. This is a substantive state-driven intervention heuristic, although its semantic signal depends on reflection-token behavior in the chosen model and language. Methodology: For each prompt, the old student policy generates a trajectory while the teacher evaluates the current prefix. At a student-generation position, the method computes the teacher top-1 token and the student top-K token set; with K=5, a trigger occurs when the teacher top-1 belongs to a 13-word reflection set, including case and leading-space variants, and the student top-K contains no reflection token. At a trigger, the teacher emits the selected reflection token and generates L additional paragraphs, with the student then resuming generation unless the maximum of M takeovers has been reached; the default is M=2 and L=3. The resulting relay trajectory contains student and teacher legs and is optimized using a PPO-clipped, single-sample reverse-KL-style objective: the advantage for each observed token is A_t = log pi_T(z_t|h_t) - log pi_old-student(z_t|h_t), combined with the ratio of current to old student probabilities and clipping range 0.2. The implementation uses one speculative-decoding engine, with the student as draft and teacher as target, and directly inserts the teacher’s trigger token; teacher parameters remain frozen and student weights synchronize to the draft model after updates. The main design choices—reflection-token triggering, paragraph-based bounded intervention, and training on actually generated relay tokens rather than teacher FKL or the student’s rejected draft tokens—are supported by preliminary intervention experiments and ablations, but the reflection vocabulary and budget remain heuristic and model-dependent. Key Results: On Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 as teacher and Qwen3-0.6B-Non-Thinking or Qwen3-1.7B-Non-Thinking as students, training uses the English DAPO-Math-17K subset, one epoch, eight H100 GPUs, temperature 1.0, and top-p 1.0. Evaluation covers AIME 2024, AIME 2025, AIME 2026, MATH500, AMC 2023, OlympiadBench, HMMT February 2026, and HMMT November 2025, using 32 samples per AIME/AMC/HMMT problem and four per MATH500/OlympiadBench problem. For the 1.7B student, Relay-OPD obtains 42.71, 32.81, 30.52, 89.50, 76.88, 58.79, 24.72, and 19.79 accuracy on the eight benchmarks, respectively, for a 46.96 average; this is +5.73 points over OPD’s 41.23 and +1.49 over FastOPD’s 45.47. For the 0.6B student, it averages 31.04 versus 28.03 for OPD and 30.42 for FastOPD. Relay-OPD is best or second-best on every listed benchmark for both students. Its best 1.7B checkpoint occurs at step 35, with 2,296 average training-response tokens versus 4,658 for OPD and 2,709 for FastOPD; the corresponding 0.6B trajectory length is 2,490 versus 6,900 for OPD. In a preliminary 128-example intervention study, replacing only a reflection token raised mean@4 accuracy from 27.73% to 34.96% while teacher tokens represented 0.35% of generated tokens; longer teacher legs reached 43.55% at L=6 but used 28.52% teacher tokens. The teacher-leg ablation improved average accuracy from 43.48% for trigger-stop to 46.25% with M=1,L=3, and the relay-token objective reached 46.96% versus 44.56% for the student-draft-token objective and 44.08% for teacher FKL. Results are promising but remain benchmark- and model-family-specific; the paper does not report uncertainty around the accuracy differences. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, and ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION: the paper introduces a trigger-based, budgeted teacher-relay variant of on-policy distillation and a unified speculative-decoding implementation, while the claimed teacher–student continuation asymmetry and local early-intervention effect are new empirical observations; the underlying reverse-KL distillation, speculative decoding, and PPO clipping are established components. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper includes useful component ablations, comparisons with SFT, KD, GRPO, OPD, TRD, FastOPD, and SKD, a sweep over L, M, and K, a trigger-stop control, and alternative teacher-leg objectives. It provides detailed hyperparameters, prompts, an algorithm, and reports a GitHub repository at https://github.com/zju-real/Relay-OPD plus a project page at https://zju-real.github.io/Relay-OPD. However, it reports no random seeds, error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests, and the paper does not state whether all code, data-processing scripts, checkpoints, or trained weights are released beyond the linked repository. The benchmark suite is narrow and the method’s K=5, M=2, L=3 configuration was tuned on the 1.7B student and reused for the 0.6B student; the sensitivity plots are not a substitute for independent validation of these choices. Baseline training configurations are described, but there is no complete wall-clock, GPU-hour, teacher-forward-pass, memory, or monetary-cost comparison, so the reported trajectory-token savings do not directly establish end-to-end efficiency. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL, with a systems implementation component. Practical: The method runs on commercially available H100 GPUs using verl and vLLM, but it requires simultaneous access to teacher logits and student generation and therefore may be expensive for larger teacher–student pairs. Efficient: Training trajectories are 50.7% shorter than OPD for the 1.7B student and 63.9% shorter for the 0.6B student, but the paper does not measure end-to-end latency, throughput, peak memory, or teacher-compute cost, so the net efficiency advantage is not established. Effective: On eight mathematical reasoning benchmarks, it improves mean accuracy over OPD by 5.73 points for the 1.7B student and 3.01 points for the 0.6B student, providing evidence on the stated math-distillation objective rather than only a proxy. Scalable: The largest tested student is 1.7B, the teacher is 4B, training uses one mathematical dataset and two student scales, and no 10×–100× scale, longer training, other model family, code, tool-use, or non-English evaluation is reported. The work delivers a software implementation through the linked GitHub repository, but no standalone library or trained model release is explicitly stated. Strengths: - The paper identifies a concrete failure mode in OPD and converts it into an online intervention rule that requires no answer labels, verifier, reward model, or process annotations. - The relay design addresses a real tradeoff: it supplies corrected context and a recovery demonstration while preserving more of the student’s state distribution than full teacher generation or offline rewriting. - The ablations separate dynamic stopping from teacher-generated correction and distinguish the observed relay-token objective from both student-draft-token and teacher-FKL alternatives. - The reported gains are consistent across two student sizes and eight math benchmarks, while the method also reduces measured training trajectory length substantially relative to OPD and FastOPD. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly restrict evaluation to mathematical reasoning and Qwen3 teacher–student pairs, leaving code generation and agentic tool use for future work. They state that the reflection-token set may need adjustment for other model families, that the method assumes the teacher redirects failed prefixes more reliably than the student, and that benefits may diminish as the teacher–student capability gap narrows. They also acknowledge that the relay budget was tuned on the 1.7B student and reused for the 0.6B student, although moderate budget sensitivity appears acceptable. These limitations are stated directly, but the paper does not quantify the extent of cross-domain degradation or the compute cost of intervention. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The trigger is a hand-engineered lexical heuristic, so the paper does not test whether it detects genuine reasoning failures rather than stylistic teacher preferences, nor does it compare against learned triggers, probability-margin triggers, semantic state divergence, or verifier-based failure detection. The evaluation lacks multiple seeds and uncertainty estimates despite several reported gains being small, particularly the 0.6B improvement over FastOPD of 0.62 points. Hyperparameter selection and checkpoint selection may be optimistic because the method is evaluated on the same benchmark suite used to select best checkpoints, and the paper does not describe a held-out validation protocol in sufficient detail. Comparisons do not isolate total teacher inference cost or wall-clock training cost, leaving open whether shorter trajectories offset the extra teacher intervention and speculative-decoding work. The paper also does not test stronger or differently trained teachers, larger students, non-Qwen architectures, domains where reflection tokens are uncommon, or cases where teacher intervention is itself wrong. Finally, claims about improved exploration based on higher policy entropy are correlational and are not tied to a direct measure of solution diversity or recovery from verified prefix errors. Bottom Line: This preprint offers a technically coherent and empirically supported improvement to math-focused on-policy distillation, and its trigger-plus-relay mechanism is worth adopting or extending, but the absence of uncertainty, end-to-end cost accounting, and cross-domain/model-family validation prevents treating it as a generally established solution.

From Proprietary to Open-Source: Bridging the Distribution Gap via Multi-Agent Protocol Distillation in Agentic Search (64 ▲ )

Junlin Liu, Jiangwang Chen, Zixin Song, Shuaiyu Zhou, Chunji Lv, Hank Wu, Kailin Jiang, Jinyang Wu, Bohan Yu, Chenxi Zhou · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 28 Jul 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Multi-Agent Protocol Distillation (MAPD), a joint reinforcement-learning and self-distillation framework that transfers proprietary-model search strategies to open-source agentic-search students through structured JSON protocols. - Why it's important: Black-box proprietary models expose neither logits nor compatible tokenizers, while direct trajectory imitation can transfer verbosity and stylistic artifacts instead of useful search and reasoning behavior. - How it does it: An offline multi-agent system decomposes questions, searches a local Wikipedia corpus, repairs failed searches, and converts verified traces into structured privileged information used by a protocol-conditioned branch of the student alongside GRPO. - The good: Across seven QA benchmarks, MAPD reaches 39.4% average success on Qwen3-1.7B and 44.4% on Qwen3-4B, improving over the strongest reported SDAR baseline by 4.8% and 3.3% relative, respectively. - The missing: The study uses only one training run per configuration, does not evaluate substantially larger models or non-Wikipedia/real-web environments, and does not isolate how much of the gain comes from answer-bearing privileged supervision rather than protocol structure. - Read it or not: Agentic-search and LLM-distillation researchers should read it for the structured-privileged-information design and ablations, but practitioners should treat the deployment and generalization claims as unverified beyond small students and a controlled QA setting.
Why this rank
