Problem & Motivation: Multi-turn agents must maintain state, learn transition rules, compose atomic skills, and execute action sequences over 1–20 steps or more. The paper targets the gap between opaque, uncontrollable Internet pre-training and the need to understand whether planning comes from memorized trajectories, internalized world models, compositional skill reuse, or post-training. It also addresses two post-training problems: outcome-based GRPO may provide unreliable credit assignment on long trajectories, and distillation from teachers with different valid procedures may overwrite rather than add knowledge. The application domain is agentic planning, but the experiments use synthetic crafting-style environments rather than computer-use, terminal, web, or physical-world tasks. Key Idea: The core insight is to distinguish low-mutual-information, reusable planning patterns from high-mutual-information, task-specific planning knowledge. The paper argues that SFT or distillation can acquire concrete procedures, RL/OPD can select generalizable reasoning patterns, and multi-teacher OPD can transfer only the planning patterns supported by and sufficiently compatible with the student and other teachers. This distinction explains the reported boundary between successful pattern shaping, failed unseen-knowledge transfer, cross-environment generalization, continual learning, and catastrophic forgetting. Methodology: The authors construct a controllable planning gym from hierarchical skill graphs in Fantasy Alchemy, Livestock Farming, and Electronic Assembly. Each domain has five levels, 200 abstract item categories, 20 concrete instances per category, AND/OR synthesis rules, distractor inventory items, and held-out entity mappings; tasks are grouped as short (1–5 actions), middle (6–8), or long (9–13 actions in the generated datasets, with inference capped at 20 steps). Models receive natural-language item/category descriptions and must repeatedly emit a reasoning trace plus an executable synthesis action. For pre-training, randomly initialized approximately 100M-parameter Qwen2.5-style causal models are trained for 9,000 steps with full-parameter SFT on controlled mixtures. The world-modeling condition explicitly verbalizes state transitions and performs an internal DFS-like backward decomposition before selecting actions; the baseline directly predicts actions. The authors vary the horizon distribution from short-only to mixtures containing 5%, 50%, or 100% middle/long trajectories, and vary optimal/suboptimal pattern mixtures such as 1 optimal, 4 optimal, and 4 optimal:8 suboptimal. For post-training, multi-turn GRPO uses a binary final-outcome reward, whereas Top-k OPD minimizes token-level reverse KL over the student’s top-100 vocabulary tokens on its own rollouts. The paper analyzes performance, training curves, token-level KL, and top-5 SVD subspace alignment of parameter updates. For multi-teacher OPD, domain-specialized teachers are distilled sequentially in the order Fantasy Alchemy, Livestock Farming, and Electronic Assembly. Critical design decisions are the synthetic skill-graph generator, explicit separation of patterns and knowledge, and controlled teacher-pattern overlap/conflict. The first two are useful for causal diagnosis but narrow the external validity; the mutual-information distinction is reasoned about conceptually rather than estimated quantitatively from learned representations. Key Results: With world-modeling traces, short-horizon avg@8 rises from 89.5% to 98.9%, middle-horizon avg@8 from 46.6% to 85.9%, and long-horizon avg@8 from 22.7% to 68.5%; corresponding pass@8 improvements are 92.1% to 99.0%, 55.4% to 88.3%, and 29.0% to 71.9%. Training only on short tasks yields pass@8 of 93.12% on short, 0.83% on middle, and 0% on long tasks. Adding 5% middle-horizon data raises middle pass@8 to 51.88%; adding 5% long-horizon data raises long pass@8 to 11.46%. With 100% short, 100% middle, and 50% long data, long-horizon pass@8 reaches 78.54%, compared with 0% under short-only training. Mixing 4 optimal with 8 suboptimal trajectories causes near-collapse: the reported long-horizon avg@8 is approximately 0% and middle-horizon avg@8 is approximately 0.4–1.6%, depending on domain. In the 4 optimal:8 suboptimal setting, OPD improves overall avg@8 by roughly 18.4–18.9 points over the instruct model, while GRPO changes performance by -1.6 to -0.3 points; for 4 optimal:4 suboptimal, OPD improves avg@8 by 15.1–16.6 points and GRPO by 10.0–13.5 points. In the clean 4-optimal setting, neither method materially improves the already strong baseline, and GRPO sometimes has a slightly higher pass@8 ceiling than OPD at larger sampling counts. Distilling a teacher using a different valid procedure reduces overall pass@8 from 44.03% for the base instruct model to 36.60%, whereas aligned-teacher distillation reaches 46.74%; on middle Fantasy Alchemy, mismatched distillation is 43.75 pass@8 points below aligned distillation. In multi-teacher experiments, shared compatible patterns transfer across domains: for the 4 optimal:4 suboptimal(a) model, middle Fantasy Alchemy avg@8 improves from 41.95% to 61.64% after Fantasy Alchemy distillation, while middle Livestock Farming improves from 34.92% to 52.58%. Under shared-but-conflicting patterns, sequential MOPD retains low-horizon avg@8 of 91.88% and 88.98% on earlier domains after learning the third domain. Without a shared pattern, later distillation can reduce Livestock Farming low-horizon avg@8 from 90.00% to 15.62%. These results are measured on the authors’ synthetic benchmark; no real-world benchmark, larger model, wall-clock comparison, or deployment-scale stress test is reported. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper provides extensive controlled comparisons, held-out concrete entity mappings, explicit dataset statistics, task-generation details, model configuration, optimizer settings, and several diagnostic analyses. However, no multiple random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, hypothesis tests, or variance estimates are reported, despite many conclusions relying on percentage-point differences. The paper compares only against direct-answer SFT, GRPO, and Top-k OPD; it does not include strong process-reward, dense-reward, curriculum, replay, anti-forgetting, parameter-efficient, or contemporary long-horizon agent baselines. The mutual-information framework is defined mathematically but the quantities are not empirically estimated. The environment, training code, models, and datasets are claimed to be released at https://github.com/Quester-one/PlanPhysCode, https://huggingface.co/MultimodalAgent/TianyiMen_PlanPhys_Models, and https://huggingface.co/datasets/MultimodalAgent/TianyiMen_PlanPhys_Datasets; the paper also provides a project page at https://quester-one.github.io/PlanPhysWebsite/. The work is an arXiv v1 preprint dated 27 July 2026, not a peer-reviewed publication according to the supplied document. The controlled benchmark is authored-generated and uses counterfactual synthesis rules, which supports internal comparisons but creates a substantial risk that conclusions depend on the benchmark’s templates, graph regularities, and tokenization. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL, with a secondary SYSTEMS aspect because the authors release a gym, code, datasets, and model checkpoints. Practical: The 100M-parameter models can run on commercially available GPUs, and training is reported on two GPUs, but the method requires interactive rollouts and teacher inference, and the paper does not establish usability on real agent environments. This is more informative than reporting only successful distillation. - The MOPD experiments connect pattern overlap to transfer and forgetting, and the token/KL and parameter-update analyses provide mechanistic evidence consistent with the performance results rather than relying solely on aggregate success rates. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly acknowledge that gold-standard trajectories provide too few error-state prefixes for recovery learning, that OPD may assign low probability to valid alternative procedures, that RL updates are too small to inject large quantities of unseen task-specific knowledge, and that MOPD cannot create planning patterns absent from the student’s pre-training support. They also acknowledge OPD’s entropy reduction and weaker scaling with larger sampling counts, GRPO’s sparse-credit limitations, the danger of catastrophic forgetting under conflicting patterns, and the use of counterfactual synthesis rules for scalable controlled data generation. These limitations are generally confronted directly, although the conclusion that the findings transfer to real-world agent development remains broader than the demonstrated evidence. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The main unresolved issue is external validity: all tasks are synthetic, structurally regular, short compared with the claimed days- or weeks-long planning horizon, and evaluated with an exact success criterion. The paper does not test OSWorld, terminal tasks, web tasks, robotics, tool-use environments, or any naturally occurring noisy trajectory corpus. It uses a randomly initialized 100M model rather than a modern pretrained foundation model, so the conclusions about pre-training acquisition may not hold when broad linguistic and procedural priors already exist. The reported OPD advantage assumes an ideal, highly accurate teacher; the paper does not evaluate teacher errors, calibration, domain mismatch beyond two synthetic procedures, or teacher uncertainty. There is no systematic seed study, no statistical testing, and no compute-normalized comparison, making the robustness of small differences unclear. The pattern labels and distributions are manually designed through templates, so the claimed pattern/knowledge separation may partly reflect the data generator rather than an intrinsic property of agent reasoning. Finally, sequential MOPD is tested in one teacher order and a small number of three-domain configurations; reverse orders, simultaneous mixtures, more teachers, replay or regularization baselines, and methods designed specifically to mitigate forgetting are absent. Bottom Line: This is a useful and unusually controlled diagnostic study for researchers investigating long-horizon SFT, GRPO, OPD, and model consolidation, but its synthetic 100M-scale setting and missing robustness and real-task evaluations make it insufficient evidence for deployment claims or broad laws about foundation-model planning.

Yuran Wang, Zekun Wang, Bohan Zeng, Ruixu Zhang, Wenxuan Liu, Liu Yang, Yifan Dai, Yang Shi, Bozhou Li, Chengzhuo Tong, Daili Hua, Yuanxing Zhang, Wentao Zhang · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 31 Jul 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Flux-OPD, an on-policy distillation algorithm that continually extracts experience contexts from student trajectories and uses them to correct a stable context-free teacher target. - Why it's important: Open-ended tasks lack dense, verifiable rewards, so the method targets a practical way to transfer evolving task preferences into smaller language models without destabilizing training. - How it does it: It combines context-conditioned teacher distributions through a normalized geometric mean, adds their log-probability difference to the context-free teacher, and scales that correction using a conflict score. - The good: Across three student–teacher configurations and two tasks, Flux-OPD obtains the highest reported aggregate task scores, including 80.18 versus 79.28 for OPD on VBench and 20.61 versus 19.63 for OPD on HealthBench in the primary settings. - The missing: The evaluation does not establish compute efficiency, broad robustness, or statistical significance across methods, and most baselines are trained only once while the proposed method uses task- and downstream-specific calibration. - Read it or not: Researchers working on on-policy distillation, context distillation, or alignment for open-ended tasks should read it for the reverse-KL analysis and method design; practitioners should wait for stronger efficiency, safety, and multi-seed evidence.

Problem & Motivation: Open-ended language-model tasks such as video-prompt optimization and medical question answering have complex preferences that are difficult to encode as verifiable rewards. Vanilla on-policy distillation supplies dense supervision from a context-free teacher but mainly transfers teacher preferences, while context distillation can expose the teacher to experience items or rubrics that encode task-specific information. Fixed contexts become less useful after their information is absorbed by the student, whereas updating contexts during training causes abrupt target-distribution shifts and conflicts between context-conditioned teachers. The paper addresses the gap between dense teacher supervision and adaptive, task-relevant preference supervision without relying on an explicitly trained reward model. Key Idea: Under the reverse-KL objective, averaging context-conditioned teachers yields a normalized geometric-mean target plus a nonnegative conflict term. Flux-OPD therefore treats the geometric-mean teacher not as the direct target but as a contextual correction to a stable context-free teacher, with the correction attenuated when the context-conditioned distributions disagree. The core insight is to use contexts as a bounded, conflict-aware residual signal rather than replacing the teacher distribution wholesale. Methodology: Flux-OPD divides one training run into iterations. At the start of iteration k, it samples eight rollouts per context-extraction batch from the current student, optionally attaches downstream video results for prompt optimization or rubrics for medical QA, and asks the frozen teacher—using three random extraction seeds—to generate new experience items that are accumulated into a context pool. During distillation, the teacher produces a context-free distribution q0 and multiple context-conditioned distributions qr for sampled contexts. It computes the unnormalized geometric mean log q̃geo(v) = (1/R)Σr log qr(v), its normalization constant Z, and the conflict score δ = −log Z. The contextual difference is Δ(v) = log qgeo(v) − log q0(v), and the target is qflux(v) = softmax(log q0(v) + λΔ(v)). The correction weight is λ = α clip(1 − δ/τ, λmin, λmax), followed by reverse-KL training DKL(student || qflux). The main design decisions are the stable context-free anchor, geometric aggregation in log space, and conflict-based weighting. The anchor is directly motivated by observed target shifts; the geometric mean follows from the reverse-KL decomposition; the weighting function is plausible but heuristic, and its thresholds and calibration ranges are selected separately for task/model settings rather than derived from an optimization principle. For computational efficiency, only the top 64 target logits are retained and renormalized. Key Results: In the primary Qwen3-VL 8B-teacher/4B-student prompt-optimization setting, Flux-OPD reaches 80.18 average VBench versus 79.69 for the initial student, 79.28 for OPD, 79.02 for OPCD, and 76.86 for OEL; on Video-Bench it reaches 3.61 versus 3.58 for the student, 3.54 for OPD, 3.57 for OPCD, and 3.31 for OEL. With a Qwen2.5-VL 32B teacher and 7B student, it reaches 80.24 average VBench versus 79.61 for the student, 79.89 for OPD, 79.65 for OPCD, and 79.75 for OEL. On HealthBench with a Qwen3 8B teacher and 1.7B student, it obtains 20.61 total versus 19.06 for the initial student, 19.63 for OPD, 19.53 for OPCD, and 19.66 for OEL; the teacher scores 37.38. On IF-Eval after medical-QA training, prompt-level strict accuracy is 34.38 for Flux-OPD, compared with 34.20 for OEL, 32.90 initially, and 31.79 for OPD. Three independent runs are reported only for OPD and Flux-OPD: VBench means are 77.39 (standard deviation 0.083) and 78.06 (0.117), while HealthBench means are 19.51 (0.323) and 20.30 (0.297), respectively. The experiments use 10K VPO prompts, approximately 18K RaR-Medicine questions, 523 VBench prompts, 419 Video-Bench prompts, and 5K HealthBench conversations. The gains are generally modest on VBench and HealthBench, and Flux-OPD does not dominate every submetric; for example, OPD or other baselines sometimes match or exceed individual dimensions. The baselines are relevant recent OPD variants, but the paper does not establish that they are tuned with equal rigor or compute budgets. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD, NEW FORMULATION, and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING: the reverse-KL geometric-mean/conflict decomposition is a useful formulation, and the proposed contextual-correction plus conflict-weighting training procedure is the main method contribution, while the empirical finding is that evolving context residuals can improve over direct OPCD/OEL and vanilla OPD in two open-ended settings; the iterative context extraction, teacher prompting, on-policy rollouts, and distillation components otherwise build substantially on existing context distillation, OPCD, OEL, and OPD techniques. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper proves the stated fixed-history reverse-KL decomposition under strictly positive teacher probabilities and correctly observes that the conflict term has no direct gradient with respect to the student distribution when contexts and teacher distributions are fixed. It includes component ablations on HealthBench: removing evolving contexts gives 19.63, OEL-style evolving contexts without correction gives 19.66, contextual correction with fixed λ values gives 19.73–20.03, and the full method gives 20.61. It also reports threshold and calibration studies, training-loss/gradient plots, conflict dynamics, and three-run comparisons for OPD versus Flux-OPD. However, the key weighting rule is heuristic, and the fixed-distribution analysis does not by itself prove stability under changing contexts, sampled histories, teacher prompting, or student-dependent context extraction. Most baseline results use one training run; only OPD and Flux-OPD receive three-run variability estimates, with no confidence intervals or significance tests. The method uses different τ, scaling, clipping bounds, and calibration choices for downstream models, creating a risk of favorable per-setting tuning; the paper does not state whether comparable tuning was applied to baselines. Top-64 target-logit truncation may materially alter the claimed KL objective, but its effect is not ablated. The paper is an arXiv preprint dated 30 July 2026, reports training on eight NVIDIA A800 GPUs, and provides prompts and pseudocode, but no code, dataset release, model-weight release, or repository URL is stated. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL, with a systems-like training pipeline but no released software artifact. Practical: The experiments run on commercially available NVIDIA A800 GPUs and use publicly named Qwen, video-generation, and benchmark models, although the teacher must be queried repeatedly for context-conditioned logits and the downstream video environment adds operational cost. Efficient: No wall-clock time, token count, teacher-query count, memory footprint, or cost comparison against OPD, OPCD, or OEL is reported; Flux-OPD likely adds context extraction, multiple teacher passes, and optional video generation relative to OPD. Effective: The measured results show improvements on VBench, Video-Bench, HealthBench, and IF-Eval over the tested student and OPD/OPCD/OEL baselines, but medical QA remains far below the teacher score and the evaluations rely partly on automated metrics and GPT-4o judging rather than direct human or clinical validation. Scalable: The method is tested with 1.7B–7B students, 8B–32B teachers, 10K–18K training examples, and context updates every 300 steps, but no 10×–100× scale experiment, long-run context-pool growth study, larger teacher, larger student, or production deployment is reported. The work delivers a training algorithm, prompts, pseudocode, and empirical model checkpoints only insofar as the experiments use them; it does not state that a reusable library, CLI, dataset, or trained model has been released. Strengths: - The reverse-KL decomposition is mathematically simple, correct under its stated positivity assumptions, and gives a principled interpretation of why context-conditioned teachers can disagree and why their geometric mean is the relevant fixed-context target. - The contextual-difference construction preserves a stable context-free teacher anchor while allowing task-specific information from evolving contexts to influence training, which directly addresses the instability observed for OEL-style target replacement. - The evaluation covers two qualitatively different tasks, three student–teacher configurations, two downstream video generators, multiple video benchmarks, HealthBench, and an out-of-distribution instruction-following test rather than relying on a single text metric. - The ablations separate evolving contexts, contextual correction, and conflict weighting, and the reported loss/gradient curves support the narrower claim that Flux-OPD is more stable than the tested OEL implementation during context updates. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The paper does not include a dedicated limitations section. It implicitly bounds the method to open-ended tasks where useful experience items or supplemental downstream feedback can be extracted, and it acknowledges that context consistency varies with teacher strength and available supplements. It does not explicitly discuss medical-safety limitations, inference/training cost, prompt-extraction errors, context-pool growth, or failure cases. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The comparison lacks matched compute and teacher-query accounting, making it unclear whether gains justify the added cost of multiple context-conditioned teacher evaluations and downstream video generation. Baseline hyperparameter tuning and random-seed coverage are not matched: Flux-OPD receives setting-specific τ and calibration choices, while most baselines are reported from one run. The paper does not compare against stronger preference-optimization, reward-model, rubric-based, or human-feedback methods, nor does it test alternative context aggregators, learned conflict functions, delayed updates, context-pool sizes, rollout counts, extraction seeds, or top-k values. The conflict score is treated as a proxy for harmful supervision disagreement, but no experiment tests whether high conflict actually predicts target error or downstream failure. The reverse-KL theorem assumes strictly positive probabilities and fixed contexts; the practical implementation truncates teacher logits and makes contexts depend on the student, so the relationship between the theorem and the complete training dynamics remains limited. Medical QA evaluation does not assess factuality, calibration, refusal quality, or clinical safety beyond aggregate HealthBench scores, and video results may be sensitive to the chosen generators and automated/GPT-4o evaluators. There is also no evidence about performance at substantially larger scale or after repeated context accumulation. Bottom Line: This is a technically coherent and empirically promising refinement of on-policy/context distillation, worth reading for its geometric-mean analysis and conflict-aware target construction, but its practical impact is not yet established because efficiency, matched tuning, statistical reliability, safety, and large-scale robustness remain under-evaluated.

Problem & Motivation The work addresses exact missing-cell prediction in spreadsheets and other tabular datasets used for analytics and data cleaning. The target users are spreadsheet users, data engineers, and organizations that need to generate reliable suggestions across large numbers of tables. Traditional constraint-based cleaning methods require known functional or conditional dependencies and cannot generally incorporate world knowledge or open-ended reasoning; statistical imputation methods optimize numerical closeness rather than exact equality; retrieval-based methods require a sufficiently redundant data lake; and vanilla language models are expensive and often overconfident. The paper frames the task as maximizing recall subject to a user-specified precision constraint, with abstention allowed when the observed table does not support a reliable answer. Key Idea The core insight is that exact missing-value prediction is heterogeneous rather than a single reasoning problem: some cells require parametric world knowledge and formatting, some require multi-step textual reasoning over rows and columns, and some require discovering and executing a column-level program. Instead of forcing one model to alternate among these behaviors, Auto-Fill assigns each behavior to a specialist and compares their calibrated probabilities. The ensemble therefore uses confidence as implicit routing while preserving abstention. This decomposition is plausible and empirically useful, although the underlying specialization, distillation, calibration, and ensembling mechanisms are individually established ideas. Methodology Training begins with complete tables from six sources: 467K spreadsheet tables, 12K business-intelligence tables, 292K Wikipedia tables, 1.6K government CSV files, 635 GitHub CSV files, and 29K GitHub Parquet files. The system randomly masks a nonempty cell and uses its original value as a free label. The knowledge specialist M_K receives direct supervised fine-tuning on 30K table-answer pairs and emits a structured value; its raw confidence is the geometric mean of token probabilities over the answer tokens. The reasoning specialist M_R is trained on 50K examples using traces generated by DeepSeek-R1: the teacher samples 10 traces without confidence, retains the shortest correct trace, then samples 10 additional traces with verbalized confidence and assigns the target confidence E[confidence | correct] multiplied by P(correct). The coding specialist M_C is trained on teacher-generated reasoning plus vectorized Python/Pandas code; accepted training programs must execute, recover the masked value, and reconstruct at least 80% of the observed cells in the target column. At inference, M_R and M_C use temperature 0.8 while M_K uses 0.1. Each specialist produces a raw score, which is mapped to empirical correctness probabilities using isotonic regression fitted on 2,000 held-out ID cases. Auto-Fill selects the highest calibrated probability and abstains if it is below threshold tau, with the principal evaluation using tau=0.9. The paper also evaluates optional GRPO reinforcement learning with a correctness-plus-Brier calibration reward, but finds only modest and inconsistent gains. The main design decisions—separate specialists, mode-specific confidence extraction, and isotonic calibration—are experimentally motivated; however, the confidence targets for reasoning rely on teacher sampling and self-reported confidence, and the 80% coding threshold is selected empirically rather than derived from a formal guarantee. Key Results The primary evaluation contains 11 benchmarks with 200 tables each, totaling 2,200 test tables: five ID sources and six OOD sources, including proprietary enterprise CSV/XLS collections, web tables, and relation-focused arithmetic, functional-dependency, and string-transformation datasets. At precision 0.9, Auto-Fill-Qwen obtains mean recall 0.628 and pAUPRC 0.613 at $0.00148 per query; Auto-Fill-GPT obtains 0.656 and 0.641 at $0.0113 per query. The strongest reported vanilla baselines by mean R@P=0.9 are o3-pro at 0.56 and o4-mini at 0.56, costing $0.177 and $0.0109 per query, while Gemini 3 Pro obtains 0.38 at $0.043. Auto-Fill-Qwen is therefore approximately 119 times cheaper than o3-pro and 29 times cheaper than Gemini 3 Pro, although the paper’s headline “less than 1%” comparison depends on the selected frontier baseline and cost accounting. Auto-Fill performs especially well on relation benchmarks: Auto-Fill-Qwen reaches 0.99 on Rel-AR, 0.89 on Rel-FD, and 1.00 on Rel-ST; Auto-Fill-GPT reaches 0.99, 0.89, and 0.99, respectively. On the difficult Pub-Web benchmark, Auto-Fill-GPT reaches 0.42 while most vanilla baselines obtain zero at the 0.9 precision operating point. Full accuracy without abstention tells a different story: Gemini 3 Pro leads at 0.786 and o3-pro reaches 0.757, while Auto-Fill-Qwen and Auto-Fill-GPT reach 0.690 and 0.727, showing that the main advantage is calibrated selective prediction rather than raw answer accuracy. The specialist ablation supports complementarity: for Qwen3-8B, M_K alone reaches 0.542 mean ID/OOD R@P=0.9, M_R 0.418, M_C 0.344, M_K+M_C 0.604, and all three 0.628. Isotonic calibration improves Qwen3 performance from 0.434 without calibration to 0.503 ID R@P=0.9 and from 0.694 to 0.733 OOD; mean ECE falls from 0.116 to 0.028. A 10-to-all-row input sampling experiment reduces recall by roughly 0.05 while reducing input-token cost, but no 10x–100x production-scale stress test is reported. Novelty Classification NEW PROBLEM, NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION. The genuinely new aspect is the explicit high-precision, abstention-aware formulation and empirical demonstration that knowledge, textual reasoning, and executable column-level computation benefit from separate calibrated specialists for missing-cell prediction; the components themselves—self-supervised masking, chain-of-thought distillation, code execution, isotonic calibration, and confidence-based ensembling—are standard or adapted combinations rather than individually new algorithms. Rigor & Reproducibility The study includes useful ablations over specialist composition, hybrid versus modular architecture, learned routing versus calibrated selection, confidence mechanisms, calibration methods, teacher sample size, code-reconstruction threshold, trace selection, row sampling, and optional RL. The strongest evidence is the consistent specialist-combination improvement and the calibration comparison: isotonic regression beats no calibration, Platt scaling, and beta calibration on the main task metrics. The paper reports training compute for Qwen models—four A100 80GB GPUs, approximately 11 hours for M_K and 40 hours each for M_R and M_C—and gives detailed hyperparameters for RL. No error bars, multiple random seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported, so the reliability of differences across 200-table benchmark subsets is unclear. The benchmark and data construction procedures are described, but the paper does not clearly state that all underlying training and evaluation tables are publicly released; some OOD sources are proprietary. The implementation is publicly linked at https://github.com/lyrain2001/auto-fill. The evaluation masks cells from otherwise complete tables, which may make the task easier and cleaner than real missingness, and relation-specific benchmarks deliberately target cells known to participate in recoverable relationships. Calibration is fitted on ID data and then applied to OOD data, but the paper does not provide a deployment recalibration protocol or calibration confidence intervals. Cost estimates cover LLM inference per query only and exclude training, hosting, orchestration, parallel specialist invocation overhead, code sandboxing, and engineering costs. Comparisons are broad, but several classical baselines are substantially adapted to the single-cell setting, and the paper does not establish equivalence to the strongest contemporary table-specific or retrieval-augmented systems beyond the listed baselines. Deployability (4-property check) Profile: SYSTEMS — the paper builds and evaluates a software-oriented missing-value prediction system rather than presenting only a model or theory. - Practical: The Qwen3 variants can run on commercially available GPUs, and the reported inference cost of $0.00148 per query for Auto-Fill-Qwen is compatible with large-scale services, although the three-specialist parallel pipeline and executable-code sandbox require production engineering. - Efficient: Auto-Fill-Qwen is reported at 0.00148 dollars per query, versus 0.0109 for o4-mini, 0.043 for Gemini 3 Pro, and 0.177 for o3-pro; however, the comparison excludes training, model serving, calibration maintenance, and non-LLM execution costs. - Effective: On the paper’s exact-match synthetic-masking task, the system achieves 0.628–0.656 recall while maintaining a measured precision target of 0.9, but this demonstrates selective prediction on a proxy rather than validated reduction of errors in live spreadsheets or downstream analytics. - Scalable: The method is tested on tables averaging 494 cells and on row-subsampled inputs, but it is not evaluated at 10x–100x table, query-volume, concurrency, or distribution-shift scale; joint missing cells and context pruning are explicitly left for future work. The work delivers a public software artifact through the GitHub repository https://github.com/lyrain2001/auto-fill, along with a benchmark suite described as 11 datasets; the paper does not establish that all proprietary data or trained model weights are publicly released. Strengths - It identifies a practically meaningful objective—maximize exact-match recall subject to high precision—and makes abstention central rather than treating every missing cell as answerable. - The specialist decomposition is supported by targeted ablations: all three specialists outperform every pairwise combination, while the coding specialist contributes near-perfect performance on relation benchmarks that text-only or statistical methods handle poorly. - The confidence design is technically differentiated by mode: token probabilities for direct completion, multi-sample teacher-derived confidence for reasoning, and execution-based reconstruction accuracy for code. This is more defensible than applying one verbal confidence prompt to all models. - The evaluation covers both ID and OOD sources, includes private enterprise tables and relation-focused datasets, and reports quality-cost trade-offs rather than accuracy alone. The residual error analysis also separates capability gaps, misrouting, and apparently unrecoverable cases. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors explicitly identify future work on jointly predicting interdependent missing cells and pruning context for large tables. They acknowledge that RL produces only modest gains and is expensive, that retrieval could improve long-tail factual lookup at additional cost, and that some cases are unrecoverable because the visible table and model knowledge do not determine the answer. Their error analysis reports 11 unrecoverable cases out of 100 sampled failures and identifies 10 misroutes, 52 knowledge-specialist failures, 23 reasoning-specialist failures, and 4 coding-specialist failures. They also recognize that coding patterns may contain legitimate outliers, motivating the 80% rather than 100% reconstruction criterion. Analyst-Identified Gaps - The central benchmark masks one observed cell in a complete table, which does not model realistic missingness mechanisms, multiple missing cells, missingness correlated with value or row type, corrupted schemas, or tables whose original ground truth is itself noisy. - Calibration and threshold selection may be optimistic because the method is calibrated on held-out ID cases from the same broad corpus family and then assessed with the same benchmark design; the paper does not report calibration drift, reliability confidence intervals, or threshold transfer across organizations. - The claim of precision at least 0.9 is supported through ranked-prefix metrics, but the paper does not provide per-dataset sample counts for accepted predictions, confidence intervals, or statistical tests, making it difficult to judge whether several small differences are meaningful. - The strongest performance is concentrated on deliberately relationship-rich Rel-AR, Rel-FD, and Rel-ST benchmarks, while the method remains substantially weaker on open-ended knowledge tables; the paper does not compare against retrieval-augmented web or enterprise search systems in the knowledge setting. - The system invokes all three specialists for every query, so the reported cost advantage may overstate the benefit of confidence-based routing relative to a cascade that cheaply detects deterministic formulas before invoking language models. - Generated Python code is executed against tables, but the paper does not evaluate sandbox security, resource limits, malicious table contents, denial-of-service behavior, or correctness under type and schema irregularities. - The method’s use of teacher-generated chain-of-thought traces and verbalized confidence inherits teacher errors and potentially unfaithful rationales; no faithfulness or robustness analysis tests whether the reasoning traces reflect the actual basis of predictions. - The paper compares against many current model names and reports API prices accessed in February 2026, but publication status, exact model versions, prompt templates, decoding settings for every baseline, and reproducible API configurations are not fully established in the provided text. Bottom Line This is a useful and technically credible systems paper for practitioners building selective spreadsheet or tabular-cleaning assistants, with strong evidence that calibrated specialist ensembles improve the quality-cost frontier, but its novelty is primarily in problem framing and integration and its deployment claims remain ahead of validation on naturally missing, jointly missing, and production-scale data.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces DataPrep-Bench, a downstream-grounded benchmark for evaluating LLM-based data construction and data-quality scoring across six domains and multiple base models, together with Data-Construction-Skill and the Distributional Alignment Score (DAS). - Why it's important: Training-data decisions are expensive and surface-level quality signals can recommend data that degrades downstream model performance. - How it does it: It holds raw sources, fine-tuning protocols, candidate pools, base models, and downstream evaluations fixed, then measures either the performance induced by constructed SFT data or the Pearson correlation between a dataset score and measured downstream utility. - The good: DAS achieves average correlations of 0.86 in Math, 0.77 in Medical, and 0.72 in Science, while Data-Construction-Skill raises Llama-3.1-8B Finance performance from 15.1 to 34.2 average points over the Dolly-only baseline. - The missing: The benchmark does not control construction-dataset size, report multiple training seeds or uncertainty intervals, or provide ablations that isolate which parts of the skill-guided agent produce its gains. - Read it or not: Researchers working on data-centric LLM training should read it for the benchmark and downstream-grounded findings, but should treat the DAS and construction-method rankings as provisional until larger candidate pools and repeated runs are evaluated.

Problem & Motivation LLM training and post-training increasingly depend on automatically prepared data, but existing construction and data-selection studies use different source corpora, generators, base models, fine-tuning recipes, and downstream tasks, making their results difficult to compare. The specific problem is to determine whether a method converts raw domain material into training data that improves a model, and whether a pre-training data-quality score predicts that improvement before fine-tuning is run. The target users are researchers and practitioners preparing instruction-tuning data for general, mathematical, scientific, medical, financial, and legal models. The benchmark addresses a gap in prior work by defining downstream training utility, rather than textual fluency, diversity, or judge scores, as the operational notion of data quality. Key Idea The central insight is to evaluate data preparation decisions only through their effect on downstream model performance, while separating two capabilities: construction from raw sources and prediction of candidate-dataset utility. For construction, the paper’s methodological idea is a reusable skill layer that exposes schemas, coverage requirements, filtering rules, and validation utilities to an agent. For evaluation, DAS treats a candidate dataset as useful when its embedding distribution is close to a domain proxy under Maximum Mean Discrepancy. The benchmark itself is the more consequential contribution; both proposed methods are relatively direct applications of agentic workflow control and distribution matching. Methodology DataPrep-Bench has two tracks. In the Data Construction Track, each method consumes the same domain source corpus, consisting mainly of long textbooks and technical materials converted to Markdown with MinerU. A method chunks the corpus and emits QA-style instruction-response pairs. Each resulting dataset is jointly fine-tuned with Dolly-15k on either Qwen2.5-7B or Llama-3.1-8B, using LlamaFactory for three epochs, learning rate 5 × 10^-6, cosine scheduling, 0.1 warmup, and a global batch size of 32; performance is averaged over domain-specific benchmark suites. Data-Construction-Skill uses an agentic, ReAct-style process: structure-aware chunking, relevance filtering, extraction of propositions, adaptive generation of concept, reasoning, and case/application QA pairs, then deduplication, grounding checks, removal of document-relative phrasing, coverage tracking, and resumable execution. Its key design decisions—explicit skill-level constraints, corpus-level coverage tracking, and post-generation validation—are plausible, but the paper does not isolate their individual effects. In the Data Quality Evaluation Track, candidate SFT datasets are scored before fine-tuning, and their scalar scores are compared with downstream performance after fine-tuning the same base model. DAS encodes up to 5,000 samples per dataset with Qwen3-Embedding-8B into 4,096-dimensional vectors, computes biased empirical MMD using a Gaussian RBF kernel with fixed bandwidth σ = 1.0 against one domain-specific proxy, and returns negative MMD so that higher scores indicate better alignment. Pearson correlation is the primary objective, with p < 0.05 used as a significance criterion. The use of a fixed encoder and kernel makes within-domain comparisons possible, but the encoder, proxy, bandwidth, sampling policy, and linear-correlation assumption are all critical unvalidated choices. Key Results The construction evaluation covers six domains and two base models, with direct prompting, DataFlow workflows, several agent backbones, and the skill-guided agent. Adding synthetic domain data to Dolly-15k often reduces performance: for Llama-3.1-8B, Dolly-only averages 11.7 in Math, 13.2 in Science, and 15.1 in Finance, while many constructed-data variants are lower. The strongest reported Data-Construction-Skill result is Llama-3.1-8B Finance, where the average rises to 34.2, a 19.1-point absolute improvement over Dolly-only; it is competitive or strong in some Medical and structured knowledge settings but performs poorly in Science, scoring 7.5 versus 13.2 for Dolly-only. On Qwen2.5-7B, DataFlow-Skill leads Finance at 64.8 and Law at 74.7, while agent methods generally perform well in Math and Medical. The comparison is not purely a quality comparison because generated dataset sizes range from 12,022–55,616 total samples for direct LLM methods, 35,699–410,170 for agents, and 745,407–849,293 for DataFlow variants; the authors intentionally treat yield as part of the method. For quality evaluation, DAS has average correlations of 0.68 in General Text, 0.86 in Math, 0.72 in Science, 0.77 in Medical, 0.18 in Finance, and 0.36 in Law across Qwen, Llama, and Mistral. It obtains correlations above 0.93 on two Math model cells and is the only metric reported to exceed 0.70 simultaneously in Math, Science, and Medical. Finance and Law remain difficult for all metrics. DAS takes 306.02 seconds per candidate dataset, compared with 459.37 seconds for BERTVendi and 434.99 seconds for Deita-Quality, but is much slower than simple lexical and n-gram heuristics. These results support the claim that distributional alignment can be predictive in some specialized domains, but they do not establish a universally reliable quality metric. Novelty Classification The contribution is primarily NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, and secondarily NEW METHOD and NEW SYSTEM/TOOL: the unified downstream-grounded protocol and released source, candidate, and ground-truth resources are the strongest novelty, while Data-Construction-Skill combines agentic processing with explicit reusable controls and DAS combines text embeddings with MMD against a proxy. The underlying mechanisms are standard combinations of agent workflows, validation rules, embeddings, kernels, and Pearson correlation rather than fundamentally new algorithms. Rigor & Reproducibility The paper releases source code at https://github.com/haolpku/Data-Preparation-Bench, datasets and a demo at https://huggingface.co/datasets/lhpku20010120/Data-Prep-Bench, and a benchmark website at https://datapreparationbench.github.io/; the skill is linked through the Clawhub repository. It fixes sources and training protocols for construction comparisons, evaluates DAS across three base-model families, includes 17 baseline operators plus DAS, reports p-values and sign consistency, and publishes candidate-level downstream records. However, no multiple random seeds, error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests for differences between methods are reported for the construction experiments. There are no ablations for skill components, chunking, validation, proxy selection, embedding choice, MMD bandwidth, or the 5,000-example sampling rule. Pearson correlations are estimated from only 8–14 candidates per domain, with particularly imbalanced Finance and Law pools containing one in-domain candidate and seven out-of-domain candidates; this creates low statistical power and makes correlation sensitive to individual points. The proxy datasets and downstream benchmarks are hand-selected, and the choice of Qwen3-Embedding-8B may favor distributional metrics that use the same representation family. The exclusion of gradient-based methods such as LESS is justified by cost and task assumptions, but it leaves out an important class of selection baselines. Unequal generated-data volumes confound data quality with quantity, so construction rankings cannot be interpreted as quality-only rankings. The paper is an arXiv preprint, not a peer-reviewed final publication, and several compared systems and models are themselves recent preprints or vendor models. Deployability (4-property check) Profile: EMPIRICAL and SYSTEMS, because the paper runs construction agents and fine-tuning experiments while releasing a benchmark, datasets, code, and a scoring implementation. - Practical: The methods can run on commercially available hardware, but construction relies on expensive external or large language models and the reported fine-tuning setup uses an 8×H20 GPU cluster; DAS also requires Qwen3-Embedding-8B inference and large-scale pairwise kernel computation. - Efficient: DAS requires about 306 seconds per candidate dataset in the reported setup, faster than BERTVendi and Deita-Quality but substantially slower than lexical, n-gram, FineWeb-Edu, and other cheap heuristics; construction cost is not reported in money, tokens, or wall-clock time. - Effective: Downstream evidence shows that DAS predicts utility well in Math, Science, and Medical and that Data-Construction-Skill helps Llama-3.1-8B Finance, but frequent regressions below Dolly-only and weak Finance/Law correlations limit the claim of general effectiveness. - Scalable: The benchmark tests 7B–8B base models, candidate pools of 8–14 datasets, and 5,000 sampled examples per candidate, but does not test 10×–100× larger candidate pools, models, source corpora, or training budgets; scalability beyond this scale is claimed through the released framework rather than demonstrated. The work delivers a reusable benchmark, raw-source corpus, candidate datasets, downstream ground-truth records, code, a skill-guided data-construction baseline, and a DAS implementation; it is not limited to a paper-only proposal. Strengths - The benchmark enforces a meaningful end-to-end target: methods are judged by the performance of models fine-tuned on their outputs rather than by surface-level QA quality or automatic judge scores. - It separates data construction from data-quality prediction and puts both under shared domain and downstream protocols, enabling analyses that prior case studies could not support. - The finding that synthetic domain data frequently harms performance is practically important and is supported by a controlled Dolly-only comparison, although the lack of repeated runs limits confidence in exact magnitudes. - DAS shows substantial cross-model correlation in Math, Science, and Medical, and the benchmark exposes domain-specific failure in Finance and Law instead of collapsing all results into a single aggregate leaderboard. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors explicitly acknowledge that Data-Construction-Skill underperforms in Science and some open-ended reasoning settings, that Finance and Law are difficult for every evaluated metric, and that those quality-evaluation pools are small and structurally imbalanced. They also state that the current candidate pools are an initial release and plan to expand them, and that DAS should be combined with reference-free quality or domain-aware signals. These limitations are confronted directly, although the discussion attributes one Science failure partly to the small candidate pool without quantifying its effect. Analyst-Identified Gaps - The construction experiment confounds sample quality, sample quantity, domain coverage, and training exposure because methods emit radically different numbers of examples and all are trained under the same three-epoch schedule; fixed-budget or matched-token comparisons are needed. - The absence of seeds and uncertainty estimates makes small differences in benchmark averages and Pearson correlations difficult to interpret, especially on candidate pools with fewer than ten datasets. - The DAS result may depend strongly on the selected proxy, Qwen3-Embedding-8B representation, fixed σ = 1.0, and candidate-pool composition; leave-one-proxy-out, encoder-transfer, bandwidth, and resampling analyses are missing. - The benchmark uses one proxy per domain and downstream suites that may share topical or stylistic properties with released SFT resources, but contamination and semantic overlap checks are not described in sufficient detail. - Data-Construction-Skill is compared as a Claude Opus 4.6 agent, so the reported skill effect is inseparable from that backbone, execution environment, generation budget, and stopping behavior; a same-backbone prompt-versus-skill ablation with matched token and sample budgets is needed. - The quality track evaluates linear Pearson association rather than the practical decision problem of selecting a dataset under a fixed budget; ranking metrics, top-k selection gains, calibration, and performance under distribution shift are not primary evaluations. Bottom Line This is a useful and potentially influential benchmark paper for data-centric LLM research, with a credible downstream-grounded framing and valuable released artifacts, but its method rankings and DAS claims should not be treated as definitive until the authors control data volume, add repeated trials and ablations, and expand the small, proxy-dependent candidate pools.

Problem & Motivation Agentic visual reasoning systems must choose between direct multimodal reasoning and tool-assisted reasoning such as cropping, annotation, image transformation, pixel computation, and numerical calculation. Existing systems often invoke tools indiscriminately or avoid them even when they are needed, causing extra computation, execution failures, and answer degradation. The paper identifies a gap in evaluation: aggregate accuracy does not reveal whether tools genuinely solve examples that tool-free reasoning cannot solve or instead introduce errors on examples already solvable without tools. It targets multimodal visual search, perception, chart, spatial, mathematical, diagrammatic, compositional, and agentic reasoning tasks. Key Idea The core insight is to treat tool use as a mode-selection problem with two separate objectives: use tools when tool-free reasoning is unreliable, and ensure that tool execution creates net capability gains rather than merely changing the reasoning trajectory. Beacon operationalizes this through group-level online labeling: if a rollout group contains a correct text-only response, correct text-only trajectories receive full reward and correct code trajectories receive partial reward; if no text-only response is correct, correct code trajectories receive full reward. A second mechanism supplies answer-free expert hints only to hard groups whose initial rollouts are all wrong, allowing RL to learn trajectories outside the policy's current capability distribution. Methodology Beacon follows an SFT-then-RL pipeline. First, the authors start from Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct and collect 212,353 examples from 16 public datasets spanning STEM, charts/OCR, perception, spatial reasoning, agentic tools, and general multimodal reasoning. They retain 15,705 difficult examples after five base-model rollouts and use Gemini 3.1 Pro to synthesize correct code-assisted trajectories, then refine or discard trajectories whose tool outputs are redundant, unused, malformed, or not causally helpful. SFT uses cross-entropy over structured trajectories containing tool calls, tool responses, observations, and answers; code output is masked during SFT, and some correct pure-text trajectories are added to avoid forcing tool use. In RL, the authors use GRPO with eight rollouts per prompt and a reward of 0.1 times format correctness plus 0.9 times the adaptive reward. The adaptive reward is 1 for correct text-only responses when any text-only response in the group is correct, 0.25 for correct code responses in that case, 1 for correct code responses when no text-only response is correct, and 0 otherwise. For all-wrong groups, Gemini 3.1 Pro generates a verified code-assisted trajectory, extracts an answer-free hint, and the policy re-rolls out with the hint; the resulting trajectories are optimized while the hint is removed from the policy input. Critical design decisions include the 0.25 partial reward, the group-conditioned online label rather than a fixed teacher label, and hint-guided exploration; the paper provides rationale for each, but does not systematically tune the reward coefficient, rollout size, or hint-generation budget. Key Results Beacon-8B reports 58.98% average accuracy across 13 benchmarks, compared with 56.67% for Metis-8B, 53.09% for the Qwen3-VL-8B base model, 48.58% for CodeV, 47.84% for Thyme, and 46.88% for DeepEyesV2. It ranks first among evaluated open-source models on 11 of 13 benchmarks and reports an average improvement of 6.07 points over Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct, although the two table-level category averages imply improvements of 5.48 and 6.76 points, respectively. On the high-resolution/spatial/perceptual group, Beacon averages 66.05% versus 64.57% for Metis and 60.57% for the base model; on quantitative/compositional/agentic tasks it averages 50.73% versus 47.46% for Metis and 43.97% for the base model. It reaches 89.00% on V*, 84.30% on HRBench 4K, 81.88% on HRBench 8K, 58.48% on ChartQAPro, 47.30% on GameQA, and 24.03% on TIRBench. Gemini 3.1 Pro remains substantially higher at 73.66% and 76.23% on the two grouped averages, so Beacon does not close the gap to the closed-source reference. On five diagnostic datasets, Beacon obtains 53.53% tool-available accuracy versus 51.57% tool-free accuracy, a +1.96-point accuracy change; its mean mode-adaptiveness score is 58.83%, with MAtool of 94.75% and MAtext of 22.91%, indicating strong tool invocation on text-hard cases but a substantial preference for tools even on text-easy cases. Tool-gain is 9.29%, tool-harm is 6.15%, and net tool effect is +3.14%, compared with approximately +0.04 to +1.74 points for the evaluated prior models. The ablation gives SFT alone 56.91% overall accuracy, SFT+GRPO 57.10%, SFT+GRPO+NAAR 57.75%, SFT+GRPO+HCE 57.62%, and the full method 58.98%; NAAR alone has the highest reported mean adaptiveness at 59.68%, while the full method has the highest overall accuracy and net tool effect. Approximately 40% of initially all-wrong groups are converted into groups with nonzero accuracy advantages through HCE. These results are promising but are mostly benchmark-level accuracy and diagnostic metrics rather than measurements of real execution efficiency. Novelty Classification NEW FORMULATION, NEW METHOD, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, and NEW SYSTEM/TOOL. The paper's most substantive novelty is the explicit decomposition of agentic visual reasoning into Mode Adaptiveness and Tool Effect, including multi-rollout definitions of text-easy/text-hard behavior, tool-gain, tool-harm, and text retention; the training method combines standard SFT, GRPO, reward shaping, and teacher-generated guidance, so its algorithmic novelty is incremental rather than a wholly new RL paradigm. Rigor & Reproducibility The paper includes component ablations for GRPO, NAAR, and HCE, detailed per-dataset diagnostic results, training dynamics, a failed-attempt analysis, and examples of tool trajectories and hints. It averages five inference runs for its main diagnostic metrics and uses fixed temperature 0.1, but it reports no error bars, confidence intervals, statistical tests, or multiple training seeds. The evaluation uses 13 benchmarks and compares against several recent open-source agentic models plus Gemini 3.1 Pro; however, some results are taken from original papers, availability differs across baselines, and the paper does not establish identical prompting, decoding, tool budgets, or training-data conditions for every comparison. Answers are judged by rule matching and, when that fails, Gemini 3.1 Pro or Gemini 3 Flash, introducing an unquantified evaluator-model dependency. Training data are filtered to remove stated test overlap, but the same broad public benchmark ecosystem supplies both data selection and evaluation, leaving potential distribution and contamination concerns. The reward and HCE mechanisms depend on Gemini 3.1 Pro-generated trajectories and hints, but there is no ablation against equally sized human or weaker-teacher data, no analysis of hint leakage beyond the stated answer-free constraint, and no test of robustness when the expert teacher is unavailable. The first page provides Code and Model icons, but no repository or model URL is stated in the parsed paper, so public release status is not verifiable from the document. Deployability (4-property check) Profile: EMPIRICAL. Practical: The 8B model can plausibly run on commercially available GPUs, but the complete inference system requires a sandboxed Python execution environment and permits up to 20 tool-call rounds in evaluation, so operational requirements are not fully characterized. Efficient: The paper motivates efficiency but does not measure latency, memory, energy, number of calls, token usage, or cost relative to text-only and competing agents; on the five diagnostic datasets Beacon invokes tools in roughly 70.65%–95.36% of responses, so practical efficiency is not established. Effective: Benchmark evidence shows a +1.96-point tool-available versus tool-free gain and a +3.14-point net tool-effect margin, but these metrics use a paper-defined solvability partition and do not directly measure real-world task completion or reliability under execution failures. Scalable: Training uses 64 NVIDIA H200 GPUs for one RL epoch, while inference is tested only with an 8B model and benchmark-sized tasks; behavior at 10×–100× workload, longer horizons, larger models, concurrent users, or more complex tool environments is not evaluated. The work delivers a trained model and an inference protocol, with code/model release links suggested on the first page but no explicit URL stated in the paper text. Strengths - The paper isolates a meaningful failure mode that aggregate accuracy conceals: existing agents may gain on tool-dependent examples while losing on examples that tool-free reasoning already solves. - The Mode Adaptiveness and Tool Effect metrics use five stochastic text-only rollouts and distinguish tool gain from tool harm, improving on a single-run binary solvability label. - NAAR addresses a real objective conflict: it discourages unnecessary code without assigning zero reward to correct tool-assisted solutions, and the ablation shows a sizeable increase in average adaptiveness from 56.30% with GRPO to 59.68% with GRPO+NAAR. - HCE targets sparse or zero-advantage RL groups rather than discarding them; the reported conversion of about 40% of all-wrong groups and the full-model improvement in net tool effect provide evidence that this mechanism contributes beyond ordinary GRPO. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The paper explicitly discusses a failed aggressive reward strategy that forced additional text-only rollouts. It reports that this caused the code-use ratio to collapse and degraded V* and HRBench performance because group labels reflected the best outcome across multiple attempts rather than the most reliable single-run mode. The authors also acknowledge, through their discussion of conventional RL with verifiable rewards, that capability expansion is difficult when the policy cannot discover successful trajectories. Broader deployment limitations, compute cost, tool-call latency, teacher dependence, and statistical uncertainty are not explicitly discussed. Analyst-Identified Gaps - The central adaptiveness labels are derived from whether one of five or eight stochastic rollouts succeeds, not from an independently established task-level necessity or expected-cost optimum; this can make MA and NAAR sensitive to rollout count and group composition. - Beacon has MAtext of only 22.91% and uses tools for roughly 70%–95% of diagnostic responses, so the evidence supports strong hard-case tool invocation more clearly than genuinely efficient conditional tool use. - No tool-call count, trajectory length, execution-error rate, wall-clock latency, or compute-cost analysis tests the paper's efficiency motivation or distinguishes useful calls from merely successful final answers. - The full method combines SFT data synthesis, trajectory refinement, NAAR, HCE, and extensive Gemini supervision; the ablations isolate NAAR and HCE but do not isolate data volume, teacher quality, refinement, pure-text injection, or the effects of training-data composition. - Results are reported without training-seed variation, uncertainty estimates, or significance tests, and several baselines rely on results reported in their original papers, limiting confidence in small differences such as the 0.62-point MathVista gain. - The paper does not compare against strong adaptive-tool baselines under a matched training-data and compute budget, nor against a simple learned tool-use classifier, a cost-regularized reward, or best-of-N routing using the same Qwen3-VL base model. - The evaluation depends partly on Gemini-based semantic judging and on benchmarks that overlap conceptually with the model's source-data ecosystem; the paper states that test overlap is removed but does not provide a complete auditable contamination analysis. Bottom Line This is a worthwhile preprint for multimodal-reasoning researchers because its adaptiveness/tool-effect framing and hint-assisted RL recipe expose and partially address a real weakness of agentic VLMs, but the lack of cost measurements, uncertainty analysis, matched controls, and deployment-scale evaluation prevents the reported benchmark gains from establishing a robust practical advantage.

Problem & Motivation The paper addresses how to measure whether AI agents can conduct genuinely open-ended AI research: selecting and refining hypotheses, deciding what evidence is sufficient, recognizing when an approach has failed, changing direction, and producing a defensible contribution. Existing evaluations largely use narrow, automatically verifiable objectives such as benchmark scores, code execution, or model performance, while end-to-end paper-generation studies often rely on noisy and underscrutinized blind peer review. The authors argue that neither setting adequately tests whether an agent can answer an ambiguous research question that has no known metric or reference solution. The practical users are AI researchers, labs forecasting AI-driven R&D acceleration, and evaluators of frontier-agent capabilities. The proposed gap is an evaluation protocol that preserves open-endedness while giving reviewers with deep task-specific expertise access to the agent’s complete output and trajectory. Key Idea The core insight is to evaluate an agent by having it “shadow” a real, unpublished research project: provide only the central question from a high-quality unpublished paper, prevent access to the original authors’ methods and findings, and ask those authors to assess the agent’s resulting work as a conference submission. This creates a task with an authentic research standard and an uncontaminated question, while replacing anonymous, time-constrained peer review with expert review from people who spent months addressing the same problem. The paper’s substantive behavioral insight is that agents can execute many research-engineering operations but fail at higher-level project control: they prematurely narrow the question, treat weak negative evidence as decisive, fail to backtrack, misallocate resources, and drift from explicit instructions. Methodology The study uses two unpublished NeurIPS 2026 research questions: decomposing and controlling LLM personas through weight-space interventions, and designing a deployment-time detector for harmful distribution shift in tabular prior-fitted networks such as TabPFN. The main runs use Claude Opus 4.8 with extra-high reasoning in the OpenClaw scaffold. Each agent receives the research question without the source paper or findings, a Linux VM on AWS, the open web, GPU resources, a six-day/120-hour nominal deadline plus a 24-hour extension, $3,000 in Anthropic API credits, and access to subagents and three external AI-review tools. The agent must conduct literature review, formulate hypotheses, implement and run experiments, solicit reviews, revise the work, and produce a conference-style paper. The authors analyze logs, code, resource trajectories, intermediate reviews, and final manuscripts; the original paper authors score the outputs on a 1–6 conference-review scale. Two pilot runs use Opus 4.8 without reasoning, while a robustness run applies GPT-5.6 Sol Ultra through Codex to the TabPFN question. Critical design decisions include using unpublished tasks to reduce training-data contamination, using original authors as expert evaluators, and using general-purpose rather than task-specific scaffolds. The first two choices directly support the stated evaluation goal, but non-blind author review and the highly limited task sample weaken causal and external validity. The paper does not specify a formal objective or optimization loss because the agent performs an open-ended workflow rather than training a new algorithm. Key Results Both main agent-generated papers were rejected by their original authors: the Personas paper received 2/6 overall and the TabPFN paper 1/6, with reviewer confidence of 4/5 and 5/5 respectively. The reviewers cited unprincipled data and experiment choices, unsupported conclusions, limited originality, and unclear writing. The agents produced some minor findings that interested the authors and completed hundreds of experiments, literature reviews, GPU operations, debugging, external-review retrieval, and LaTeX compilation without human help. However, both agents used less than half of their available API budget: the Personas run spent $1,130 of $3,000 and the TabPFN run $1,235 of $3,000; the agents also completed major exploration phases after approximately 5 hours and roughly 40 hours earlier than planned, respectively. Across 15 self-review rounds, the agents never received an acceptance verdict, yet they made mostly incremental revisions rather than abandoning their core approaches. The agents’ self-reviews usually rated the papers as “Weak Reject,” whereas the human experts judged them unambiguous rejects; two external Stanford reviews reportedly recommended acceptance despite the human assessments. In the robustness run with GPT-5.6 Sol Ultra and Codex, the agent again failed to run adequately powered experiments or produce a novel contribution, exhausted the $3,000 token budget in just over two days, and left nearly 100 hours remaining, although it did use a real-world shifted dataset and maintained accurate reporting of negative findings. The paper reports no conventional accuracy, F1, speedup, or statistical-significance headline because the dependent variable is expert assessment of open-ended research quality. The main qualitative finding is a five-part failure pattern: poor judgment about the publication bar, uncreative responses to criticism, ineffective project-level backtracking, poor resource awareness, and instruction drift. Novelty Classification NEW EVALUATION METHOD; NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING; NEW PROBLEM FORMULATION. The genuinely new contribution is the shadow-evaluation protocol for assessing open-ended AI R&D with uncontaminated research questions and task-specific expert grading, together with early trajectory evidence that frontier agents can automate research engineering but not reliably perform high-level scientific judgment. The underlying agent components—LLM planning, subagents, web tools, GPU execution, automated review, and paper generation—are standard combinations rather than new algorithms, and the empirical conclusion remains preliminary because it comes from two core case studies. Rigor & Reproducibility The paper provides unusually extensive process evidence for an open-world agent evaluation: full expert reviews, pre-experiment survey responses, agent repositories, logs, resource trajectories, and reproduction materials at https://cruxevals.com. It documents human interventions, including an OpenClaw bug fix, a 24-hour deadline extension, and a readability rewrite, and it includes pilot runs plus a second model/scaffold robustness experiment. The logs support the reported failure modes, and the human experts’ detailed criticisms overlap with problems visible in the agents’ own reviews. However, the study has no meaningful statistical inference, error bars, inter-rater reliability, blinded independent evaluation, or controlled human baseline. The main evidence consists of two tasks and two primary runs using the same model family and scaffold; the robustness check covers only one task and uses a different budget-consumption profile. The original authors’ reviews are necessarily non-blind and may favor their own framing or penalize AI-generated work. The agents were also informed that they were being evaluated under a NeurIPS rubric, which may affect behavior. The paper acknowledges most of these concerns, but the evaluation cannot establish that the observed failures are model-level limitations rather than interactions among task selection, scaffold design, time budgeting, prompt design, and author-specific standards. Deployability (4-property check) Profile: EMPIRICAL. Practical: The evaluated workflow can run on commercially available cloud VMs and GPUs, but the reported setup required approximately $3,000 in API credits plus GPU resources and a custom scaffold, and it encountered repeated harness failures. Efficient: The agents completed substantial engineering work but used only about 38% and 41% of the stated API budgets in the two main runs, so the evidence shows poor resource utilization rather than an efficiency advantage over human researchers or other agents. Effective: The evidence supports the narrower claim that these runs produced rejected papers while completing research engineering; it does not establish that agents generally cannot answer open-ended research questions or that the five identified failure modes are necessary properties of current frontier models. Scalable: The work was tested over roughly six days and two research questions, with one cross-model replication, but it did not test 10×–100× more tasks, longer projects, stronger models, larger scaffolds, or substantially different domains. The work delivers a reproducible evaluation protocol, released logs and repositories, and the OpenClaw-based CRUX scaffold rather than a production research-agent system or trained model. Strengths - The shadow-evaluation design targets an important measurement gap: it tests ambiguous, long-horizon research while avoiding direct contamination from the original paper’s public methods and findings. - The paper combines outcome evaluation with full-trajectory analysis, allowing it to distinguish research-engineering competence from judgment, exploration, feedback use, and project management. - The evidence is unusually transparent for an agent capability claim: the authors release reviews, surveys, repositories, logs, and resource traces, and explicitly document interventions and possible biases. - The cross-scaffold/model run reproduces several failures, including underpowered experimentation, lack of novelty, budget mismanagement, and instruction problems, which weakens—but does not eliminate—the explanation that OpenClaw alone caused the result. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors explicitly acknowledge the sample size of only five total runs, including pilots, two main runs, and one robustness check; non-blind review by the original authors; selection of only two empirical research questions; scaffold and model limitations; evaluation awareness; interpretive ambiguity in labeling failures as creativity, judgment, or epistemic lock-in; and the lack of an objective ground truth. They also acknowledge that the two tasks may not represent incremental research, theoretical work, or research that can be reduced to hill-climbing objectives, and that open-world evaluation involves substantial researcher discretion. They discuss possible bias from the core team’s views on recursive self-improvement, release artifacts for scrutiny, and state that stronger models, vendor scaffolds, and larger follow-up studies are needed. This candor is a material strength, although the paper still sometimes draws broader implications than the two-case evidence directly supports. Analyst-Identified Gaps - The study does not include a human-researcher control under the same six-day, compute, API, and information constraints, so it cannot quantify how unusual the agents’ performance is relative to competent researchers or research assistants. - The original authors are the sole substantive evaluators for the two main tasks, and the paper does not report blinded independent ratings, inter-rater agreement, or an adjudication procedure; this leaves the magnitude of the rejection effect uncertain even if the papers were plainly weak to the participating authors. - The task-selection process is not operationalized enough to establish representativeness: two unpublished NeurIPS submissions selected by collaborators may overrepresent particular styles of empirical ML research and particular author expectations. - The qualitative coding of logs into five failure modes lacks a formal coding protocol, independent coders, agreement statistics, or a preregistered taxonomy, making it difficult to separate observed behavior from post hoc interpretation. - The study does not isolate model capability from scaffold and prompt quality through factorial comparisons of models, reasoning levels, budget allocations, exploration gates, review policies, and restart mechanisms; the single robustness run is insufficient for that attribution. - The paper infers that additional wall-clock time would probably not help, but neither main run exhausted its API budget and both received human deadline extensions, so the effect of substantially different budget scheduling or explicit human-like project management remains unevaluated. - The claim that AI review could serve as a useful verifier is underdetermined: all evaluated papers were poor, so the experiments measure rejection behavior but cannot establish verifier calibration, selectivity, or ability to distinguish good from merely plausible research. Bottom Line This is a valuable and unusually transparent early evaluation of autonomous AI research, worth reading for its shadow-evaluation protocol and failure analysis, but its evidence supports only a cautious case-study conclusion—not a general verdict that frontier agents cannot conduct open-ended AI research.

ACE-Data-0: Human-Centric Ambient Capture as Embodied Data Engine (34 ▲ )

Yukang Cao, Haozhe Xie, Beichen Wen, Runmao Yao, Yinghao Liu, Yue Huang, Zhichao Liao, Yunxiang Wang, Haiheng Liu, Xingshun Tian, Dawei Su, Long Zhuo, Dacheng Tao, Xiaogang Wang, Liang Pan, Ziwei Liu · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 31 Jul 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces the Ambient Capture Engine (ACE) and releases ACE-Data-0, a synchronized multimodal dataset of household human-object and human-scene interactions with egocentric/exocentric video, motion capture, object trajectories, audio, tactile pressure, and annotations. - Why it's important: Embodied-AI systems lack data that jointly records perception, body motion, object state, contact, and long-horizon behavior in realistic domestic environments rather than isolated laboratory clips. - How it does it: ACE combines table-scale and room-scale sensor installations with an OptiTrack-referenced synchronization and calibration pipeline, then assigns goal-level household tasks to participants so that diverse action sequences emerge without fixed scripts. - The good: The dataset unifies 150+ hours, 17M frames, 75,000+ episodes, 50 participants, 200 task categories, synchronized first- and third-person views, metric human/object motion, and tactile supervision in a single physical timeline. - The missing: The paper does not demonstrate that ACE-Data-0 improves robot policy learning, world modeling, or vision-language-action performance, and the benchmark uses only existing pretrained models without training, ablations, uncertainty estimates, or deployment experiments. - Read it or not: Researchers working on embodied perception, egocentric hand/body reconstruction, vision-to-touch prediction, or multimodal human demonstrations should read it for the capture design and data resource; readers seeking a new learning algorithm or evidence of robot-level impact can skip it.
