The dataset and capture design provide meaningful Novelty (72) and Non-Obviousness (68), particularly through synchronized room-scale and table-scale sensing with tactile and metric state supervision. Rigor (65) and Resilience (60) are limited by the absence of downstream robot-learning experiments, uncertainty and dropout analyses, participant- or environment-disjoint validation, ablations, and statistical testing, despite detailed calibration reporting. Problem & Motivation: Embodied AI needs observations that connect visual appearance with the physical state and consequences of action: body and hand kinematics, object motion, contact, sound, and task progression. Existing resources generally trade off naturalistic scale against physical supervision: egocentric datasets provide long and varied behavior but lack metric body/object state and synchronized external views, while motion-capture HOI datasets provide accurate geometry but use laboratory or tabletop settings, omit tactile sensing, and usually contain short atomic interactions. The target domain is household activity involving manipulation, locomotion, furniture interaction, and multi-step goals. The paper argues that the missing resource is a synchronized, spatially registered perception-action record in a furnished home, although its claim that no existing dataset satisfies the full combination is comparative rather than independently established beyond the cited dataset table. Key Idea: The central insight is to treat synchronized multisensory capture—not an individual modality or annotation—as the basic unit of embodied data. ACE resolves the conflict between fine manipulation coverage and room-scale locomotion by using two complementary configurations: dense close-range sensing around a table and wide-baseline sensing across a furnished apartment. Goal-level instructions, rather than step-by-step scripts, are used to induce variation in ordering, routes, object choices, hesitation, and recovery. The synchronization and calibration procedures are technically important, but the conceptual contribution is primarily a new dataset/capture paradigm rather than a new inference algorithm. Methodology: ACE records four 1088×1280 egocentric fisheye streams at 20 FPS, eight 1920×1080 exocentric streams at 30 FPS, 60-Hz optical motion capture, articulated hand sensing, full-palm tactile pressure, IMU data, and multichannel audio. The room-scale setup covers an approximately 200 m² furnished apartment with eight ZED cameras and 12 OptiTrack cameras; the table-scale setup covers a 30 m² workspace with eight GoPro cameras and 16 OptiTrack cameras. The OptiTrack clock provides the temporal reference. Room-scale RGB streams share a hardware trigger and are aligned to motion capture through a displayed QR-code clock; egocentric streams use a deliberate clock glance; table-scale GoPro streams are aligned through audio and then connected to the common clock; tactile gloves are aligned to the headset using correlated IMU motion. Static exocentric cameras are calibrated through an ArUco board carrying retroreflective markers, while moving egocentric cameras use marker-based rig tracking and hand-eye calibration with bundle adjustment. Objects receive scanned or 2D Gaussian-splat meshes and marker-based 6-DoF trajectories; participants wear a 41-marker body suit, Manus gloves for room-scale hand motion, and tactile gloves. The collection pipeline creates atomic HOI takes of roughly three minutes, 20–30-minute chains of HOI tasks, and approximately five-minute human-scene-interaction takes. Derived annotations include poses, projections, boxes, object trails, contact maps, audio alignment, and language descriptions generated by Gemini-3.1-pro-preview and manually checked. Critical design decisions—two spatial scales, measured rather than image-estimated camera/body/object states, and goal-level task specification—are well motivated for coverage and physical fidelity, but the paper does not quantify the relative contribution of each choice through controlled comparisons. Key Results: ACE-Data-0 contains more than 150 hours, 17M video frames, 75,000+ episodes, 200+ task categories, 50 participants, two environments, and more than 50 tracked object instances; the frame distribution is 6.2M atomic-HOI frames (36.5%), 7.3M chain-of-HOI frames (42.9%), and 3.5M human-scene-interaction frames (20.6%). The authors hold out 10 hours for testing. Calibration reports median held-out reprojection errors below 3 pixels for exocentric cameras and about 2 pixels for egocentric cameras; synchronization residuals are reported at the millisecond level, with re-estimated offsets under 4 ms. On tactile-from-egocentric-video prediction, PressureVision obtains temporal accuracy 0.0093, contact IoU 0.0007, volumetric IoU 0.0000, and center-of-pressure error 10.9807; EgoPressureDiff obtains 0.2912, 0.0197, 0.0025, and 8.5152; TouchAnything is best at 0.7095, 0.1646, 0.1357, and 6.5846, respectively. For full-body motion from single-view exocentric video, the best listed temporal method, SMPLest-X, reports PA-MPJPE 55.7 mm, MPJPE 58.8 mm, and PVE 67.6 mm, while its world-frame trajectory metric is not reported; Human3R has the best listed scene-aware world-frame error at 180.2 mm. Egocentric body methods are substantially worse, with EgoAllo reporting MPJPE 147.9 mm and WA-MPJPE 252.2 mm. For egocentric hand reconstruction, WildHands achieves PA-MPJPE 11.2 mm, MPJPE 12.6 mm, F@15 0.774, and AUCJ 0.776, while Dyn-HaMR and HaWoR report world-trajectory errors of 98.2 mm and 102.1 mm. For exocentric hands, WiLoR reaches PA-MPJPE 9.1 mm, MPJPE 9.9 mm, F@5 0.313, and AUCJ 0.819; HaPTIC reports a 63.0 mm trajectory error. The results support the narrower claim that current methods degrade under occlusion, contact ambiguity, egomotion, and long temporal horizons. They do not establish downstream gains in imitation learning, control, world models, or VLA systems. Baselines are mostly recent and include methods from 2024–2026, but the comparisons are inference-only evaluations using released checkpoints rather than retrained models optimized for ACE-Data-0. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK, NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, and ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION, with a secondary NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING classification. The genuinely new contribution is the released, physically synchronized combination of home-scale and tabletop capture, egocentric/exocentric views, motion, object trajectories, audio, and tactile sensing plus a three-level diagnostic benchmark; the underlying sensors, optical motion capture, hand-eye calibration, camera synchronization, pose representations, and evaluated perception models are established techniques combined and engineered for this setting. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper provides detailed hardware, synchronization, calibration, task, and annotation procedures and links a project page at https://ace-data-engine.github.io/ACE-Data-0/ and a Hugging Face dataset at https://huggingface.co/datasets/ACERobotics/ACE-Data-0. It reports held-out calibration errors and a 10-hour test split, and evaluates 3 tactile, 22 body-motion, and 3 or 5 hand-motion baselines depending on viewpoint. However, it reports no multiple-seed experiments, error bars, statistical significance tests, annotation inter-rater agreement, sensor-level uncertainty, missing-data rates, per-participant or per-environment split analysis, or ablations of synchronization, calibration, modalities, task design, or scale. Most labels are measured or projected from tracked states, but tactile glove accuracy, optical-marker tracking failures, hand-ground-truth coverage, and the reliability of the Gemini-generated temporal descriptions are not quantitatively validated. The table-scale hand ground truth is triangulated and manually refined rather than directly glove-measured, and evaluation masks joints visible in too few views, which may remove the hardest cases. The paper also does not specify whether participant, task, object, and environment identities are disjoint across training and test data, leaving possible leakage and generalization concerns. It is an arXiv v1 preprint dated 30 July 2026, not a peer-reviewed publication according to the supplied document. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS, because the work builds a capture infrastructure and releases a dataset, while also running empirical benchmark evaluations. - Practical: The learning baselines can run on conventional research hardware, but reproducing ACE requires specialized OptiTrack systems, 24 RGB cameras across configurations, motion-capture suits, Manus and tactile gloves, trusses, marked objects, dedicated recording hosts, and instrumented environments; the paper does not report end-to-end capture cost or operational throughput. - Efficient: The system produces approximately 1 TB of raw data per recording hour and uses substantial sensing and storage infrastructure, so it is materially more expensive than camera-only alternatives; no compute, bandwidth, annotation, or maintenance comparison is reported. - Effective: The benchmark demonstrates that existing perception methods encounter measurable failures on contact, occlusion, egomotion, and long sequences, but it does not measure whether the released data improves task success, policy quality, transfer to robots, or any other direct embodied-AI objective. - Scalable: The paper claims a scalable data-engine paradigm but tests only two sites, 50 participants, 200 task categories, and one 10-hour held-out evaluation; it provides no 10×–100× scale study, cross-site generalization experiment, or evidence that marker-based tracking and object preparation remain tractable at larger deployment scale. The work delivers a public dataset and associated capture/data-processing resource; it does not deliver a robot policy, learning library, or demonstrated deployed control system. Strengths: - The synchronized combination of egocentric video, multi-view exocentric video, measured full-body and hand motion, object 6-DoF state, audio, and tactile pressure addresses a real supervision gap that most prior datasets leave fragmented. - The two-scale design is a concrete response to incompatible sensing requirements: close-range capture supports dexterous contact, while room-scale capture preserves locomotion and furniture occlusion in furnished domestic scenes. - The benchmark reveals diagnostically distinct failure modes rather than collapsing performance into a single task score: tactile models detect contact more readily than pressure location, body estimators recover local pose more accurately than global trajectories, and fixed exocentric views outperform moving egocentric views for world-space hand motion. - The calibration workflow is unusually explicit for a dataset paper, including a QR-code optical clock, marker-bridged camera calibration without camera co-visibility, measured headset pose, and reported pixel/millisecond residuals. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state that ACE covers only two sites and therefore has limited variation in layouts, furnishings, and lighting; ground truth is restricted to instrumented entities, with tracked objects requiring advance scanning and marker attachment; articulated mechanism state, fluids, and deformable materials are not annotated; and suits, gloves, headsets, and markers remain visible and may create dataset-specific visual cues. They also leave object-pose benchmarking to future work because they identify too few applicable methods. These limitations are directly acknowledged, although the paper does not quantify their effect on model performance or generalization. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The benchmark does not include the most consequential downstream validation: no imitation-learning, policy-learning, robot-retargeting, world-model, VLA, or task-success experiment uses ACE-Data-0. The two environments and instrumented object set may permit memorization of layouts, appearances, object identities, or capture artifacts, but the paper does not establish participant-, object-, task-, or environment-disjoint splits or cross-site transfer. The reported dataset scale is large in frames but modest in independent environments and participants, and 75,000 episodes are segmented within continuous takes, so episode count may overstate independent behavioral diversity. The paper does not report participant demographics, consent-release details beyond a general statement, demographic balance, or whether all participants completed the same tasks in comparable conditions. It also does not quantify tracking dropouts, marker occlusion, tactile sensor calibration, hand-label accuracy, language-label correction rates, or the proportion of sequences with complete modalities. The comparison against official pretrained checkpoints may measure domain shift rather than the achievable performance after ACE-specific training, and the absence of trained baselines makes the benchmark less informative about dataset utility. Finally, the claim that the corpus is scalable is not supported by cost, throughput, or expansion experiments, and direct tactile sensing may make the proposed vision-to-touch task less representative of deployed robots whose camera and tactile geometries differ from the glove setup. Bottom Line: ACE-Data-0 is a valuable and technically well-specified multimodal capture resource for embodied-perception research, but its importance currently rests on the quality and availability of the dataset rather than demonstrated improvement in robot learning or real-world control.

CLBench-V: Evaluating Multimodal Context Learning from Grounding to Knowledge Acquisition (40 ▲ )

Lai Wei, Chengqi Li, Jiapeng Li, Ruina Hu, Yue Wang, Weiran Huang · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 30 Jul 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces CLBench-V, a 3,443-instance multimodal context-learning benchmark that organizes tasks into context grounding, new-information application, and new-knowledge learning. - Why it's important: Multimodal systems increasingly need to use information from unseen documents, figures, tables, maps, and reports rather than relying only on parametric knowledge, yet existing context-learning evaluations are predominantly textual. - How it does it: It converts public multimodal benchmarks and constructs medical-paper and financial-report tasks under a unified inference and scoring framework, then diagnoses errors by capability level and failure type. - The good: Across six recent multimodal models, the best overall score is only 0.2847, and the level-wise divergence—InternVL3.5-30B-A3B leading grounding and knowledge learning while Qwen3.5-Plus leads information application—supports the claim that multimodal context use is not a single capability. - The missing: The benchmark lacks repeated-seed variability, confidence intervals, strong human-validated calibration for LLM judges, and controlled experiments establishing that its three levels measure distinct capabilities rather than mixtures of perception, reasoning, domain knowledge, and format compliance. - Read it or not: Benchmark designers and researchers studying multimodal long-context reasoning should read it for its taxonomy and task collection, while practitioners seeking a deployment method can skip it because it contributes evaluation infrastructure rather than a model or algorithm.

Problem & Motivation Real-world multimodal tasks require systems to extract task-specific evidence from documents, scientific figures, financial reports, maps, sports scenes, web pages, and multiple images, then apply or generalize that evidence. Existing context-learning benchmarks primarily test textual contexts, while multimodal and long-context benchmarks often emphasize retrieval, perception, document understanding, or multi-image reasoning without isolating whether a model found evidence, applied newly supplied values, or learned context-defined rules and conclusions. CLBench-V addresses this diagnostic gap by treating multimodal context learning as a progression from grounding evidence, through applying new information, to acquiring new knowledge. The target users are researchers evaluating multimodal large language models and developers diagnosing failures in document-centric or evidence-grounded systems. Key Idea The central insight is to classify context-learning tasks by what the supplied context contributes: L0 Context Grounding requires locating and binding evidence; L1 New Information Application requires using context-specific facts, values, or cases with otherwise familiar reasoning; and L2 New Knowledge Learning requires inducing and transferring rules, procedures, empirical patterns, or conclusions defined only by the context. This hierarchy provides a more interpretable alternative to a single aggregate score, although the levels are cumulative in practice and are not experimentally shown to be independent. Methodology CLBench-V normalizes two sources of data into a common model-input, metadata, answer-extraction, and evaluation interface. The integrated public portion includes ReasonMap-Short/Long/Plus, InSight-O3, ZeroBench, CourtSI, MIRBench, Pix2Fact, MMLongBench-Pic, BrowseComp-V3, PRISMM-Bench, and an image-rendered CL-Bench table subset; the newly constructed portion includes 206 financial-report ROE instances and 581 medical-paper conclusion-inference instances. Candidate public examples are filtered using visual-dependency, low-irrelevant-context, multi-hop, and scope-exclusion criteria, with Qwen3.5-Plus used as a primary automated inspector followed by manual review. Financial-report instances require extracting net income, revenue, total assets, and equity from converted reports and applying the DuPont identity, ROE = net profit margin × asset turnover × equity multiplier. Paper-conclusion instances provide content before the Results section and ask models to generate 4–8 findings, scored as max(0, (Nhit − Nextra) / Nref). Structured tasks use option extraction, exact or tolerance-based numeric matching, route-topology validation, or task-specific metrics; open-ended tasks use extracted answers and LLM judges. Important design choices include the three-level capability assignment, automated filtering to reduce shortcut-solvable examples, and hybrid deterministic/LLM evaluation. The taxonomy and evaluator choices are motivated, but the paper does not provide controlled ablations showing the effect of filtering, level assignment, prompt design, or conversion format. Key Results The benchmark contains 3,443 instances: 2,137 primarily L0, 629 primarily L1, 826 primarily L2 or boundary cases under the table’s dataset counts and assignments, with MIRBench and PRISMM-Bench treated as boundary datasets in aggregation. Six models are evaluated: InternVL3.5-30B-A3B, Qwen3.6-27B, Qwen3.5-Plus, Doubao-Seed-2.0-Lite, Kimi-K2.6, and GPT-5.4. InternVL3.5-30B-A3B obtains the highest weighted overall score, 0.2847, and leads L0 at 0.3080 and L2 at 0.3536; Qwen3.5-Plus leads L1 at 0.2954, narrowly ahead of Qwen3.6-27B at 0.2878. The remaining overall scores are 0.1991 for Kimi-K2.6, 0.1958 for Qwen3.6-27B, 0.1894 for GPT-5.4, 0.1862 for Qwen3.5-Plus, and 0.1850 for Doubao-Seed-2.0-Lite. Dataset-level leadership is heterogeneous: Kimi-K2.6 leads all three ReasonMap subsets; Qwen3.6-27B leads InSight-O3 at 0.5724, Pix2Fact at 0.2941, and CL-Bench-Table at 0.0938; Qwen3.5-Plus leads MMLongBench-Pic at 0.3621 and PRISMM-Bench at 0.5061; GPT-5.4 leads BrowseComp-V3 at 0.2105, CourtSI at 0.1783, and Financial Report ROE at 0.1262; and InternVL3.5-30B-A3B leads Paper Conclusion at 0.4120 and MIRBench at 0.4807. InternVL3.5-30B-A3B scores 0.0000 on Financial Report ROE because its run exceeded the maximum context length, illustrating an operational failure rather than task accuracy alone. Judge choice materially changes semantic-task scores: Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct has an average of 0.2122 across two prediction sets, versus 0.1564 for Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct. For Qwen3.6-27B, token length is nearly uncorrelated with score (Pearson r = −0.0042; Spearman rho = 0.0500), while image count is weakly negative (Pearson r = −0.0756; Spearman rho = −0.0739); for InternVL3.5-30B-A3B, correlations change after excluding overlong financial reports, suggesting context-limit effects dominate simple length trends. These results are preliminary benchmark measurements, not evidence that the proposed hierarchy causally explains model behavior. Novelty Classification The contribution is primarily a NEW BENCHMARK, NEW FORMULATION, and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, with a secondary NEW DATASET contribution through financial-report ROE and medical-paper conclusion tasks. The genuinely distinctive element is the explicit L0/L1/L2 multimodal context-learning formulation and its use to organize heterogeneous tasks diagnostically; most individual task formats, model evaluations, conversion procedures, and automatic filtering components combine existing ideas rather than introduce new algorithms. Rigor & Reproducibility The paper reports deterministic evaluators where possible, publishes task counts and prompts, describes the data-conversion and filtering pipeline, includes failure case studies, and states that code is available at https://github.com/IamLihua/CLBench-V. It promises release of data, documentation, provenance, and evaluation scripts, but the supplied text does not establish whether the full data, model outputs, judge prompts, or processed files are already publicly released. No ablations, multiple random seeds, error bars, confidence intervals, statistical significance tests, inter-annotator agreement, or human-versus-LLM judge validation are reported. The use of Qwen3.5-Plus as an automated candidate inspector may introduce model-dependent selection bias, while the use of Qwen3.6-27B as the primary judge and the large score shifts across judges make several headline results evaluator-dependent. The benchmark combines heterogeneous source datasets with different annotation styles, metrics, and difficulty distributions; sample-weighted aggregation therefore reflects dataset composition as much as capability. The evaluation also includes a model run that exceeded context limits, and some models are proprietary or have unspecified inference settings, limiting exact reproducibility. There is no systematic leakage audit beyond selecting recent medical papers, and no comparison against text-only, image-only, or retrieval-augmented baselines to quantify the multimodal and context-learning increments. Deployability (4-property check) Profile: SYSTEMS — the paper delivers a benchmark and evaluation framework, although it does not evaluate deployment in a production environment. Practical: The benchmark can run on commercially available hardware or through model APIs, but the paper does not report the hardware, inference cost, latency, or memory requirements for its models and long-document inputs. Efficient: Efficiency is not evaluated; inputs range from short visual tasks to financial reports exceeding 128k tokenizer tokens, and the paper provides no throughput or cost comparison against alternative evaluation pipelines. Effective: The low measured scores and interpretable failure examples show that the benchmark exposes weaknesses in evidence binding, context-specific value use, and context-defined knowledge induction, but the paper does not establish that performance predicts success on real operational tasks rather than benchmark-specific proxies. Scalable: The framework scales in dataset size through automated construction and filtering, but model-side scalability is unresolved: financial reports include 135 examples in the 64k–128k bucket and 70 above 128k, and one evaluated model exceeded its maximum context length; no 10×–100× stress test or scaling-law analysis is reported. The work delivers a software artifact consisting of a benchmark/evaluation codebase and, subject to the stated release, datasets and evaluation scripts; it does not deliver a trained model, inference algorithm, or deployable application. Strengths - The L0/L1/L2 hierarchy gives researchers a useful vocabulary for separating evidence access, context-specific application, and context-defined knowledge acquisition, which are often conflated in multimodal evaluations. - The benchmark covers unusually varied multimodal contexts, including scientific figures, financial reports, long documents, maps, sports scenes, web-style evidence, and multi-image inputs, rather than concentrating on one document or VQA format. - The paper reports concrete evidence of capability specialization: the best model changes by level and dataset, and no model dominates across the 14 listed components. - The explicit judge comparison and failure taxonomy acknowledge that evaluation reliability and error localization are part of the benchmark problem rather than treating scores as automatically trustworthy. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors explicitly acknowledge heterogeneous annotation styles and evaluation protocols, small subsets that should be treated as diagnostic probes, possible model-specific bias from LLM judges, and incomplete scoring of intermediate DuPont reasoning in the financial-report task. They also describe the benchmark as an initial release and label the experiments preliminary. These limitations are confronted directly, but the paper does not quantify their effect on rankings or aggregate scores. Analyst-Identified Gaps - The paper does not validate the proposed capability hierarchy against controlled task pairs in which grounding, information application, and knowledge learning are varied independently; consequently, level scores may partly measure dataset composition, domain familiarity, answer format, or context length. - It lacks strong non-multimodal and multimodal baseline conditions, such as text-only inputs, image-only inputs, oracle evidence, retrieval-assisted systems, or human performance, so the source of the observed errors remains underdetermined. - Automated filtering with Qwen3.5-Plus and manual curation are not accompanied by agreement rates, rejection statistics, leakage audits, or an analysis of whether filtering preferentially removes easy or model-specific examples. - The open-ended scores depend substantially on the judge model, yet there is no human adjudication, calibrated rubric study, judge ensemble, or confidence interval for judge-induced variation. - Aggregate rankings are difficult to interpret because datasets differ greatly in size and metric semantics; the 645-instance CourtSI and 1,063-instance MIRBench subsets can dominate weighted scores relative to small but potentially important tasks. - The financial task evaluates only final ROE and includes severe context-length incompatibility for at least one model, while the paper conclusion task uses reference findings generated from truncated papers and a list-level judge; both designs require stronger validation before supporting claims about general knowledge acquisition. - The paper reports only preliminary single-run results and does not provide inference hardware, API versions, decoding parameters, or cost, which limits reproducibility and practical comparison among the evaluated models. Bottom Line CLBench-V is worth reading as a useful early benchmark design for multimodal context use and failure localization, but its preliminary rankings should not be treated as definitive until hierarchy validity, judge reliability, leakage, baseline coverage, and statistical reproducibility are established.

A New Role for Relevance: Guiding Corpus Interaction in Agentic Search (83 ▲ )

Jiangnan Li, Yuqing Li, Mo Yu, Jinchao Zhang, Jie Zhou · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 29 Jul 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces the Relevance-Aware RipGrep Search Agent (RARG), which uses document-level relevance to order ripgrep traversal, query-relevant paragraphs to initialize search, and match-level relevance to rerank excerpts exposed to an LLM. - Why it's important: Direct corpus interaction can preserve fine-grained evidence discovery but wastes interactions on irrelevant matches, while conventional retrieval can hide decisive evidence; reducing this trade-off matters for the cost and reliability of deep-research agents. - How it does it: RARG treats embedding retrieval as an execution prior rather than an evidence-selection bottleneck, preserving ranked document paths during sequential `rg` scanning and reranking truncated matches before they reach the model. - The good: On the 100-query BrowseComp-Plus evaluation with GPT-5.4-mini, RARG++ reaches 84% accuracy with 23.9 average tool calls, versus 78% and 28.7 for RISE and 78% and 99.1 for DCI. - The missing: The study does not establish robustness across independent seeds, substantially different LLM backbones, open-web corpora, or real wall-clock and monetary latency, and its strongest comparisons partly reuse results cited from prior work. - Read it or not: Researchers building agentic retrieval or direct-corpus-interaction systems should read it for the execution-prior design and useful ablations, while practitioners seeking production cost estimates should treat the evidence as preliminary because tool calls are only a proxy for system cost.

Rigor (65) and Resilience (65) are limited by the 100-query primary evaluation, imported baseline results, absent confidence intervals and seeds, imperfect prompt/configuration matching, and reliance on tool-call counts as a cost proxy. systems Novelty 75 Rigor 65 Non-Obv 78 Completeness 72 Resilience 65 Impact 72
Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation The work addresses multi-hop question answering and reasoning-intensive document retrieval over large local corpora. Retrieval agents typically expose top-ranked documents or snippets, which can omit decisive spans, duplicate evidence, or fail when a document becomes useful only after an intermediate entity is discovered. Direct Corpus Interaction (DCI), based on shell tools such as `grep`, `read`, and `cat`, supports exact lexical search, evidence localization, entity following, and cross-document composition, but searches in a largely relevance-agnostic order. As corpora grow, irrelevant matches can dominate truncated tool outputs and force the LLM through many unproductive interactions. Prior systems such as RISE and DR-DCI use relevance to construct or expand a searchable workspace, but the paper identifies a narrower gap: relevance is not propagated into document traversal order or into the selection of local matches visible under an observation budget. Key Idea The core insight is to use relevance as a search-execution prior rather than as a hard filter on evidence. Global relevance determines which documents `rg` scans first, allowing relevant clues to appear early while retaining access to lower-ranked documents; local relevance determines which individual matches survive output truncation. RARG+ adds a query-relevant paragraph preview as an entry point, and RARG++ uses embedding-based reranking of a larger match pool. The contribution is therefore not a new retrieval model, but a new interface-level role for relevance in direct corpus interaction. Methodology RARG is built on DCI-Agent-Lite, in which an LLM controls `Bash` and `Read` tools. First, the agent calls `embed_recall(scope_query)`, which uses an embedding model to rank corpus paths and writes up to 10,000 paths to a scope file without returning document contents as the primary evidence channel. The agent then executes `cat scope.txt | xargs -d '\n' rg "PATTERN"`; a rule-based wrapper injects `rg -j1` so matches are emitted in document-ranking order rather than thread-completion order. The agent can create additional scopes after exploring the current one. RARG+ splits paragraphs from top-ranked scope documents into 400–1000-character chunks, embeds them against the scope query, and appends the top 10 paragraphs to the recall output as an initial search hint; these paragraphs are not intended to serve as the final answer and are cleared during context compaction. RARG++ collects up to M=500 matches from an `rg` operation, constructs a reranking query from the global scope query and the extracted local `rg` keywords, and exposes only the top m matches, with m=30 for BrowseComp-Plus and 60 for BRIGHT. A generative reranking-query variant instead asks the LLM to supply a natural-language local query, but it performs worse. The underlying agent uses level-3 context compaction, retaining recent tool results and scope mappings. Critical design decisions are the use of sequential scanning to preserve relevance order, the separation of relevance guidance from retrieved content, and match-level reranking under truncation; the paper motivates each choice empirically, although it does not optimize or formally model the latency introduced by sequential scanning and embedding reranking. Key Results On the 100-query, 100K-document BrowseComp-Plus setting, GPT-5.4-mini obtains 84% accuracy with RARG++, compared with 78% for RISE and DCI, 77% for RISE-BM25, and 68% for the conventional Retrieval-Agent baseline. RARG++ uses 23.9 average tool calls, versus 28.7 for RISE and 99.1 for DCI. The progression across RARG variants is 80% accuracy and 29.8 tools for RARG, 81% and 29.6 for RARG+, and 84% and 23.9 for RARG++. With GPT-5.4-nano, RARG++ reaches 79% and 36.1 tools, versus 71% and 126.5 for DCI and 68% and 28.7 for RISE; with GPT-5.4, it reaches 91% and 25.43 tools, versus 82% and 34.30 for RISE. On a 1M-document BrowseComp-Plus corpus formed by adding 900K long FineWeb-Edu documents, RARG++ reaches 79% accuracy with 24.7 tools, compared with 69% and 32.1 tools for RISE-BM25; RARG, RARG+, and RARG++ fall from 80/81/84% at 100K documents to 78/78/79% at 1M. On four BRIGHT domains, RARG+ obtains average nDCG@10 of 53.36, ahead of NeMo at 52.89, DCI at 48.43, RARG at 51.75, RARG++ at 50.55, and RISE-BM25 at 41.60. The variant ordering reverses on BRIGHT: entry-point initialization helps, but match-level reranking hurts broad candidate recall. Scope recall for GPT-5.4-mini is reported as 96.3% at 100K and 95.4% at 1M, while `rg` coverage falls from 82.7% to 75.9%; GPT-5.4-nano has 91.8% scope recall and 78.5% coverage. These results support the claimed mechanism, but the reported cost axis is based mainly on tool-call counts rather than measured wall-clock latency, GPU time, token use, or monetary cost. Novelty Classification The contribution is primarily a NEW METHOD and NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, with a secondary NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING: it operationalizes document relevance as traversal order and match visibility inside a DCI agent, rather than merely combining retrieval with shell interaction as a pre-filter. The embedding models, LLM agent, ripgrep search, paragraph scoring, and semantic reranking are existing components; the novel element is their coarse-to-fine execution interface and the empirical observation that its optimal granularity depends on whether the task rewards rapid convergence or broad recall. Rigor & Reproducibility The paper includes component comparisons among RARG, RARG+, RARG++, and the generative reranking variant, plus comparisons with DCI, RISE, RISE-BM25, dense-retrieval RISE, Retrieval-Agent, and NeMo. The variant results provide useful evidence that initialization and constructed match reranking matter, and the behavioral analyses measure scope recall, `rg` coverage, hit distributions over scope ranks, and command composition. However, no multiple random seeds, confidence intervals for accuracy or nDCG, statistical significance tests, or per-query variance are reported. The error bars shown for scope recall and `rg` coverage are standard deviations across the three RARG variants, not independent experimental repetitions. Several baseline numbers in the main BrowseComp-Plus table are cited from RISE rather than rerun, and the paper notes that RISE uses a different thinking-effort configuration in at least one GPT-5.4 comparison. The evaluation uses only a 100-query BrowseComp-Plus sample and four BRIGHT subsets, while the LLM-as-judge accuracy uses GPT-5.1 and the agents use GPT-5.x models. The authors provide a GitHub link, `github.com/LeqsNaN/RARG`, and state that the implementation is in Python and was tested on Linux with one H20 GPU; the paper does not clearly state whether benchmark corpora, all prompts, model weights, trajectory logs, and exact evaluation scripts are released. The use of the same benchmark corpora to tune prompts, tool limits, and embedding choices creates some risk of benchmark-specific optimization, although the authors do include a corpus-expansion test and a separate retrieval benchmark. Deployability (4-property check) Profile: SYSTEMS — the paper builds and evaluates an LLM-driven corpus-search tool rather than presenting a purely theoretical result. Practical: The implementation runs on Linux with one commercially available H20 GPU and uses standard Python, embedding models, an LLM API, and ripgrep, so a comparable deployment is technically feasible, although the required proprietary GPT-5.x models and embedding inference costs are not fully characterized. Efficient: RARG reduces average tool calls substantially on BrowseComp-Plus—23.9 versus 99.1 for DCI and 28.7 for RISE in the GPT-5.4-mini setting—but sequential `rg -j1`, up to 500-match reranking, and embedding inference add unmeasured wall-clock and hardware overhead; tool-call counts are not a complete efficiency comparison. Effective: The evidence shows improved answer accuracy and BRIGHT ranking quality on the tested benchmarks, including 84% versus 78% on BrowseComp-Plus and 53.36 versus 52.89 average nDCG@10 against NeMo, but it does not directly measure factuality, citation correctness, answer calibration, or performance on live web search. Scalable: The method retains a 10-point accuracy advantage over RISE-BM25 after expanding BrowseComp-Plus from 100K to 1M documents, but RARG++ still drops from 84% to 79% and `rg` coverage falls from 82.7% to 75.9%; behavior beyond 1M documents or at 10×–100× larger scale is not evaluated. The work delivers a software artifact and a publicly named GitHub repository, but not a new dataset, trained model, or reusable formal proof technique. Strengths - It identifies a concrete interface mismatch between document-level relevance and direct corpus interaction, then expresses the fix as an executable system design rather than only a prompt-level recommendation. - The coarse-to-fine decomposition is technically meaningful: document ordering improves early evidence exposure, paragraph initialization reduces the time to a useful search anchor, and match reranking addresses output truncation and document-level embedding dilution. - The experiments separate task objectives effectively. RARG++ is best for BrowseComp-Plus question answering, whereas RARG+ is best on BRIGHT, exposing a real recall-versus-convergence trade-off instead of presenting one variant as universally optimal. - The 1M-document stress test and hit-distribution analysis provide evidence about mechanism and failure mode: long noisy documents preserve scope recall but reduce the fraction of useful matches recovered by `rg`. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors explicitly report dependence on embedding quality and note that document-level and short-match relevance may require different embedding models; they use NV for BRIGHT document ranking and Qwen3-Embedding-4B for match reranking. They acknowledge the latency cost of single-threaded `rg` and match reranking, sensitivity to LLM instruction following, degradation from long noisy documents, the accuracy loss of the generative reranking-query variant, and the limited coverage of GPT-5.x backbones, BrowseComp-Plus, BRIGHT, and closed-corpus settings. They also state that match-level reranking only partially mitigates corpus-induced interference and leave broader validation and improved local matching for future work. These limitations are confronted directly, although the quantitative latency and cost implications remain underreported. Analyst-Identified Gaps The central efficiency claim relies on tool-call counts even though RARG changes the meaning and computational cost of a call: an embedding recall, sequential scan, reranked scan, and ordinary `rg` call are not equivalent. The paper does not report wall-clock latency, embedding FLOPs, GPU utilization, token consumption, or monetary cost, so the claimed accuracy–efficiency frontier may not translate to deployment cost. Baseline fairness is imperfect because some results are imported from RISE, thinking-effort settings differ, the DCI BRIGHT prompt is modified, and the study does not report a fully controlled retriever-quality and prompt-matched comparison across all agents. The 100-query BrowseComp-Plus sample is small for accuracy comparisons, and the paper does not provide per-query paired significance tests or robustness to prompt/order changes. The method hard-caps scopes at 10,000 paths and requires order-preserving single-threaded traversal, but there is no sensitivity analysis for scope size, paragraph count, match pool size, output limits, or the `-j1` implementation. The evaluation also lacks adversarial lexical-match cases, document duplication tests, corrupted or incomplete corpora, and open-web freshness/noise. Finally, the analysis establishes that relevance changes hit distributions, but it does not isolate whether the gains arise from better document ordering, extra paragraph content, reranking, altered prompts, or changed context-compaction behavior under a common computational budget. Bottom Line This is a useful and technically credible systems paper for researchers working on agentic search because it turns retrieval relevance into an explicit execution-control signal and demonstrates consistent benchmark gains, but its practical efficiency claims need stronger cost accounting, controlled baselines, and broader robustness tests before it can support production deployment.

CAST: Game Solvers as Turn-Level Teachers for LLM Agents (29 ▲ )

Yu Wang, Yi-Kai Zhang, Wentao Shi, Ziang Ye, Yuchun Miao, Yueqing Sun, Qi Gu, Xunliang Cai, Lan-Zhe Guo, Han-Jia Ye, Fuli Feng · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 30 Jul 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces CAST, an RLVR training method that converts changes in a game solver’s cost-to-go into turn-level action-credit signals for LLM agents. - Why it's important: Sparse win/loss rewards provide weak supervision for long-horizon decisions, while solver queries can provide denser guidance without requiring teacher logits or large process-reward models. - How it does it: CAST computes the drop in solver cost-to-go after each sampled action, applies asinh compression and batch RMS normalization, and adds the resulting signal to DAPO’s trajectory-level advantage. - The good: On a 4B Qwen3 policy, CAST improves the average in-domain success rate from DAPO’s 44.7% to 62.1% and the unseen-difficulty rate from 18.7% to 28.4% across Sokoban, Minesweeper, and Rush Hour. - The missing: The claimed generality is not established beyond three small, solver-friendly games and two zero-shot text benchmarks, and the central distillation theorem depends on strong soft-optimality, small-signal, and frozen-visitation assumptions. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on process supervision or RL for language agents and want a practical solver-derived credit signal; skip it if you need evidence for large-scale, solver-free, open-world deployment.
Why this rank
Profile: systems. Novelty (72) and Non-Obviousness (73) are solid: using solver cost-to-go changes as turn-level LLM-agent credit is a useful integration of oracle querying and process supervision, though related to potential-based shaping and oracle distillation. Rigor (72) benefits from three runs, matched baselines, ablations, timing analysis, and code, but is reduced by preprint status, missing significance tests, and theoretical assumptions that do not closely match the implemented Minesweeper and deterministic-solver settings. Completeness (68) and Resilience (65) reflect the honestly discussed but substantial limits on solver availability, transfer, scale, and checkpoint-selection evidence, while Impact (75) is relatively strong for an open-source, practically measurable training recipe; weighted composite: 0.15*72 + 0.15*72 + 0.10*73 + 0.15*68 + 0.15*65 + 0.30*75 = 71.
systems Novelty 72 Rigor 72 Non-Obv 73 Completeness 68 Resilience 65 Impact 75
Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation The work addresses credit assignment for language-model agents acting over many interaction turns with sparse, verifiable terminal rewards. The target domains are structured games and, by extension, agentic environments in which early actions can create irreversible consequences. Outcome-only RLVR assigns essentially the same trajectory-level advantage to every token or turn, making it difficult to identify which decisions caused success or failure. Existing alternatives—search, learned process reward models, critics, and cross-trajectory comparisons—trade off computation, additional supervision, and signal reliability. The specific gap is a cheap, state-grounded process signal that can evaluate learner-visited states rather than only expert trajectories or recurrent comparison states. Key Idea The central insight is to use a solver’s change in cost-to-go as action credit: if an action reduces the solver-estimated remaining work by one step, it receives positive credit; if it makes no progress or leads toward failure, it receives zero or negative credit. This is a recognizable combination of oracle querying, potential-based progress attribution, and policy optimization, but the framing as logit-free on-policy distillation from a scalar solver value is the paper’s main conceptual angle. The insight is strongest when an accurate solver can evaluate arbitrary learner-visited states and when cost-to-go is meaningful, deterministic, and inexpensive. Methodology The agent operates in a finite-horizon multi-turn MDP and generates one action per turn from a textual state representation. For Sokoban and Rush Hour, the solver cost N(s) is the shortest number of actions remaining; for Minesweeper, K(s) is the number of reveals required by a deterministic constraint/probability-based solver, with failure assigned infinite cost and then capped for training. For a transition, CAST forms the shifted progress signal N(s_t)-N(s_{t+1}), equivalent to the change in the potential -N(s); an optimal shortest-path action receives approximately +1, a neutral action 0, and harmful actions negative credit. The signal is transformed with g(x)=asinh(x), which compresses large dead-state penalties, and divided by a batch-level RMS without mean subtraction so that zero retains its interpretation as no progress. The final per-turn advantage is A_outcome plus alpha times the normalized solver signal, and this value is broadcast to all tokens generated during that turn inside a DAPO-style clipped policy objective. The main design decisions—using solver values rather than expert actions, retaining the terminal reward alongside auxiliary shaping, and applying asinh/RMS stabilization—are motivated operationally and tested in ablations, although alpha is tuned only on Sokoban and the transformations are not evaluated across all games in a full factorial design. The theoretical interpretation assumes a soft-optimal solver with pi_solver(a|s) proportional to exp(Q_solver(a,s)/tau), yielding A_solver=tau log pi_solver; a first-order expansion of asinh around the optimal-action point then gives an approximate cross-entropy distillation objective under a frozen state-visitation surrogate. Key Results On 200 held-out instances per game and four rollouts per instance, with means over three independent training runs, CAST is the best trained method in every reported game and split. In-domain success rates are 77.0% for Sokoban, 44.7% for Minesweeper, and 64.7% for Rush Hour, averaging 62.1%, versus DAPO’s 71.9%, 29.8%, and 32.5% and average 44.7%; GRPO averages 44.9% and GiGPO 45.4%. On harder unseen-difficulty instances, CAST scores 34.8%, 11.0%, and 39.5%, averaging 28.4%, versus DAPO’s 31.3%, 7.3%, and 17.4%, averaging 18.7%. The largest in-domain gain over the strongest trained baseline occurs on Minesweeper, where CAST reaches 44.7% versus DAPO’s 29.8%. CAST reaches DAPO’s peak validation performance after 120 versus 200 steps on Sokoban, 200 versus 400 on Minesweeper, and 140 versus 240 on Rush Hour, described as 1.7–2.0x fewer training steps. Zero-shot transfer is reported on seen-validation ALFWorld and the 500-instruction WebShop test set: CAST averages 37.9% on ALFWorld and 22.7% on WebShop, compared with the strongest trained-baseline averages of 32.1% and 17.9%, respectively, for an overall average of 30.3% versus 24.7%. The transfer evidence is suggestive but not conclusive: the absolute scores remain low, the held-out tasks share the same single-action multi-turn scaffold, and no broad suite of environments is tested. Solver queries account for 8.4% of an environment step, 0.01% of a trajectory, and an estimated 73 parts per million of a batch training step in the reported Sokoban timing setup. A DQN-based Rush Hour value network trained without solver-distance targets retains much of the exact-solver benefit, but the paper reports this mainly through curves rather than a complete numerical table. Novelty Classification NEW METHOD, NEW FORMULATION, ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION, and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING: CAST contributes a solver-value-difference process signal integrated into LLM RLVR, together with a scalar-only distillation interpretation and stabilization scheme; the underlying ingredients overlap with potential-based shaping, AggreVaTe/DAgger-style oracle querying, search distillation, and process-credit methods, so the strongest novelty is their particular integration and empirical demonstration in LLM game training rather than a wholly new RL principle. Rigor & Reproducibility The paper is an arXiv preprint, version 1 dated 28 July 2026, and reports three independent runs for the main trained methods, standard deviations as bands in training curves, explicit data-generation and split procedures, fixed 200-instance evaluation sets per game tier, shared Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 backbones, and detailed hyperparameters. It provides a code URL, github.com/Wloner0809/CAST, but the text does not state whether all generated instances, exact solver implementations, checkpoints, or value-network weights are released. Ablations cover alpha values of 0.01, 0.1, 0.3, and 0.5 and independently remove asinh or RMS normalization, showing that alpha=0.1 and both transformations perform best on Sokoban. Comparisons against GRPO, GSPO, DAPO, and GiGPO use the same base model and nominal training configuration, which is a strength, although the baselines’ tuning equivalence is not independently verified. The theoretical result is conditional rather than a guarantee for the implemented algorithm: the solver is deterministic and usually hard-optimal rather than demonstrably soft-optimal, the asinh linearization is assumed for most signals, GRPO’s group-relative advantage is treated as unbiased, and the state-visitation derivative is frozen. Minesweeper’s oracle is not an optimal value function in the ordinary MDP sense and can include probabilistic failures, weakening the direct connection between the implementation and the theorem. No statistical significance tests or per-instance confidence intervals are reported, and the proprietary-model references use a single run. Deployability (4-property check) Profile: SYSTEMS/EMPIRICAL hybrid — the paper trains and evaluates an implemented LLM-agent system and also measures solver runtime. Practical: The method can run on commercially available hardware in principle because it uses a 4B open-source policy, local solver queries, and standard DAPO-style training, although the paper does not report GPU type, total hardware count, memory use, or monetary training cost. Efficient: In the reported small-game setup, solver queries are cheap relative to generation—6.23 ms of a 73.91 ms environment step and an estimated 73 ppm of a 190-second training step—but this measurement does not establish efficiency for larger state spaces or expensive search-based solvers. Effective: The evidence shows substantial gains in success rate over matched outcome-only and process-level baselines on the three training games and modest gains on ALFWorld/WebShop, but it measures task success rather than solution optimality, robustness, calibration, or recovery across a broad range of environments. Scalable: The method is tested only on 6x6 or 7x7 boards with two or three Sokoban boxes, seven or ten Minesweeper mines, and seven or nine Rush Hour vehicles; behavior at 10x–100x scale, with long contexts, larger action spaces, or unavailable exact solvers is not evaluated. The paper delivers an open-source code artifact and game-specific solver integrations, plus a learned Rush Hour value-network variant, but not a general solver library or released trained model explicitly identified in the text. Strengths - It identifies a concrete way to convert an external solver’s state evaluation into on-policy, learner-visited process supervision without requiring teacher logits. - The controlled DAPO comparison isolates a large empirical contribution: average in-domain success rises from 44.7% to 62.1%, and unseen-difficulty success rises from 18.7% to 28.4%. - The method combines global terminal credit with turn-level progress rather than replacing the actual win objective, reducing the risk that shaping alone optimizes a proxy. - The paper tests exact solvers, an approximate learned value network, within-game difficulty shifts, and cross-domain transfer, and reports solver timing rather than only claiming low overhead. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors explicitly recognize that the theory requires a soft-optimal solver, that the asinh-to-log-probability equivalence relies on a small-signal regime, that GRPO introduces finite-sample variance, and that the frozen-visitation surrogate omits long-range occupancy-gradient terms. They also acknowledge that Minesweeper’s partial observability complicates deterministic cost-to-go and that the learned value-network analysis is approximate. However, the paper does not present a dedicated limitations section or quantify how often the theoretical assumptions fail, and it generally frames the solver assumptions as well-justified for the selected games. Analyst-Identified Gaps - The method is evaluated in domains deliberately chosen to have efficient, reliable, game-specific solvers; this leaves the central practical question—whether useful state evaluators can be obtained in domains without exact solvers—largely open. The single DQN experiment on Rush Hour is not a substitute for evaluation across diverse approximate critics. - The OOD transfer protocol is narrower than the headline suggests: ALFWorld uses its seen validation split, WebShop is a fixed simulated benchmark, and both reuse the same text-action loop, so the results do not establish transfer to genuinely different interfaces or real-world interaction. - The theorem’s soft-optimal solver assumption is not empirically validated. A deterministic shortest-path oracle does not naturally define the stated nonzero-temperature teacher distribution, and Minesweeper’s heuristic/probabilistic solver is not demonstrably optimal. Thus “equivalent to on-policy distillation” should be treated as a conditional interpretation, not a measured property of the implemented training signal. - Ablations are concentrated on Sokoban; there is no alpha sweep or transformation ablation on Minesweeper and Rush Hour, no comparison against direct solver-action imitation, and no study of imperfect, adversarial, stale, or systematically biased value estimates. - The main results use final checkpoints selected at fixed training steps rather than a clearly preregistered model-selection protocol, and no confidence intervals or significance tests accompany the 200-instance success rates. The apparent gains may therefore be sensitive to checkpoint choice and run variance. - The claimed 1.7–2.0x sample-efficiency improvement is measured by reaching DAPO’s peak validation value, not by equal-compute area-under-learning-curve, environment-interaction count, or wall-clock cost; the solver’s contribution to total optimization cost is also estimated from one Sokoban configuration. Bottom Line CAST is a useful and empirically strong recipe for solver-rich game RL, with a credible process-credit mechanism and clear gains over matched LLM-RL baselines, but its broader claims about general agent training and logit-free distillation remain insufficiently supported outside small environments with unusually favorable oracle access.

SceneActBench: Can Agents Act on the 3D Scenes They See? (4 ▲ )

Yifei Zhao, Xiangxin Zhou, Wenhao Yang, Jiaqi Tang, Pu Jian, Huanjin Yao, Jiarui Yao, Haowei Lin, Chunchao Guo, Zhuo Chen, Wenkai Lyu, Jianzhu Ma, Xueqian Wang, Wenxi Zhu · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 27 Jul 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces SceneActBench, an executable benchmark that evaluates vision-language model agents acting on complete 3D scenes through five tasks: Layout, Camera, Articulated, Reconstruction, and Dynamic. - Why it's important: Existing 3D benchmarks often score text answers, isolated objects, or task success, leaving coordinated multi-object scene action—and its geometric correctness—poorly measured. - How it does it: It places every agent in a shared inspect–execute-Blender-code–render–revise loop and scores the final GLB scene, animation, or camera pose against hidden 3D ground truth with task-specific geometric metrics. - The good: The benchmark exposes failure stages that aggregate scores hide: for example, Claude Opus moves 255/391 articulated parts while Doubao moves only 13/391, despite similar maximum-part-error scores of 0.375 and 0.404. - The missing: The main study lacks task-specialist baselines, open-weight models, repeated runs or seed variation, and a sufficiently broad Dynamic set—the latter contains only 10 scenes and strongly affects the overall ranking. - Read it or not: Read it if you evaluate multimodal agents, Blender/code agents, or 3D reasoning; skip it if you need a demonstrated algorithmic improvement rather than a benchmark and diagnostic framework.
Why this rank
Profile: empirical. Novelty (82) and Non-Obviousness (75) are strong because SceneActBench formulates executable, hidden-ground-truth evaluation of coordinated 3D scene action with useful failure diagnostics. Rigor (58), Completeness (72), and Resilience (65) are pulled down by single runs, proprietary-only models, absent specialist baselines, only 10 Dynamic scenes, and metric asymmetries; Impact (70) reflects a potentially useful executable benchmark whose release contents are not fully verifiable. Weighted composite: 0.20*82 + 0.25*58 + 0.15*75 + 0.15*72 + 0.15*65 + 0.10*70 = 69.7, rounded to 70.

Problem & Motivation The work addresses the problem of measuring whether a vision-language agent can convert visual evidence into geometrically correct actions in a multi-object 3D environment. Relevant users include researchers building multimodal agents, procedural graphics systems, embodied agents, and 3D content-generation tools. Prior benchmarks such as ScanQA, SQA3D, and Spatial457 primarily evaluate textual answers, while code-driven or embodied benchmarks often target a single object, a static edit, or binary task success. The specific gap is an evaluation that combines spatial grounding, egocentric camera reasoning, articulated motion, shape reconstruction, and multi-object dynamics under one executable interaction protocol and evaluates the resulting 3D artifact rather than only the agent's language. Key Idea The core insight is to make 3D understanding an executable, hidden-ground-truth matching problem: the agent must construct or modify a Blender scene using tools, and the benchmark evaluates the final geometric state independently of the agent's textual explanation. The benchmark's distinctive contribution is not a new inference algorithm; it is the unified fixed agent–environment loop plus task-specific geometric evaluation and denominator-aware diagnostics across heterogeneous scene-action capabilities. Methodology SceneActBench is assembled from 210 source instances and 520 task cases, including paired input conditions. Layout uses 100 3D-FRONT rooms with 3–7 standardized, anonymized furniture assets placed at the origin; the agent receives either one or approximately 11 calibrated views and predicts object world positions and yaw rotations, scored primarily by Hungarian-matched ADD-S surface distance. Camera uses the same furnished scenes with one image and known field of view; the agent predicts a six-degree-of-freedom camera pose, scored by position error and angular viewing-direction error. Articulated uses 100 anonymized objects from the S2O Articulated Containers Dataset, 32 ordered open–close frames, and a closed GLB; the agent identifies movable parts and infers joint type, axis, pivot, and range, exporting 32 scene states scored by Maximum Part Error, which combines geometry error and unreproduced travel. Reconstruction gives the agent approximately 11 room views and an empty Blender scene; it identifies furniture, constructs meshes and base colors with Blender code, and is scored by object-level F@5% after fixed-scale ICP, clustering, matching, and per-object recentering. Dynamic contains 10 custom multi-object scenes built from Kenney assets, a component GLB library, a 144-frame video, and a known camera; the agent reconstructs static layout, mover identities, starting positions, and trajectories in an animated GLB, scored by Maximum Mover Error and static Layout Error. All tasks use a shared MCP interface for scene inspection, code execution, rendering, and—in Dynamic—reference-frame retrieval, with budgets of 30, 30, 60, 35, and 80 steps respectively. Overall maps native metrics to 0–100 using fixed reference thresholds, averages cases within each task, and equally weights the five tasks; multi-view Layout and photorealistic Dynamic remain outside Overall. These design decisions are mostly explicit and operationally reproducible, but the justification for the particular normalization constants, equal task weighting, and primary metric choices is limited; the authors acknowledge that normalization constants are design choices. Key Results The paper evaluates eleven configurations from ten proprietary VLMs, all through the same harness, with one completed run per configuration–case pair. Overall scores range from 38.6 to 50.2. Doubao Seed 2.0 Pro High ranks first at 50.2, followed by Claude Opus 4.6 High at 48.9 and GPT 5.4 Medium at 48.7; GPT 5.4 High reaches 48.7 despite leading Layout at 84.1, Articulated at 73.8, and Reconstruction at 12.3, because its Dynamic score is only 46.7. Doubao leads Layout with ADD-S 0.905 and score 77.4, Camera with position/angular errors of 4.825 m/54.5 degrees and score 34.5, and Dynamic with MME/LE of 0.471/0.150 and score 70.7. Claude Opus leads Articulated with MPE 0.375 m and score 63.7. GPT 5.4 Medium leads Reconstruction with F@5% 0.104 and score 10.4, although reconstruction performance is very low for all systems. Multi-view Layout improves nine of eleven configurations, with gains as high as 12.1 points for Claude Sonnet 5 High, while photorealistic Dynamic improves four and harms six; GPT 5.4 High gains 17.3 points, whereas Step 3.7 Flash and Sonnet 5 lose 10.3 and 10.2 points. The ranking is sensitive to benchmark composition: Doubao ranks first in 64% of 50,000 paired case resamples, compared with 19% for Claude Opus and 17% for GPT 5.4 Medium, and its advantage over Claude is concentrated in two Dynamic scenes, raceloop and factory. Diagnostic results show severe failure despite moderate aggregate scores: in Articulated, Doubao moves only 13/391 ground-truth parts, while Claude Opus moves 255/391; in Reconstruction, the top three systems match 425–432 of 515 targets but cover only 24–44 targets at the reported coverage criterion; and in Dynamic, Doubao matches 28/29 movers but gets direction correct on only 7/16 eligible tracks. More interaction does not predict better performance across configurations; task-balanced realized budget and Overall have descriptive Spearman correlation rho = -0.68, not a causal effect. Novelty Classification NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK, NEW EVALUATION FORMULATION, and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely new contribution is a benchmark formulation that evaluates executable, multi-object 3D action across five capabilities under a fixed agent loop with hidden geometric scoring and failure-stage diagnostics; the Blender control, rendering, GLB outputs, standard metrics, and VLM comparisons are combinations of existing components rather than a new learning method. Rigor & Reproducibility The paper specifies data construction, anonymization and asset standardization, task prompts, step budgets, output formats, evaluator rules, matching procedures, thresholds, invalid-output handling, score normalization, and diagnostic metrics in the appendix. It reports per-case sample standard deviations across instances, but these are not repeated-run error bars: every configuration–case pair was run once, so stochastic execution variance, provider nondeterminism, and statistical significance of leaderboard gaps are not measured. No component ablations isolate the effect of the shared MCP interface, prompts, rendering checks, tool availability, or individual task design choices. A separate Claude Sonnet 5 comparison between the shared harness and official Claude Code CLI is informative but confounded by different system prompts, context policies, image readers, and interaction packaging; it does not identify a causal interface effect. The main comparison uses proprietary models and omits task-specialist 3D systems such as layout generators, camera estimators, and reconstruction models, which the authors explicitly identify as future work. Code, project page, and Hugging Face links are displayed on the first page, but their actual URLs or release contents are not stated in the parsed text; public availability of the complete benchmark data, evaluator, prompts, and model outputs is therefore not verifiable here. Potential metric incentives remain: unmatched predicted/ground-truth objects are excluded from primary Layout ADD-S, extra predicted movers do not enter Dynamic MME, and Reconstruction uses ICP alignment plus cluster recentering, so the primary metrics do not uniformly penalize all forms of incorrect scene structure. Deployability (4-property check) Profile: EMPIRICAL, with a benchmark harness rather than a deployed production system. Practical: The evaluated loop runs headless Blender through Python/MCP tools on commercially available hardware in principle, but the paper does not report hardware, wall-clock latency, or infrastructure requirements. Efficient: Compute, memory, token, and rendering costs are not quantified; the main protocol permits up to 30–80 agent steps per case and uses 520 cases, so relative cost versus specialist pipelines is not established. Effective: The benchmark measures final geometric agreement and reveals substantial capability gaps, but it is a proxy for real-world 3D action because scenes are synthetic or standardized, actions occur in Blender rather than physical environments, and no downstream application success is measured. Scalable: The paper tests rooms with 3–7 objects, 100 articulated objects, and only 10 dynamic scenes, with no 10×–100× stress test; broader-scene scalability is claimed as future work rather than demonstrated. The work delivers an executable benchmark/evaluation harness and associated datasets or assets if the linked release is complete, but the parsed paper does not verify the release contents or URLs; it does not deliver a trained model or an algorithm intended to improve agent performance. Strengths - It identifies a meaningful evaluation gap between textual 3D understanding and executable scene manipulation, and operationalizes that gap across spatial, camera, kinematic, shape, and dynamic reasoning. - The common inspect–act–render loop controls a major source of comparison noise: all eleven configurations use the same Blender environment, core tools, prompts, task budgets, and final-output evaluators. - The task-specific metrics and denominator-aware failure funnels provide more actionable information than a single success rate. The articulated analysis separates failure to select moving parts from joint-type and direction errors, while the reconstruction analysis separates object matching from actual surface coverage. - The paired input-condition experiments reveal configuration-dependent robustness: more views usually help Layout, but photorealistic Dynamic references help some systems and substantially hurt others. The paper also correctly labels single-run comparisons and bootstrap rank sensitivity as non-causal or non-repeated-run evidence. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors explicitly state that the main study uses proprietary VLM configurations and one completed run per configuration–case pair; that the Dynamic set contains only 10 scenes and should be treated as a targeted stress test; that Overall depends on fixed normalization constants; and that comparisons with task-specialist 3D pipelines remain future work. They also note that the benchmark should be expanded to broader scenes, open-weight models, and richer interactions. These limitations are confronted directly rather than hidden, although their consequences for ranking reliability and external validity remain substantial. Analyst-Identified Gaps - There is no comparison against strong non-agentic specialist baselines, human performance, classical geometric methods, or a simple scripted oracle, so the benchmark does not establish whether the unified agent protocol is competitive with existing task-specific solutions. - The Dynamic ranking is vulnerable to composition effects because only 10 scenes are used and two scenes account for most of Doubao's advantage over Claude Opus; the bootstrap quantifies sensitivity but cannot repair the narrow sample. - One execution per case prevents reliable conclusions about stochastic agent behavior, and the paper does not provide repeated-run confidence intervals, significance tests, or provider/version stability analysis. - The primary metrics have asymmetric handling of omissions and extras: Layout ADD-S averages only matched objects, Dynamic MME ignores extra predicted movers, and Reconstruction grants fixed-scale ICP and object recentering. Audits partly address these issues, but leaderboard rankings rely on the primary metrics. - The benchmark evaluates mostly synthetic, anonymized, or low-poly assets and constrains agents to Blender code and fixed tool interfaces; transfer to cluttered real scans, unknown asset libraries, noisy perception, physical manipulation, or longer-horizon interaction is not measured. - The paper does not report wall-clock time, token consumption, GPU/CPU hardware, Blender rendering cost, or benchmark execution cost, limiting practical comparisons among high-effort proprietary configurations. Bottom Line SceneActBench is a useful and technically specified benchmark for diagnosing executable 3D-agent failures, but its modest and partly composition-sensitive evaluation, absent specialist baselines, and single-run proprietary-model study make it stronger as an evaluation proposal and diagnostic resource than as evidence of a definitive model ranking or solved method.

X $^ 3$-OPD: Distilling Reasoning into Large Audio-Language Models via On-Policy Alignment

D Fu, D Cao, X Cheng, Z Zhang, W Jia, Y Chen, S Ji… · arxiv.org · Recommended articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces X³-OPD, a cross-modal on-policy distillation framework that transfers reasoning from a frozen text teacher into a large audio-language model using student-generated acoustic reasoning trajectories. - Why it's important: Audio-language models retain prosodic and environmental information unavailable in transcripts but lack the large-scale, high-quality reasoning supervision available to text models. - How it does it: It pairs audio with semantically matched text, has the audio student sample multiple trajectories, and scores each sampled token with a text teacher conditioned on the paired text and gold answer after a short offline warm-start. - The good: On the reported benchmarks, X³-OPD raises BIG Bench Audio from 87.9 to 93.6 over its Qwen3-Omni-Thinking initialization and limits out-of-domain WorldSense/DailyOmni degradation to 1.2/2.3 points versus 5.3–6.6 points for SFT and GKD. - The missing: The evaluation does not isolate the method from the large, heavily curated synthetic and caption-mediated training corpus with sufficient independent seeds, statistical uncertainty, or a broader set of strong contemporary on-policy and audio-reward baselines. - Read it or not: Audio-language-model researchers should read it for the paired-data and on-policy-distillation design, but practitioners should treat the gains as provisional until leakage, teacher-answer conditioning, reproducibility, and real-audio robustness are better validated.
Why this rank
Scored using the Empirical profile. Novelty (78) and Non-Obviousness (80) reflect a meaningful cross-modal adaptation of on-policy distillation in which an audio student supplies the supervised states while a text teacher provides dense reasoning feedback. Rigor (62), Completeness (72), and Resilience (65) are pulled down by absent uncertainty estimates and released artifacts, synthetic and caption-mediated data dependence, answer-conditioned teacher scoring, and limited contemporary on-policy baselines. Impact (60) is constrained by the very high teacher and hardware requirements, missing cost analysis, and lack of robustness tests on uncontrolled audio, accents, languages, and long contexts. Weighted composite: 0.20*78 + 0.25*62 + 0.15*80 + 0.15*72 + 0.15*65 + 0.10*60 = 69.65, rounded to 70.
