Problem & Motivation Content moderation systems must classify prompts, model responses, images, and multimodal combinations under policies that vary by application, domain, strictness, language, and risk tolerance. Existing guard models generally emit labels tied to a fixed taxonomy, making it difficult to consolidate heterogeneous datasets or express deployment-specific criteria—for example, content acceptable in cybersecurity research but inappropriate in a mental-health product. The paper targets the gap between fixed-category moderation and inference-time policy adaptation, while also addressing the compute cost of using much larger models for multimodal safety classification. Key Idea The core insight is to treat moderation as semantic entailment of a natural-language policy question: given an instruction, a yes/no query, and content, the model predicts whether the content satisfies the query. The training signal is strengthened by pairing identical content with both matching and non-matching category queries, and by generating unsafe rewrites that target one category while avoiding a sibling category. This makes policy adaptation a query-conditioned discrimination problem rather than a fixed-label classification problem. The binary-question formulation itself is a straightforward repurposing of generative language-model inference; the more distinctive contribution is its combination with large-scale heterogeneous-data unification and category-contrastive synthetic generation. Methodology Shieldstral starts from the multimodal Ministral-3B-Base-2512 causal language model with a Pixtral vision encoder. Every example is serialized with a fixed system prompt and user fields `<Instruct>`, `<Query>`, and `<Document>`, where the document may contain a prompt, response, prompt–response pair, image, or image plus text. Fine-tuning uses LoRA on language-model parameters and full-vocabulary cross-entropy at a single output position; inference extracts the logits of the “yes” and “no” tokens and computes s = exp(z_yes)/(exp(z_yes)+exp(z_no)), using threshold 0.5 for classification. The data pipeline has four stages: manually designed dataset processors map 45.2M open-source text examples into common templates with paraphrased task framings, strictness levels, queries, and document formats; contrastive curation pairs content with category-matching and category-mismatching questions and uses an LLM for label cross-validation; contrastive generation creates approximately 4.4M examples by rewriting safe text toward one of 73 training leaf categories while avoiding a sibling category, then generates positive, negative, and ancestor-category queries; and image processing produces approximately 4.5M multimodal samples from moderation, clean-image, and general-purpose image datasets, with query mutation, taxonomy mapping, LLM-generated hard negatives, and vision-language-reranker filtering. The authors train a public-data checkpoint P and a public-plus-generated-data checkpoint PG, then merge PG, P, and the Ministral-3B-Instruct checkpoint using SLERP weights 0.6, 0.3, and 0.1. The principal design choices—binary serialization, contrastive same-content pairing, and synthetic hierarchical rewrites—are motivated by taxonomy heterogeneity and policy generalization, but the paper does not provide a formal analysis of why the fixed 0.5 threshold, LLM filtering, or SLERP weights should transfer across deployments. Key Results The paper evaluates 16 benchmarks across 21 splits and compares against 10 baselines ranging from 4B to 20B parameters. On text safety, Shieldstral reports 84.9% overall F1, equal to GPT-OSS-Safeguard-20B and above Qwen3Guard-8B at 84.0%, Nemotron-3.5-Safety-4B at 83.3%, PolyGuard-Qwen-7B at 82.1%, Nemotron-Safety-8B at 81.8%, WildGuard-7B at 79.5%, OmniGuard-7B at 77.4%, LlamaGuard-4-12B at 69.1%, and ShieldGemma-9B at 54.7% under the reported settings. On refusal detection, Shieldstral obtains 90.2% overall F1 across WildGuardTest, XSTest, and PolyGuard, below GPT-OSS-Safeguard-20B at 93.7% but above Qwen3Guard-8B at 90.7%, WildGuard-7B at 87.5%, and PolyGuard-Qwen-7B at 84.5%. On the fine-grained adaptability benchmark, it reports 93.2% precision, 89.6% recall, and 91.3% F1; GPT-OSS-Safeguard-20B leads at 94.1% F1, while Nemotron-3.5-Safety-4B reaches 91.8%. On multimodal safety, Shieldstral reports 83.8% overall F1 across VLGuard, UnsafeBench, and LlavaGuard, compared with OmniGuard-7B at 77.6%, Nemotron-3.5-Safety-4B at 73.9%, LlavaGuard-7B at 71.6%, ShieldGemma-2-4B at 57.5%, and LlamaGuard-4-12B at 37.5%; it leads on VLGuard and UnsafeBench but not on LlavaGuard. The training-stage ablation moves fine-grained-taxonomy F1 from 0% for the untuned base model to 61.1% with public data and 84.4% after generated taxonomy data; the final three-way merge reaches 88.7% on the taxonomy validation set and 88.0% on Aegis v2 validation, versus 61.1% and 88.5% for the public-only checkpoint. Full SFT and LoRA are close: 87.8% versus 87.1% F1 on Aegis v2 validation and 83.9% versus 84.4% on taxonomy validation. Results are strongest on standard English and several multilingual response tasks; prompt-classification F1 falls to 77.9% for Arabic and 55.5% for Indonesian, and the authors note weaknesses in other low-resource languages. The evaluated scale is standard benchmark scale, with individual public test sets ranging from 100 to 42,239 samples; no stress test at 10×–100× scale is reported. Novelty Classification The contribution is primarily NEW METHOD, NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, with a supporting NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK contribution: the paper combines query-conditioned binary moderation, heterogeneous dataset processors, same-content category contrastives, LLM-generated hierarchical rewrites, and multimodal augmentation into Shieldstral, while introducing a fine-grained adaptability evaluation set; binary question answering, LoRA, LLM data generation, contrastive negatives, and SLERP model merging are individually established techniques rather than new primitives. Rigor & Reproducibility The paper includes useful component ablations: public versus generated data, LoRA versus full SFT, and several SLERP mixtures. These show that generated data primarily raises unseen-taxonomy recall and that merging recovers benchmark performance while retaining adaptability. However, the reported evidence lacks multiple random seeds, error bars, statistical significance tests, threshold sweeps, calibration metrics, confusion matrices, and robustness tests under policy paraphrase or adversarial prompt injection. The custom adaptability benchmark is generated and cross-verified by LLMs, with different generation and verification models from training, but the paper does not report human annotation, human agreement, contamination audits beyond the stated model separation, or the exact benchmark sample count. Much of the training data is derived from open-source sources and synthetic transformations, but the text does not state that the 54.1M-sample dataset, preprocessing code, trained weights, or evaluation code are publicly released; no URL or repository is mentioned. Comparisons are broad and include recent baselines, but settings are not fully matched: GPT-OSS-Safeguard uses high reasoning effort, Qwen3Guard uses averaged strict/loose mappings, and some systems use different output formats and inference procedures. The evaluation also uses the authors’ own generated taxonomy and fixed canonical queries, creating a risk that the benchmark measures competence on the generation protocol or category separability more than real deployment policy interpretation. Deployability (4-property check) Profile: SYSTEMS, because the paper builds and evaluates a 3B multimodal moderation model, although it does not report a production deployment. Practical: The 3B-parameter model is plausibly runnable on commercially available GPUs, but the paper reports neither memory requirements, quantized configurations, supported hardware, nor a released inference package. Efficient: Single-token yes/no inference and LoRA-based training should reduce inference and training cost relative to reasoning-based 20B guards, but the paper provides no latency, throughput, energy, batch-size, or end-to-end image-processing measurements, so the claimed efficiency is not quantitatively established. Effective: F1 results show strong performance on the selected text, multimodal, and synthetic policy-adaptability proxies, but they do not establish performance under live policy authoring, distribution shift, calibrated risk thresholds, or human-reviewed moderation workloads. Scalable: The model trains on 54.1M examples but is evaluated only on fixed benchmark sets and a generated taxonomy; behavior at 10×–100× traffic, policy volume, image complexity, context length, or language coverage is not tested. The work delivers a trained-model artifact in paper description, but no software, dataset, model-weight, or repository release is stated. Strengths - The instruction–query–document representation provides a concrete mechanism for consolidating datasets with incompatible label spaces without forcing them into a single universal taxonomy. - Same-content positive/negative query pairing directly targets a known failure mode of safety classifiers: predicting general harmfulness while ignoring which policy is being evaluated. - The ablations support the role of synthetic taxonomy data: it raises unseen-taxonomy F1 from 61.1% to 84.4%, while the three-way merge reaches 88.7% on the validation taxonomy and partially restores public-benchmark performance. - The model combines text and image moderation in a compact 3B-parameter system and reports competitive aggregate multimodal results, including 83.8% overall F1 versus 77.6% for the next listed baseline. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The paper explicitly acknowledges weaker prompt-classification performance in Arabic, Indonesian, and other low-resource languages. It also notes that the generated-data checkpoint can suffer distribution drift and that adding taxonomy data slightly degrades Aegis v2 performance, motivating model merging. The authors discuss the relative scarcity of visual safety data and compensate with general-purpose safe images, but they do not present a broader limitations section covering synthetic-label validity, calibration, adversarial robustness, or deployment cost. Analyst-Identified Gaps - The central adaptability benchmark is author-constructed through LLM rewriting and LLM verification; without independent human annotation or a naturally occurring policy-shift dataset, the 91.3% F1 result may overstate real-world policy generalization. - The benchmark taxonomy is described as independent at the leaf level, but 10 of 12 evaluation superclasses have high-level counterparts in training, and the evaluation categories are deliberately action-oriented and separable; this weakens the claim that the test measures entirely novel policies. - The paper does not quantify the contribution or quality of each of the 45.2M open-source, 4.4M synthetic, and 4.5M multimodal samples, nor does it report dataset deduplication, source-level contamination checks, or sensitivity to sampling ratios. - LLM-based cross-validation and vision-language reranking can remove legitimate minority or ambiguous examples and may encode the same policy biases the classifier is intended to make configurable; no human audit or subgroup analysis is reported. - A fixed 0.5 threshold is used for headline F1 despite moderation deployments having asymmetric false-positive and false-negative costs; precision–recall tradeoffs and per-category calibration are absent. - The efficiency claim is comparative and architectural rather than measured: there are no latency, throughput, memory, cost-per-million-examples, or image-resolution experiments. - The multimodal evaluation is small and narrow, and one LlavaGuard comparison uses an unavailable-image subset; robustness to OCR, memes, compositional image-text attacks, culturally specific content, and generated imagery is not established. - No public release is stated for the model weights, data processors, synthetic dataset, benchmark, or evaluation scripts, limiting independent reproduction. Bottom Line This is a strong engineering and empirical contribution for compact, query-conditioned safety classification, but practitioners should read it as a promising recipe rather than conclusive evidence of real-world policy adaptability until independent human-labeled evaluations, calibrated operating-point analysis, efficiency measurements, and reproducible artifact releases are provided.

PhiZero: A World Model Built Around Physical Language (150 ▲ )

Shuyao Shang, Yuqi Wang, Ruopeng Gao, Xu Chen, Tieniu Tan, Lue Fan, Zhaoxiang Zhang · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 31 Jul 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces PHIZERO, a video world model that learns a 256-symbol discrete representation of visual state transitions, predicts that representation autoregressively, and renders it into future video with a diffusion decoder. - Why it's important: Physically inconsistent consequences such as failed collisions, implausible object motion, and incorrect causal evolution limit the use of video generators as simulators for robotics, driving, and Physical AI. - How it does it: A transition-level Q-Former and finite scalar quantizer separate state changes from appearance, while a pretrained VLM predicts the resulting discrete transition sequence before a pretrained video diffusion model renders it. - The good: PHIZERO reports the best scores among listed systems on Physics-IQ Verified (IQ-Score 41.2), PhyGround (Physics Score 3.01; Overall 2.97), and WorldModelBench (Physics Adherence 4.88; Total 8.19), with supporting tokenizer ablations. - The missing: The paper does not provide quantitative evidence for long-horizon stability, real control or robot execution, inference cost, multiple-seed variability, or whether its claimed appearance/embodiment transfer works without domain-specific tokenizer adaptation and external image editing. - Read it or not: Researchers working on video world models, latent-action representations, or physically grounded generation should read it for the reason-then-render design, but practitioners should treat the robotics and sim-to-real demonstrations as qualitative rather than deployment evidence.

Problem & Motivation Video world models are expected to predict how the physical world evolves, but most current systems predict future pixels or latent visual states directly, leaving dynamics implicit and often producing visually plausible yet physically incorrect outcomes. The problem affects world simulation, autonomous driving, robotics, and embodied AI, where correct consequences of collisions, gravity, deformation, fluid motion, and causal interactions matter more than appearance alone. The paper targets the gap between compact, reusable representations of state transitions and existing latent-action or video-tokenization methods that are usually tied to particular tasks, embodiments, or visual domains. It also argues that natural language is too coarse to encode fine-grained physical transitions, while continuous visual latents retain too much appearance information and do not provide an explicit reasoning interface. Key Idea The central idea is to learn a discrete “physical language” from video reconstruction, using the first frame to carry static appearance and a compact sequence of transition tokens to carry future state evolution. The same token sequence is then used as an explicit prediction target for a VLM, producing a reason-then-render decomposition: infer the transition in a symbolic-like discrete space, then synthesize pixels conditionally. The representation is not a symbolic physics language or a set of interpretable physical variables; it is a learned empirical code whose claimed semantics arise from reconstruction, prediction, transfer, and benchmark performance. Methodology PHIZERO factorizes future-video modeling as p(V,z|I0,c)=pθ(z|I0,c)pψ(V|I0,z), where I0 is the first frame, c is a textual action intent, z is the physical-language sequence, and V is the future video. The tokenizer first applies a spatiotemporal encoder to a video, forms representations for each adjacent pair of latent temporal states with a shared transition-level Q-Former, concatenates the resulting features in temporal order, projects them to a low-dimensional space, and quantizes them with finite scalar quantization. The configuration uses 32 queries per adjacent transition, nine temporal latent states for a 33-frame clip, and therefore 256 tokens; FSQ levels (8,5,5,5,5,5) yield a 25K-symbol vocabulary. A pretrained Wan2.2-5B diffusion model serves as decoder: its text condition is replaced by the quantized transition context, and the first frame is supplied as a clean visual condition. Decoder training uses a flow-matching objective, with an initial pure-noise warm-up intended to prevent the pretrained denoiser from ignoring the new transition condition. The reasoner is initialized from Qwen3-VL-4B, extends its vocabulary with FSQ symbols, and predicts the 256-token sequence autoregressively using cross-entropy under teacher forcing. Training uses roughly 10K hours of filtered real video for tokenizer pretraining, 5M four-second real/simulated clips for tokenizer SFT and reasoner continued pretraining, and 1M motion-rich clips for reasoner SFT; training reportedly uses 128 NVIDIA A100 GPUs. The main design choices—appearance conditioning through the first frame, local adjacent-state Q-Former processing, and pure-noise warm-up—are supported by reconstruction ablations, although the paper does not isolate all interactions among them or establish that the learned code is physically rather than visually predictive. Key Results On Physics-IQ Verified, evaluated over 66 controlled real-world experiments, PHIZERO obtains S-IoU 58.2, ST-IoU 36.8, WS-IoU 27.6, and IQ-Score 41.2, compared with Wan2.2-14B at 51.1/20.5/28.5/32.2 and the listed Cosmos3-Super at IQ-Score 39.5. On PhyGround’s 250 image-text conditions covering 13 physical laws, it obtains General Quality 2.93, Physics Score 3.01, and Overall 2.97; Wan2.2-14B obtains 3.00/2.90/2.95 and Veo3.1 obtains 3.01/2.85/2.93. On WorldModelBench’s 350 conditions, it reports Physics Adherence 4.88, Common Sense 1.71, and Total 8.19, versus Wan2.2-5B at 4.51/1.41/7.98 and Runway at 4.27/1.65/8.08. For understanding, it reports 56.34% overall on IntPhys2, 41.7% average error on LikePhys, and YoCausal RSI 55.54%, CCI 6.20%, and aggregate rank 2.0; these results are competitive, not uniformly dominant, and the LikePhys table shows a particularly strong rigid-body result but weaker fluid and optical results. The tokenizer reconstructs 500 four-second real videos at 512x896 using 256 discrete tokens, achieving PSNR 28.9, SSIM 0.903, and LPIPS 0.087, versus VideoFlexTok with 288 tokens at 25.2/0.858/0.177 and the Wan VAE with 44,800 tokens at 37.7/0.957/0.042. Removing the diffusion decoder lowers PSNR/SSIM from 28.9/0.903 to 26.6/0.875, removing the transition Q-Former gives 28.2/0.896, and removing warm-up gives 27.9/0.894. On Physics-IQ, the reasoner score falls from 41.2 to 37.7 without simulation data and 39.2 without two-stage training; prompt enhancement applied to Wan2.2-5B reaches only 26.6 versus the baseline 21.2. The broader driving, robotics, interactive rollout, cross-embodiment, and sim-to-real results are presented as qualitative demonstrations rather than quantitative control or transfer evaluations. All headline experiments use short four-second clips, except for qualitative sliding-window rollouts. Novelty Classification NEW METHOD; NEW FORMULATION; NEW SYSTEM/TOOL; NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely new element is the explicit use of a learned, discrete, transition-focused video representation as the intermediate prediction language in a reason-then-render world model; the tokenizer itself combines established Q-Former compression, FSQ quantization, pretrained diffusion decoding, and VLM autoregressive prediction, and the empirical evidence suggests this combination improves physical-video benchmark scores but does not establish interpretable physical laws. Rigor & Reproducibility The paper includes useful component ablations for the tokenizer and reasoner, reconstruction comparisons against compressed video tokenizers, multiple benchmark families, and explicit training configurations. However, it reports no error bars, confidence intervals, multiple random seeds, statistical significance tests, or per-category variance. Several evaluations rely on specialized VLM judges or benchmark likelihood protocols, so the results may inherit evaluator biases; some baselines are commercial or self-reported systems, and the paper does not establish identical sampling, compute, or checkpoint conditions across all comparisons. The reasoner’s video-understanding evaluation uses physical-language likelihoods of sequences generated by the tokenizer, creating a coupled tokenizer/reasoner evaluation that may reward agreement with the learned representation rather than independently verified physical understanding. The training corpus contains 2.5M in-house clips in the SFT mixture, but its composition, licensing, and exact filtering reproducibility are not fully stated. The paper gives a project URL, https://Phi-Zero.github.io/, but does not state that code, datasets, checkpoints, or model weights are released; no repository URL or downloadable artifact is identified in the text. The use of VLM-based filtering, VLM-generated captions, simulation data, and benchmark-specific adaptation also creates possible selection and supervision biases that are not fully quantified. Deployability (4-property check) Profile: EMPIRICAL and SYSTEMS. Practical: The model uses a Wan2.2-5B diffusion decoder and Qwen3-VL-4B reasoner and can in principle run on commercially available GPUs, but the reported training recipe requires 128 NVIDIA A100 GPUs and inference latency, memory, and hardware requirements are not reported. Efficient: The 256-token representation is far smaller than the 44,800-token Wan VAE representation in the reconstruction comparison, but autoregressive prediction of 256 tokens followed by diffusion sampling may be slower or more expensive than direct video generation; no end-to-end throughput, latency, memory, or cost comparison is provided. Effective: Benchmark scores indicate improved physical plausibility and causal preference on several proxies, but the paper does not measure whether generated predictions support successful robot control, driving planning, policy learning, or real-world task completion. Scalable: The demonstrated model operates primarily on 33-frame, four-second clips; longer interaction is produced by qualitative sliding-window autoregression, with no quantitative 10x–100x horizon, scene-memory, drift, or closed-loop stability test. The work presents a software/modeling system and a project webpage, but the paper does not confirm a released library, CLI, dataset, trained model, or weights. Strengths - The reason-then-render factorization gives a concrete architectural answer to the problem of separating transition inference from pixel synthesis, rather than merely adding a physics loss to a video generator. - The first-frame conditioning plus compact FSQ bottleneck is a plausible mechanism for discouraging redundant appearance encoding, and the 256-versus-44,800 token comparison quantifies the intended compression tradeoff. - The evaluation spans physical generation, physical plausibility discrimination, intuitive physics, causal video understanding, and qualitative controllability, with improvements on several independent-looking benchmark families. - The paper includes targeted ablations showing measurable contributions from the diffusion prior, transition-level Q-Former, pure-noise warm-up, simulation data, and staged reasoner training. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors explicitly state that physical language is an empirical representation rather than an interpretable symbolic formulation of physical laws; that observational video cannot adequately cover visually ambiguous or inaccessible phenomena such as tactile interactions and microscopic dynamics; and that the current model and training corpus remain small relative to the diversity of the physical world. They also identify fixed-duration modeling and propose hierarchical or recurrent extensions for long-horizon prediction. These limitations are acknowledged directly, but the paper does not quantify their impact or evaluate the proposed extensions. Analyst-Identified Gaps - The claimed “zero-shot” cross-embodiment and sim-to-real transfer is not fully zero-shot at the representation level: the tokenizer is briefly fine-tuned on each source domain, and GPT-Image 2.0 is used to edit the target first frame. There is no comparison against no adaptation, direct motion-transfer baselines, or quantitative transfer metrics. - The main physical-generation claims depend heavily on VLM-judged or benchmark-specific metrics, with no human study, simulator-grounded trajectory error, conservation-law measurement, object-state tracking, or independent physics evaluator. - The paper does not test whether the reasoner predicts physically correct transitions when the textual action intent is novel, underspecified, contradictory, or outside the curated motion-rich training distribution. - The four-second training and evaluation horizon leaves unresolved whether autoregressive rollouts accumulate state drift, lose object identity, violate temporal causality, or become inconsistent under repeated controls. - The token representation may encode appearance, camera motion, or dataset-specific correlations despite the transfer demonstrations; the paper provides no mutual-information, intervention, counterfactual, or cross-domain generalization analysis that isolates dynamics from visual content. - There is no quantitative evaluation of action-conditioned driving or robotics accuracy, no real-robot execution, and no evidence that generated videos are useful for downstream planning or policy learning. - Compute-normalized comparisons, inference sampling settings, sample counts, confidence intervals, and independent replication are missing, making the magnitude and robustness of the reported improvements difficult to assess. Bottom Line PHIZERO is a substantial and technically coherent preprint whose discrete transition interface and reason-then-render decomposition merit attention, but its strongest evidence remains short-horizon benchmark performance and qualitative transfer, so it should not yet be treated as validated physical simulation or deployable robotics infrastructure.

CoRT: Counterfactual Replay for Token-Level Rubric-Guided Policy Optimization (75 ▲ )

Bo-Wen Zhang, Junwei He, Wen Wang, Song-Lin Lv, Wentao Ma, Rongyi Lin, Shuhan Zhong, Lan-Zhe Guo · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 30 Jul 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces CoRT, a token-level credit-weighting method that redistributes rubric-derived GRPO advantages using counterfactual replay of the same response under a criteria-free prompt. - Why it's important: Response-level rewards assign identical credit to every generated token, wasting structured rubric information and potentially reinforcing irrelevant text during language-model post-training. - How it does it: CoRT contrasts per-token log probabilities with and without rubric criteria, maps the contrast through a bounded sigmoid, normalizes weights within each response, and multiplies them by the signed GRPO advantage. - The good: Across Qwen3-4B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Qwen3-14B experiments, CoRT generally improves matched GRPO and is competitive with the learned RTT token-relevance baseline; for example, Qwen2.5-7B under CSR gains 11.85 points on MultiDimIF. - The missing: The paper does not report multiple seeds, error bars, significance tests, wall-clock training cost, or a direct evaluation showing that high-contrast tokens are causally better credit assignments rather than merely rubric-sensitive tokens. - Read it or not: Researchers working on rubric-based LLM reinforcement learning should read it for the simple policy-internal credit-allocation mechanism and diagnostics, but practitioners should wait for stronger variance and cost evidence before adopting it.

Problem & Motivation: Rubric-guided instruction-following RL provides criteria such as correctness, formatting, safety, and length, but GRPO typically collapses these judgments into a scalar response reward and broadcasts the resulting group-relative advantage uniformly over all generated tokens. This creates a credit-assignment mismatch: tokens that express a criterion receive the same update as incidental explanation or filler tokens. The target domain is language-model post-training for open-ended and multi-constraint instruction following, where exact token-level supervision is expensive and auxiliary relevance models add training and deployment complexity. The paper aims to close the gap between structured criterion-level feedback and uniform token-level policy updates without changing the verifier, scalar reward, or rollout procedure. Key Idea: The central insight is to treat the criteria-free likelihood of the already sampled response as a local counterfactual baseline. Tokens whose likelihood drops substantially when rubric criteria are removed are interpreted as more dependent on the rubric context; their bounded contrast-derived weights receive more of the original signed response advantage. This is a heuristic dependence signal, not a calibrated causal measure of token importance or correctness. Methodology: For each prompt group, the old policy samples eight responses from the full prompt x+ containing the user request and rubric criteria. A rubric verifier produces scalar rewards, either Constraint Satisfaction Rate, the fraction of positive criteria satisfied, or All-or-Nothing reward, which GRPO converts to Ai = (ri - mean(r))/(std(r) + epsilon). CoRT reuses the full-prompt per-token log probabilities and performs one additional forward scoring pass over the fixed response under the criteria-free prompt x−. It computes the contrast Delta_i,t = log pi(y_i,t | x+, y_i,<t) - log pi(y_i,t | x−, y_i,<t), then applies s_i,t = sigmoid(tau(Delta_i,t - b)) - 1/2 and provisional weights 1 + eta lambda_k s_i,t. The weights are response-mean normalized so their average is one, and the clipped PPO/GRPO surrogate uses stop-gradient shaped advantages Ahat_i,t = w_i,t Ai. The default settings use eta = 0.5, zero-centered unit-temperature contrasts, a 100-step SmoothStep ramp, prompt batches of 64, eight responses per prompt, maximum prompt/response lengths of 2048/4096, learning rate 10^-6, and clipping bounds of 0.2 and 0.27. The three critical design decisions are the criteria-free fixed-response intervention, the bounded sigmoid transform, and response normalization plus gradual activation. The first is intuitively motivated and supported by case studies, but its attribution interpretation is not formally validated; the latter two are supported by stability ablations but introduce additional hyperparameters and training-schedule dependence. Key Results: On Qwen3-4B with CSR reward, CoRT improves matched GRPO by 1.77/1.27 points on IFEval prompt/instruction accuracy, 2.18/2.81 on IFBench prompt/instruction accuracy, 6.10 on MultiDimIF, and 3.16 on AdvancedIF overall, reaching 86.06, 90.48, 34.49, 36.24, 80.48, and 49.18 respectively across the reported metrics. Under AON, it improves GRPO on most metrics, including +7.35 on MultiDimIF, but trails GRPO on AdvancedIF overall and improves only 0.41 there. On Qwen2.5-7B with CSR, gains over GRPO are +3.36/+3.10 on IFEval, +6.40/+6.45 on IFBench, +11.85 on MultiDimIF, and +3.27 on AdvancedIF overall; under AON it loses 2.31/1.91 points on IFBench while gaining 10.22 on MultiDimIF. Qwen3-14B results show CSR improvements on all five reported metrics and AON improvements on IFBench and MultiDimIF, but decreases on IFEval. CoRT also improves all five DAPO metrics and four of five GSPO metrics under CSR on Qwen3-4B, with a small GSPO decrease on MultiDimIF. The headline average gain of 4.4 percentage points is reported by the authors across comparisons, but the paper does not provide uncertainty estimates. Evaluation uses IFBench, IFEval, MultiDimIF, and judge-based AdvancedIF, with five sampled responses at evaluation time; the main tables select the best checkpoint within the first 500 training steps for three benchmarks, while AdvancedIF is evaluated at step 500. These are standard or recent instruction-following benchmarks, but the main baselines and reference rows are taken from RTT rather than rerun by the authors, and the training scale remains relatively small: 4B, 7B, and 14B models, one 16k-example HIR training set, and 500 trainer steps. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD and ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION: the paper introduces counterfactual fixed-response likelihood contrasts as a rubric-dependent token-credit signal and combines them with bounded weighting, response normalization, and scheduled activation, while the underlying GRPO/PPO objective, rubric rewards, and policy-gradient machinery remain standard; the closest competing method, RTT, already targets the same response-to-token credit problem with a learned relevance discriminator. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper includes ablations removing response normalization, the SmoothStep ramp, or both, plus a CoRT-only perturbation that removes the normal GRPO advantage path. These diagnostics show that unnormalized weights drift toward approximately 1.04 and coincide with late increases in clipping, gradient norm, and entropy, while removing the ramp causes abrupt late instability. Criterion-wise and matched-context case studies provide qualitative evidence that local formatting-related criteria produce localized likelihood contrasts. However, no multiple random seeds, error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported. The main comparison uses baseline numbers copied from RTT, which limits controlled reproducibility even though the authors claim a shared protocol. The evaluation is concentrated on HIR-derived rubric instruction following and related benchmarks, and the attribution signal is developed and tested in the same rubric-conditioned setting. No code, dataset release, model-weight release, or URL is mentioned. The extra forward pass is described, but actual wall-clock, memory, throughput, and total compute measurements are absent. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL, with a systems-like training modification but no released software artifact. Practical: The method can run on commercially available accelerator hardware because it adds only a forward scoring pass over existing response tokens and uses ordinary GRPO/PPO operations, although the paper does not report hardware requirements. Efficient: Relative to matched GRPO, it adds approximately one criteria-free forward pass per sampled response and therefore likely increases training compute substantially, but no measured latency, memory, or throughput overhead is provided; it avoids the separate relevance-model training required by RTT. Effective: The evidence supports improved instruction-following benchmark scores over matched GRPO in most reported comparisons, but it does not establish that the method improves true token-level causal credit assignment or generalizes beyond rubric-sensitive proxy metrics. Scalable: The method is tested on 4B, 7B, and 14B models but not at 10x–100x training or model scale, long multi-turn horizons, tool use, or large production workloads; scalability beyond the extra forward-pass cost is claimed rather than demonstrated. The paper delivers an algorithmic training recipe, not a released library, CLI, dataset, or trained model artifact. Strengths: - The method addresses a precise mismatch between rubric-level supervision and token-level policy updates without changing the reward interface or requiring token-level annotations. - Fixed-response counterfactual replay is operationally simple: it reuses sampled trajectories, needs no extra generation or verifier call, and requires only one additional scoring pass. - Response normalization gives a clear invariant: the mean shaped advantage remains equal to the original GRPO advantage, separating within-response redistribution from response-level reward scaling. - The experiments cover two model families, three model sizes up to 14B, two reward granularities, four instruction-following benchmarks, and compatibility with DAPO and GSPO; the stability ablations test the proposed integration controls rather than only reporting final scores. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state that replay signals can be weak when criteria have little effect on token likelihoods, when criteria duplicate information already present in the original prompt, or when response-level rewards are noisy. They also acknowledge that the current method estimates criteria reliance along observed trajectories and identify criterion-specific allocation, finer-grained interventions, and longer-horizon credit across turns, actions, and tool calls as future work. These limitations are confronted directly in the conclusion, but the paper does not quantify their frequency or impact. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The central assumption that rubric dependence is useful credit is not adequately separated from rubric dependence that is irrelevant, stylistic, or caused by prompt-length and context-distribution changes. The case studies show alignment with visible formatting cues, but not that weighting those tokens improves causal policy outcomes compared with alternative attribution signals. The criteria-free prompt is a strong intervention that changes the input distribution and may remove semantic context or alter tokenization behavior, so matched-context controls are helpful but insufficient as a general confound analysis. The paper lacks seed-level variance and statistical testing, making the reported small gains and metric-specific regressions difficult to assess. Best-within-500-step checkpoint selection can favor favorable validation noise, and the authors do not provide an equally transparent selection protocol for all baselines. The evaluation uses a single HIR-16k training source and closely related instruction-following benchmarks, with no out-of-domain alignment, safety, multi-turn, or production workload test. RTT and other baselines are not fully rerun, and the method's compute overhead is not measured. Finally, the narrow multiplier range of 0.75–1.25 limits how much credit can actually be redistributed, so the paper does not establish whether the gains arise from the proposed attribution signal or from a mild regularized perturbation of GRPO. Bottom Line: This is a useful and reasonably well-motivated preprint for researchers designing rubric-guided LLM RL, but its practical and scientific claims remain provisional because attribution validity, statistical reliability, compute cost, and out-of-domain scalability are not measured.

Zijun Lin, Zeqing Wang, Cheston Tan, Bihan Wen, Yeying Jin · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 30 Jul 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces StatePlay, a game world model that jointly predicts internal game states and generates action-conditioned video frames for mechanically consistent gameplay. - Why it's important: Pixel-plausible game rollouts can violate essential rules such as skill-meter requirements and game termination, making them visually convincing but not genuinely playable. - How it does it: It adds a 0.76B-parameter state branch to a 5B video diffusion model, preserves modality-specific processing with a mixture-of-transformers architecture, and exchanges information through bidirectional joint attention while training states with Smooth L1 regression and video with flow matching. - The good: On a 10,000-clip Street Fighter 3 dataset, StatePlay reaches 0.947 state alignment and 82.3%/78.3% mechanics fidelity under Gemini-3.1-Pro/GPT-5.5 evaluation, versus 63.7%/59.7% for the strongest stateless fine-tuned baseline. - The missing: The evaluation uses only 100 generated test samples from one fighting game, relies substantially on large-language-model visual judges, and does not test long-horizon rollouts, multiple games, independent engine-state verification, or the cost of inference. - Read it or not: Researchers working on interactive video generation and game world models should read it for the explicit-state formulation and ablations, but practitioners seeking a deployable game simulator should treat the results as an initial single-game demonstration rather than validated infrastructure.

Problem & Motivation: Action-conditioned game world models generate future frames that may follow player inputs and look realistic, but pixel supervision alone does not reliably capture hidden, rule-governed variables such as health, skill meters, timers, and terminal status. This creates rollouts in which a character attacks after reaching zero health, a special move occurs without sufficient meter, or a match continues after a knockout. The problem affects interactive game generation and any downstream system that requires valid closed-loop gameplay rather than a visual approximation. The specific gap is the absence of explicit internal-state prediction and evaluation of whether state modeling improves mechanics fidelity, although the paper's claim that prior work entirely lacks state modeling should be interpreted narrowly because it cites contemporaneous state-annotated datasets and related work. Key Idea: The central insight is to treat game state as a low-dimensional, rule-sensitive modality that should be predicted explicitly and coupled to video generation, rather than forcing the video model to infer mechanics indirectly from pixels. StatePlay uses separate state and visual experts, then lets each modality attend to the other so predicted health, meters, timers, and related temporal dynamics can influence frame generation while visual dynamics inform state estimation. Methodology: The authors construct synchronized gameplay data from Street Fighter 3 using the Stable Retro/Gymnasium interface. Agents act in an 11-dimensional space comprising four movement actions, six normal attacks, and one super-art action; the collection pipeline records frames, actions, timer, both characters' health points, and both skill meters. Episodes are segmented into 5-second clips at 20 FPS, and 10,000 clips are balanced across result-win, result-lose, macro-success, macro-fail, and normal categories, with Gemini-3.1-Pro-assisted NPC strategy descriptions. The model starts from Wan2.2-TI2V-5B and adds a 0.76B state branch, for 5.759B parameters overall. The state sequence is perturbed as \(s_t=(1-t)s_0+t\epsilon_s\), encoded, temporally self-attended, and decoded with Smooth L1 regression; visual VAE latents are perturbed analogously and trained with the flow-matching objective \(L_{video}=E[\|v_\theta(x_t,t)-(\epsilon_v-x_0)\|_2^2]\). Action embeddings enter both branches, and bidirectional cross-modal attention updates the visual and state representations before modality-specific feed-forward and decoding layers. The total objective is \(L_{train}=\lambda_{state}L_{state}+\lambda_{video}L_{video}\), with both weights set to 1. At inference, the first-frame state is supplied and later states are initialized from noise and predicted. Critical design decisions are the separate modality branches, direct regression rather than flow matching for state prediction, and noise-based state initialization; the paper provides ablations supporting each choice, but does not deeply justify the supplied-initial-state protocol or establish that the predicted states causally enforce game rules. Key Results: On the state-aware fine-tuning comparison, StatePlay obtains SSIM 0.378, LPIPS 0.424, movement accuracy 92.5%, attack accuracy 95.0%, state alignment 0.947, and mechanics fidelity of 82.3% ± 0.5 under Gemini-3.1-Pro and 78.3% ± 0.5 under GPT-5.5. The strongest stateless baseline, ReactiveGWM, obtains SSIM 0.376, LPIPS 0.439, movement accuracy 95.0%, attack accuracy 100.0%, and mechanics fidelity 63.7% ± 2.1 and 59.7% ± 0.9, respectively. Thus, StatePlay improves mechanics fidelity by 18.6 percentage points under Gemini and 18.6 points under GPT relative to ReactiveGWM, although the paper describes this as an 18.6% improvement. Zero-shot baselines have mechanics fidelity below 53.0% under both judges, with ReactiveGWM reaching 48.0% and 43.3% while achieving the best zero-shot visual metrics among the listed models. In the architecture ablation, MoT-style coupling with regression reaches 82.3%/78.3% mechanics fidelity versus 64.7%/67.7% for the shared backbone with regression; replacing regression with flow matching reduces state alignment from 0.947 to 0.845 and mechanics fidelity from 82.3%/78.3% to 60.7%/62.0%. The reported test scale is small: 100 generated samples evenly covering mechanics categories, with judge results averaged over three runs. The paper does not report long-horizon rollout length, real-time throughput, latency, GPU memory, or results at larger datasets or model scales. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD, NEW DATASET/benchmark, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, and ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION: the main contribution is an explicit state-and-video game world model with modality-specific branches and cross-modal attention, supported by a newly constructed 10,000-clip annotated fighting-game dataset and evidence that state supervision improves mechanics-fidelity scores; the architecture combines established transformer, diffusion/flow-matching, attention, and regression components rather than introducing a new learning theory or hard rule-enforcement mechanism. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper includes useful component ablations for shared versus MoT-style coupling, flow matching versus regression state losses, and broadcast versus noise-based state inputs. It reports mean ± standard deviation over three evaluator runs, but not multiple training seeds, confidence intervals, statistical significance, or variance across independently trained models. The mechanics metric depends on Gemini-3.1-Pro and GPT-5.5 judging generated videos from prompts and reference images; this provides two evaluators but remains a proxy rather than an executable game-engine check. Attack accuracy uses ClipAttackNet, a custom classifier trained on about 5,000 clips, and movement accuracy relies on SAM2.1 and Grounding DINO with predefined thresholds; classifier and tracking errors are not independently quantified. The test set contains only 100 generated samples, and the paper does not clearly specify train/test episode separation, dataset release, annotation quality checks, or whether the game-engine state trace is available for every generated rollout. The project page is provided at https://jimntu.github.io/stateplay_page/, but code, dataset, model weights, and a repository are not stated as publicly released. Comparisons are reasonably informative against ReactiveGWM under matched fine-tuning, but LingBot-World models are excluded from fine-tuning because of their size, and the zero-shot comparisons do not provide equivalent action-control or state metrics. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL. - Practical: The 5.759B-parameter model is plausibly runnable on commercially available high-memory GPUs, but the paper reports no hardware configuration, inference latency, memory requirement, or real-time performance. - Efficient: StatePlay adds 0.76B parameters, approximately 15.2% over the 5B visual branch, but the paper provides no compute, sampling-step, throughput, or energy comparison with the baselines. - Effective: The evidence shows improved state alignment and judge-based mechanics fidelity on selected Street Fighter 3 clips, while movement and attack control remain close to the strongest baseline; it does not establish reliable executable gameplay or eliminate visual-state contradictions. - Scalable: Scalability is not evaluated: experiments use one game, 10,000 training clips, 100 generated test samples, and short 5-second clips, with no 10×–100× data, horizon, game-genre, or environment-scale test. The work delivers a model design and an annotated dataset construction procedure, but no publicly documented software, dataset, or trained-model artifact is stated beyond the project page. Strengths: - It identifies a meaningful failure mode—mechanics violations that pixel-level metrics can miss—and turns it into an explicit modeling and evaluation target. - The state/video factorization is technically coherent: separate experts preserve the different statistical structures of low-dimensional rule variables and high-dimensional visual latents while joint attention allows information exchange. - The controlled ablations support the main design choices, with regression improving mechanics fidelity over flow matching and MoT-style coupling substantially outperforming the shared-backbone variant. - The matched fine-tuning comparison against ReactiveGWM shows that the gain is not simply attributable to using a stronger visual backbone, although the evaluation remains narrow. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state that the evaluation is restricted to Street Fighter 3 because synchronized state-frame-action datasets are scarce, and they call for broader validation across genres and larger, more diverse datasets. They also report occasional inconsistencies in pixel-level health bars and skill meters and degraded visual quality when multiple mechanics occur simultaneously, such as a super art coinciding with match termination. These limitations are confronted directly, but the discussion does not quantify their frequency or evaluate the proposed method beyond the single-game setting. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The most important unacknowledged concern is that mechanics fidelity is judged by LLMs using visible result screens and visual heuristics rather than by replaying generated actions in the original game engine or comparing every predicted transition against an authoritative simulator. The protocol also supplies the initial state at inference, which may make the task easier and leaves unclear how state estimation behaves from pixels alone or after compounding rollout errors. The 100-sample evaluation is too small to support strong claims about rare failures, and the balanced training distribution may overrepresent terminal and super-art events relative to natural gameplay. The paper does not report independent human validation of the LLM judges, exact train/test split construction, training-seed variance, long-horizon consistency, model sampling cost, or cross-game transfer. It also does not test whether explicit state prediction improves actual interactive control in closed loop, as opposed to improving classification of short generated clips. Bottom Line: This is a worthwhile early demonstration that explicit latent game-state modeling can improve mechanics-consistency scores in action-conditioned video generation, but its single-game, short-horizon, small-sample, LLM-judged evaluation is not yet sufficient to support claims of general playable-world modeling or practical deployment.

VideoCoCo: Code-as-CoT for Physically-Consistent Video Generation via an Agentic Dual-Engine System (61 ▲ )

Haodong Li, Tianfei Ren, Xiaoxiao Ma, Chunmei Qing, Zhen Fang, Sipeng He, Ziyu Guo, Haoyu Wu, Juanxi Tian, Yihang Zou, Ruichuan An, Dongzhi Jiang, Boxue Yang, Ji Xie, Xu Huang, Wenhao Yan, Jialv Zou, Zhengrong Yue, Yaxin Luo, Xiaotong Li, Yuzhu Wang, Junyan Ye, Jinjing Zhao, Zehui Chen, Lin Chen, Renye Yan, Feng Zhao, Pheng-Ann Heng · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 31 Jul 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces VideoCoCo, a dual-engine text-to-video system that converts prompts into executable Blender simulations and uses the resulting drafts to guide photorealistic video editing. - Why it's important: Physically plausible dynamics remain unreliable in text-to-video systems, especially for processes such as melting, sublimation, collapse, shattering, and buoyancy where visual plausibility can mask causal errors. - How it does it: A coding agent writes and executes Blender Python code to create a deterministic, temporally dense white-clay draft, while an adapted video editor restyles that draft under an appearance-focused instruction. - The good: On the reported benchmarks, VideoCoCo improves OmniWeaving from 0.475 to 0.558 on PhyGenBench and from 52.18% to 77.88% on VBench-2.0, with ablations indicating that executable drafting contributes independently of editor tuning. - The missing: The paper does not report inference latency, compute cost, multiple-seed variability, human evaluation, or controlled comparisons against other physics-aware methods using the same base model and data budget. - Read it or not: Researchers working on physics-aware video generation, controllable generation, or executable intermediate representations should read it for the system design and ablation, but deployment-oriented readers should wait for latency, robustness, and artifact-release details.

Novelty (80) and Non-Obviousness (77) are solid because executable Blender programs provide an inspectable process-level intermediate, while the ablation supports a real contribution from draft conditioning. Rigor (55) and Resilience (58) are weakened by heterogeneous unmatched baselines, synthetic teacher targets, GPT-based scoring, no human or simulator verification, and missing runtime and failure-rate analysis; Impact (60) reflects a potentially useful pipeline and linked repository but no confirmed artifact contents. Problem & Motivation: Text-to-video models must infer a complete spatiotemporal process from a compressed natural-language description while also synthesizing appearance. This creates a gap between semantic intent and physically coherent evolution: models may generate attractive frames while violating gravity, material behavior, thermal transitions, or causal ordering. The target users are researchers and developers building physically faithful video-generation and world-modeling systems. Prior approaches use textual plans, layouts, keyframes, intermediate visual states, search, simulators, rewards, or preference optimization, but the paper argues that these representations are either non-executable, temporally sparse, tied to fixed phenomena, or indirect. The central gap is an inspectable intermediate representation that instantiates the full process before photorealistic synthesis. Key Idea: The core insight is to treat executable Blender code—not text plans, isolated keyframes, or latent intermediate states—as a process-level chain of thought. Code forces the agent to specify objects, properties, interactions, and temporal evolution; execution converts that specification into a dense deterministic draft; and draft-conditioned editing separates “what happens” from “what it looks like.” The conceptual novelty lies primarily in applying executable Code-as-CoT to complete temporal video processes rather than image previews, although the overall architecture combines established program synthesis, simulation, video editing, diffusion fine-tuning, and agentic instruction generation. Methodology: At inference, a coding agent maps a prompt p to a self-contained Blender Python program c = A_code(p). The program defines the scene, objects, physical properties, animations, and event evolution. A sandboxed Blender environment executes c and renders a low-fidelity white-clay draft d = B(c), intended to provide a temporally dense structural scaffold rather than a final visual output. A second instruction agent consumes the original prompt and draft and produces an appearance-focused editing instruction e = A_edit(p,d), describing subjects, materials, lighting, camera, and cinematic style while being instructed not to redefine motion. A draft-conditioned video editor then generates the final video v_hat = G_theta(d,e). To adapt the editor, the authors construct VideoCoCo-3K, containing 3,000 draft–instruction–target triplets. Each target is generated once by the Seedance 2.0 teacher editor from the simulated draft and instruction; benchmark prompts and near-duplicates are reportedly excluded. The editor is initialized from OmniWeaving and trained with a standard conditional diffusion denoising loss, E[||epsilon - epsilon_theta(z_t,t,d,e)||_2^2], using either full fine-tuning or LoRA. Three important design decisions are: using Blender code as the process representation, separating dynamics from appearance through draft-conditioned editing, and using teacher-generated triplets for adaptation. The paper motivates all three, but does not quantify code-generation success rates, simulator failure rates, draft fidelity, instruction-agent reliability, or the degree to which the editor actually preserves draft motion. Key Results: On PhyGenBench, the OmniWeaving base scores 0.475 overall, while VideoCoCo with LoRA adaptation scores 0.558, exceeding Wan2.2-TI2V-5B at 0.544. VideoCoCo reports category scores of 0.558 for mechanics, 0.613 for optics, 0.511 for thermal, and 0.525 for material; the largest gains over OmniWeaving are material, increasing from 0.392 to 0.525, and thermal, increasing from 0.433 to 0.511. On VBench-2.0, the average rises from 52.18% to 77.88%, with mechanics improving from 62.79% to 92.31%, thermotics from 52.08% to 72.92%, and material from 41.67% to 68.42%. This is the best reported average on both benchmarks, although VideoCoCo trails CogVideoX-1.5 on VBench material, 68.42% versus 83.19%. The ablation on PhyGenBench shows 0.506 for tuning-free draft conditioning, 0.535 for full tuning, and 0.558 for LoRA tuning, compared with 0.475 for OmniWeaving. Thus, the reported evidence supports independent contributions from drafting and editor adaptation, and LoRA outperforms full fine-tuning despite updating fewer parameters. The evaluation uses standard physics-focused benchmark suites at standard benchmark scale, but the paper provides no sample counts, confidence intervals, per-prompt variance, number of generated samples, or latency measurements. The physical metrics rely on GPT-4o judging for PhyGenBench and benchmark protocols for VBench-2.0, so the results measure benchmark-assessed plausibility rather than verified physical correctness. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD, NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, NEW DATASET/RESOURCE, and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely distinctive contribution is the use of executable Blender programs and rendered simulations as dense, inspectable process-level intermediates for video generation; VideoCoCo-3K provides aligned supervision for this interface, while the dual-engine design and LoRA adaptation are largely combinations of existing program synthesis, simulation, video editing, and diffusion adaptation techniques applied to physical video generation. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper includes a useful component ablation: tuning-free draft conditioning isolates a gain from the executable draft, while full tuning and LoRA tuning test editor adaptation. It also compares against several closed and open video generators and reports per-category metrics on two physics-oriented benchmarks. However, it reports no error bars, multiple random seeds, significance tests, human judgments, confidence intervals, or statistical analysis. The central results compare the proposed pipeline, built on OmniWeaving, against heterogeneous standalone generators with different architectures, training data, parameter counts, and conditioning mechanisms; there is no matched-compute or matched-base-model comparison against other physics-aware methods such as simulator-guided or preference-optimized systems. The targets in VideoCoCo-3K are synthetic teacher outputs from Seedance 2.0 rather than human-authored ground truth, which risks transferring teacher artifacts and makes the training and evaluation assumptions difficult to audit. The paper states that benchmark prompts and near-duplicates were excluded, but gives no procedure or quantitative overlap analysis. A project page and GitHub URL are provided (https://github.com/micky-li-hd/VideoCoCo), but the paper does not state whether the code, VideoCoCo-3K data, Blender programs, trained weights, teacher outputs, or exact evaluation scripts are released. The work is an arXiv v1 preprint dated July/August 2026, not a peer-reviewed publication according to the supplied document. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS, with empirical evaluation. Practical: The pipeline can in principle run on commercially available hardware using Blender, an LLM/code agent, and an open video model, but the paper does not specify hardware, software versions, API dependencies, or end-to-end runtime. Efficient: It adds code generation, sandbox execution, draft rendering, instruction generation, and video editing; no latency, memory, FLOP, token, or cost comparison is reported, and the authors explicitly acknowledge additional inference latency. Effective: Benchmark evidence shows large gains in automated physical-plausibility scores, but it does not establish verified physical correctness, improved visual quality, robustness to failed or incorrect code, or performance on applications outside the two benchmarks. Scalable: The paper tests 3,000 training triplets and standard benchmark prompts, but does not test 10×–100× larger data, longer videos, higher resolutions, complex multi-object scenes, or phenomena beyond Blender’s expressiveness; it explicitly identifies turbulent fluids and other complex dynamics as difficult. The work delivers a claimed software artifact through the linked project page and GitHub repository, plus a claimed dataset and adapted model, but the supplied paper does not confirm the release contents. Strengths: - It identifies a concrete failure mode in text-to-video generation and supplies an intermediate representation that is executable, temporally dense, and inspectable rather than merely descriptive. - The tuning-free ablation provides evidence that the draft itself contributes to physical-consistency gains, rather than attributing all improvement to additional editor training. - The dual-engine separation is technically sensible: a simulator handles explicit process structure while a generative editor handles appearance, reducing the need for one model to infer dynamics and photorealism simultaneously. - The method produces reusable intermediate artifacts—code, draft video, and editing instruction—that could support debugging, manual revision, and future distillation into end-to-end models. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that the method introduces additional inference latency and is limited by the expressiveness of Blender. They specifically identify highly complex phenomena such as turbulent fluids as challenging to synthesize zero-shot. They propose specialized physics engines such as Taichi and knowledge distillation as future directions. These limitations are acknowledged directly, but the paper does not quantify latency, simulator failure frequency, or the range of phenomena that fail. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The evaluation omits direct comparisons with the strongest physics-aware generation systems cited in the related-work section under a controlled protocol, making it difficult to separate the value of executable drafting from the choice of OmniWeaving and editor adaptation. The large VBench-2.0 improvement may reflect benchmark-specific alignment or judge behavior, yet there is no human evaluation, physical-verification test, prompt-level breakdown, or robustness analysis. The use of Seedance 2.0 to generate every training target creates a teacher-dependence and possible contamination concern, and the paper does not measure whether targets preserve the Blender draft or whether the adapted editor copies teacher artifacts. It does not report code-generation validity, sandbox crash rates, revision policies, simulator parameter accuracy, render cost, video quality trade-offs, or failure cases where the code agent writes an incorrect process. It also lacks tests of prompt ambiguity, out-of-distribution phenomena, longer temporal horizons, camera changes, scene composition, and manual code editing. Claims of controllability and reproducibility therefore exceed the reported evidence. Bottom Line: This is a worthwhile preprint for researchers exploring executable intermediates and physics-aware video generation, with credible benchmark gains and a meaningful draft-versus-tuning ablation, but its practical and scientific impact remains uncertain until matched baselines, independent physical or human evaluation, failure analysis, and runtime and artifact-release details are provided.

Visual prompt engineering for video models (11 ▲ )

Robert Geirhos, Yuxuan Li, Thaddäus Wiedemer, Neha Kalibhat, Zi Wang, Mani Malek, Oyvind Tafjord, Kevin Swersky, Been Kim, Priyank Jaini · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 29 Jul 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces visual prompt engineering (VIPE), a test-time pipeline that edits a task image into alternative visual presentations before a video model attempts the associated reasoning task. - Why it's important: Video-generation models often fail on abstract or synthetic visual inputs despite succeeding on visually equivalent realistic scenes, so changing the input may improve reliability more cheaply than generating many additional videos or retraining the model. - How it does it: A human or VLM ideates a structure-preserving visual transformation, an image editor samples candidate images, an optional VLM filter selects a faithful candidate, and the video model generates and is scored on a solution attempt. - The good: On VPCT, Veo 3.1 accuracy increases from 41.3% on sketches to 59.3% after VIPE, while the paper’s realism ablation indicates that realistic texture—not merely adding 3D depth—drives much of the gain. - The missing: The strongest automated results rely on selecting the best of up to 20 variants using task- or sample-level oracle selection, and the study does not establish comparable gains under a strictly held-out, non-oracular deployment protocol across larger and independent benchmarks. - Read it or not: Read it if you study video-model reasoning, test-time compute, or multimodal evaluation; practitioners should treat the gains as promising evidence of representation bias rather than as a validated general-purpose production method.
