Problem & Motivation Video generation models are increasingly used as visual reasoners: given an image and a textual instruction, they generate a video that is intended to enact a solution to a maze, physics, sorting, search, or puzzle task. Existing evaluations generally treat the visual prompt as fixed, even though its rendering style can determine whether the model maintains object identity, scene geometry, and temporal consistency. The paper addresses the gap between poor performance on abstract sketches or synthetic diagrams and substantially better behavior on semantically equivalent realistic scenes. The target users are researchers evaluating video models and developers seeking higher test-time reliability without changing model parameters. The central practical concern is that a benchmark may measure failures of visual representation and generation consistency rather than the underlying reasoning capability. Key Idea The core insight is that visual prompt optimization can bridge a representation or training-distribution gap: transforming a flat sketch into a realistic, materially grounded scene gives a video model visual patterns and object dynamics that are more familiar, improving persistence and reducing hallucinated scene changes. The paper argues that this is distinct from simply adding spatial depth; its “unnatural textures” control retains 3D-looking geometry but removes realism and generally fails to reproduce the VIPE gain. The idea is conceptually simple and closely parallels text prompt engineering, but the application to image-conditioned video reasoning and its connection to temporal scene consistency are the main intellectual contributions. Methodology VIPE represents each task as an image-text pair and replaces the image with a candidate variant while attempting to preserve task logic, spatial layout, element count, and correspondence. The pipeline has three stages: (1) an ideator, implemented either manually, with Gemini 3.1 Pro for freeform proposals, or with the ACE atomic-concept-editing framework, produces a natural-language image-edit instruction; (2) an image editor, primarily Nano Banana Pro or Nano Banana 2, samples \(m=5\) edited images; and (3) an optional Gemini-based filter chooses the most faithful candidate. The selected image is passed with a task text prompt to a video model, chiefly Veo 3.1, and the generated video is scored by deterministic or VLM-based autoraters. Freeform ideation is open-loop and generates 20 variants; ACE performs a three-level tree search with branching factors 6, 5, and 3, uses autorater feedback, and learns task-specific “constitutions” describing successful mutations. The paper also evaluates majority-vote self-consistency over up to 20 video generations, compares image and text prompt engineering, tests native image-generation models, and constructs a realism progression experiment. Critical design decisions are the preservation constraints in the image editor and filter, the use of realism/material changes as the dominant search direction, and the reliance on downstream autoraters for variant evaluation. The first two are plausible but not fully causally isolated; the third creates opportunities for evaluator-induced selection effects. Key Results On the 100-sample VPCT physics dataset averaged over 10 runs of the full dataset, Veo 3.1 improves from 41.3% accuracy on sketches to 59.3% with VIPE; Omni Flash improves from 56.3% to 67.5%. Wan2.2 improves from near-chance baseline performance—32.4% for TI2V English, 35.0% for TI2V Chinese, 42.3% for I2V English, and 35.6% for I2V Chinese—to 42.3%, 43.3%, 43.5%, and 40.3%, respectively. The unnatural-texture ablation reaches 44.0% for Veo 3.1 and 64.5% for Omni Flash, suggesting that 3D structure alone does not explain the gain. With Veo 3.1 on VPCT, 20-way majority voting raises the baseline from 41.3% to 50.0%, whereas one VIPE prompt reaches 59.3% and VIPE plus 20-way voting reaches 68.0%; the paper reports that, for a fixed API budget, allocating resources to more VIPE variants generally outperforms generating more videos per variant. Across six task families—four maze splits, two RushHour levels, VPCT, Conjunctive Search, Connect the Dots, and Sort 3 Numbers—the automated experiments generate 18,160 videos. Reported best-variant error reductions range from 2.6% on Maze 7×7 and 8.0% on RushHour Level 3 to 42.9% on VPCT, 60.4% on Conjunctive Search, 70.0% on Sort 3 Numbers with freeform VIPE, and 40.0%, 75.0%, and 100.0% for ACE on Conjunctive Search, Connect the Dots, and Sort 3 Numbers; these are best-variant figures rather than average deployment performance. In the text-versus-image comparison, best text/image variants achieve 62%/73% on VPCT, 12%/62% on Conjunctive Search, 86%/76% on Sort 3 Numbers, and 35%/8% on Connect the Dots, from baselines of 57%, 4%, 4%, and 3%. On native image models, VIPE is inconsistent: Nano Banana Pro image Pass@1 is 45% on sketches versus 50% on VIPE, Nano Banana 2 image falls from 37% to 21%, and Nano Banana 2 text is best on sketches at 58% Pass@1 and 80% majority-vote accuracy. A realism progression on a synthetic motion task increases human-rated scene consistency from 0% to 11%, 24%, and 59% as railway tracks, wagons, and background are added. The strongest surprising result is that Gemini 3.1 Pro reaches 96% on original VPCT sketches but only 4% on upside-down-bucket controls despite 100% accuracy at identifying whether buckets are upside down, indicating shortcut-sensitive physics reasoning; this control concerns a VLM rather than the main video-generation experiments. Novelty Classification NEW METHOD, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION. The genuinely new contribution is the formulation and empirical demonstration of editing an image-conditioned video model’s visual prompt as a test-time reasoning lever, together with evidence for a realism/representation bias and its interaction with temporal consistency; the ideator, image editor, filtering, ACE search, self-consistency, and VLM autorating components are established techniques combined in this setting rather than new algorithms. Rigor & Reproducibility The paper includes useful controls, 95% confidence intervals for many plots, repeated runs, an unnatural-texture ablation, language-versus-image comparisons, native image-model comparisons, a realism progression, and autorater validation against humans. It reports human agreement for rubric-based autorating on roughly 216 videos, VPCT autorating on 100 videos, maze autorating on 100 videos, and RushHour parsing on 120 videos. However, the experimental design has important selection and evaluation concerns. Figure 3 emphasizes the best of 20 variants per task/split and an oracle best variant per sample; those numbers do not represent the expected performance of an automatically selected variant on unseen samples. The automated ideators and filters are Google models, the principal reasoner is largely the closed-source Veo 3.1, and the image editor, VLM autorater, and video model share a vendor ecosystem, limiting independent reproducibility. The paper provides prompts and dataset descriptions but does not state that code, edited datasets, model weights, or a complete reproducible pipeline are released; no repository URL is given. Several task datasets are very small or author-generated: Conjunctive Search and Sort 3 Numbers have five images, Connect the Dots has six, and many automated experiments use only the first 10 samples of larger splits. The paper reports inconsistent autorater-validation figures: the prose states 85.6% agreement and Cohen’s kappa 0.711 for one validation, whereas Table 9 reports 87.0% and 0.732; the table itself appears to be the more specific account. No significance testing across model/task aggregates, independent image editors, held-out ideator prompts, or cross-provider raters is reported. The use of a VLM filter and VLM autorater also leaves open whether variants are selected partly because they are easier for the evaluator to recognize rather than because the video model performs the underlying task more faithfully. Deployability (4-property check) Profile: EMPIRICAL. Practical: The pipeline can run on commercially available hardware through image/video-model APIs, but the principal video models are proprietary and API availability, latency, and pricing may change. Efficient: The reported 720p, 8-second Veo 3.1 video costs about USD 3.20, while a five-edit VIPE loop costs about USD 0.40, so VIPE is roughly one-eighth the cost of one video generation under the paper’s stated 2026 pricing, although it adds image-editing and filtering latency. Effective: The evidence shows substantial improvements on selected visual-reasoning proxies, but it does not establish robust reasoning independent of rendering consistency, and several headline results use best-variant or oracle selection. Scalable: Experiments cover up to 20 variants and 20 video attempts, 18,160 generated videos, and standard small-to-moderate task instances, but the paper does not test 10×–100× larger datasets, more complex scenes, longer videos, or production-scale request loads. The work provides prompts, an experimental pipeline, and task-specific edited examples, but no stated software library, CLI, released model, or complete public dataset artifact. Strengths - It identifies a concrete and underexplored intervention for image-conditioned video reasoning: optimize the visual conditioning image rather than only the text instruction or model parameters. - The realism ablation and stepwise consistency experiment connect performance gains to temporal scene persistence, not merely to a generic change in appearance; the synthetic-to-realistic progression reaches 0%, 11%, 24%, and 59% human-rated consistency. - It compares VIPE with self-consistency and text prompt engineering, showing that visual variants can be more cost-effective than repeated video sampling and can outperform text variants on some tasks. - It includes cross-model evidence from open Wan2.2 and closed Veo 3.1/Omni systems and shows that the effect is not universal: native image-generation models receive little or negative benefit, which supports a representation-gap interpretation rather than a claim that realism always helps every model. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors explicitly identify dependence on image-editor fidelity: edits may change the task or introduce artifacts, requiring VLM filtering and manual verification. They also acknowledge the additional cost of visual prompt engineering, while arguing that image editing is substantially cheaper than video generation. They note that freeform ideation can struggle to find one variant that works across task splits and that joint text-plus-image variants were less effective than image-only variants in their experiments. They present the realism explanation as a hypothesis and acknowledge uncertainty about whether abstract scenes are out of distribution or trigger different learned priors. These limitations are confronted directly, but the discussion does not fully address oracle selection, small task sizes, proprietary-model dependence, or evaluator coupling. Analyst-Identified Gaps - The main automated claim is not tested under a clean train/search/test separation: variant discovery and selection use downstream autorater feedback or best-of-20 reporting, so gains may reflect extensive test-time search and post hoc selection rather than a generally transferable visual prompt policy. - The paper does not quantify average performance over all generated variants as the primary metric, nor does it report the probability that an automatic filter selects a variant that improves performance on previously unseen samples. - Realism is confounded with many other changes, including object material, contrast, scale, background, semantic framing, and salience. The unnatural-texture ablation isolates one aspect but does not distinguish photorealism from object enlargement, contrast enhancement, target isolation, or familiar-domain priors. - The evaluation is narrow and often tiny: several core tasks contain five or six images, many results use only 10 samples per split, and the benchmark families come mainly from closely related prior work. Independent datasets, naturalistic tasks, longer temporal horizons, and adversarial structure-preservation tests are absent. - VLM-based autoraters are involved in ideation, filtering, rubric generation, and scoring, creating possible feedback loops; the paper does not provide a fully independent human evaluation of the headline best-variant gains. - The recommendation to stop evaluating abstract tasks is stronger than the evidence supports: VIPE may measure a model under a more favorable rendering distribution, but the same intervention can alter the practical task interface and may conceal failures that matter when real inputs are abstract. - The cost comparison omits image-editing latency, filtering calls, failed edits, engineering time, and the cost of manual verification; it also relies on vendor API prices that may not generalize to local or multi-provider deployments. Bottom Line This is a useful and empirically substantial preprint for understanding visual-distribution bias in video reasoners, but its central improvement claims should be read as best-of-variant test-time prompting results rather than as evidence of a robust, independently validated reasoning advance.

Practical Impact (58) reflects a useful repository and field map but no validated data recipe, benchmark, or deployable software artifact.

Problem & Motivation: Embodied manipulation requires training signals that connect observations to physical state, action, contact, and consequences. The relevant data sources differ sharply in collection cost, robot and embodiment alignment, physical fidelity, diversity, and transferability. Real-robot trajectories provide executable closed-loop supervision but require hardware, operators, resets, maintenance, and safety oversight; general image, video, and language data scale cheaply but lack robot actions and contact dynamics. UMI-style demonstrations and human egocentric/exocentric recordings occupy intermediate positions, while simulation provides scalable robot-oriented trajectories with imperfect dynamics. Prior surveys primarily organize model architectures or narrow subproblems, and prior pyramid views are often tied to one model's training recipe. The paper addresses the resulting lack of a category-level, data-centric synthesis of how heterogeneous sources are collected, represented, aligned, mixed, and used for embodied foundation models. Key Idea: The paper's core insight is to treat embodied data as a structured trade-off between scalability and robot alignment, rather than as a single quality-ordered dataset pool. It places five sources in an approximate pyramid—from real-robot data at the apex to general data at the base—and supplements the two primary axes with quality, diversity, reusability, and physical fidelity. The ordering is explicitly a synthesis rather than a monotonic ranking: simulation can be more robot-aligned than human video but less physically faithful, while general data can dominate semantic scale despite weak action grounding. Methodology: This is a literature survey and taxonomy rather than a new learning algorithm. The authors first define five data categories: real-robot trajectories; robot-free UMI-style demonstrations with end-effector supervision; egocentric and exocentric human recordings; simulation and learned-world-model data; and general image, video, language, spatial, planning, grasping, and physical-reasoning data. For each category, they review embodiments and sensors, collection paradigms, annotation or supervision construction, dataset scale and diversity, transferability, and limitations. They then analyze representative embodied foundation models, grouping them into embodied brain models, vision-language-action models, and world-action models, and relate data sources to perception, reasoning, planning, action generation, and future-world prediction. A second analytical axis concerns alignment: embodiment-specific projection, fixed-dimensional or zero-padded action interfaces, semantic action slots, and robot-, camera-, or wrist-centric geometric representations. The paper also catalogs simulation infrastructure, including robot assets, scenes, object assets, physics/rendering backends, human teleoperation, scripted execution, trajectory replay, autonomous rollouts, and LLM-assisted generation. Critical design choices are the five-way categorization, the two-axis organization, and the separation of action-free from action-labeled supervision; these are conceptually motivated, but the paper does not validate their superiority through an explicit annotation protocol, inter-rater study, or downstream controlled experiment. Key Results: The paper reports descriptive scale statistics rather than new model-performance results. Its tables cite real-robot datasets ranging from 50K trials in Pinto and Gupta and 580K in QT-Opt to approximately 1M trajectories and 2,976 hours for AgiBot World Beta, over 310K trajectories and 1,000+ hours for RoboMIND 2.0, and more than 2.4M trajectories in Open X-Embodiment. UMI examples range from 514 demonstrations in UMI on Legs and 2.5K in UMI to 100K in FastUMI-100K, 274.7K in Daimon-Infinity, and 789.8K in RealOmni. Egocentric resources range from 3,670 hours in Ego4D to 100,405 hours in Egocentric-100K and 967,000 hours in HumanNet. Simulation resources include 427M dexterous grasps in DexGraspNet 2.0, 1B samples in Dex1B, 637K trajectories and 7,400 hours in InternData-A1, and 1.7M trajectories and 5,800 hours in MolmoB0T. General-data examples include 1.1B masks in SA-1B, 1.43M affordance-point questions in RoboPoint, and 1B grasp labels in GraspNet-1Billion. These figures are heterogeneous—different sources count demonstrations, hours, clips, question-answer pairs, or synthetic grasps—so they do not support direct scale comparisons. The review reports a trend toward heterogeneous mixtures and larger pretraining corpora, including cited claims of approximately 38,100 hours for Qwen-RobotManip and over 100,000 hours for Xiaomi-Robotics-1, but it does not provide accuracy, success rate, F1, transfer, compute, or statistically tested improvements attributable to the taxonomy or to any particular data recipe. The baselines are therefore descriptive prior literature, not experimentally controlled comparators. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION; NEW EMPIRICAL/SYNTHETIC FINDING; NEW SYSTEM/TOOL. The genuinely new contribution is the explicit data-centric formulation of embodied learning as a five-layer scalability/alignment pyramid with four complementary dimensions, together with a cross-model synthesis and the announced "Awesome Embodied Data Pyramid" repository; the underlying collection technologies, action representations, and model architectures are largely established ideas reviewed and recombined rather than new algorithms. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper cites a large body of prior work and provides structured tables for datasets, sensors, modalities, scales, embodiments, annotations, simulation environments, and representative VLA/WAM data recipes. It distinguishes claims from known limitations in many places, including sim-to-real mismatch, tracking errors, embodiment gaps, action-space incompatibility, and annotation noise. However, it has no formal systematic-review protocol, search strategy, inclusion/exclusion criteria, quality-control process, uncertainty estimates, inter-annotator agreement, or quantitative synthesis of evidence. It reports no ablations, multiple seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or compute-matched comparisons because it does not run a new model study. Many scale and capability claims are compiled from papers, technical reports, dataset pages, and vendor or institutional self-reports; the confidence level is consequently uneven, especially for many 2025–2026 preprints and technical reports. The paper names an open-source repository, "Awesome Embodied Data Pyramid," and provides the project name but no repository URL in the supplied text. It does not release a machine-readable taxonomy, benchmark protocol, or evaluation code. The review also risks temporal and bibliographic instability: the manuscript is an arXiv preprint dated July 27–28, 2026 and includes many very recent or future-dated resources whose availability and reported statistics may change. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL, using the survey's cataloged dataset and system evidence rather than a new experimental evaluation. - Practical: The taxonomy and curated repository can be used on commercially available hardware, but the reviewed collection and deployment pipelines range from low-cost wearable or UMI interfaces to expensive robot fleets, tactile systems, and GPU simulation infrastructure. - Efficient: The review identifies the principal cost differences—real-robot collection requires hardware, operators, resets, maintenance, and safety supervision; UMI, web data, and simulation reduce marginal collection cost—but it does not provide a common compute, labor, storage, or energy accounting. - Effective: The synthesis plausibly explains which sources provide semantics, temporal structure, executable actions, contact information, or privileged labels, but it does not measure whether the proposed pyramid or any mixture improves real-robot success, robustness, recovery, or transfer. - Scalable: The paper documents scaling from thousands to millions of trajectories, hundreds of thousands of hours, and billions of synthetic grasps, but it does not test 10x–100x scaling under fixed quality, compute, or deployment constraints and explicitly states that optimal data recipes remain unresolved. The work delivers a curated repository/resource list and a reusable conceptual taxonomy, but no new software library, CLI, dataset, trained model, or validated data-mixture optimizer is established in the supplied paper. Strengths: - The scalability-versus-robot-alignment framing gives a useful common language for comparing data that are otherwise difficult to place on one axis; the paper correctly notes that the pyramid is an aggregate synthesis rather than a strict ranking on every dimension. - The separation of UMI-style data from ordinary egocentric video is technically meaningful: UMI preserves explicit relative end-effector trajectories and gripper state while removing target-robot dependence, making retargeting and cross-embodiment deployment central analytical issues. - The review connects data-source properties to model roles instead of merely listing datasets: action-free sources support semantic, temporal, and physical priors; action-labeled sources ground executable control; and world-action models require action-conditioned transitions for simulator or policy-evaluation use. - The treatment of missing interaction signals is concrete. It identifies tactile sensing, failure and recovery trajectories, coordinate-frame conventions, and compute-matched data recipes as bottlenecks rather than assuming that more trajectories automatically produce better policies. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly acknowledge that real-robot data are costly and embodiment-specific; UMI data suffer from tracking, calibration, missing proprioception, and limited force feedback; egocentric data have occlusion, partial observability, missing robot dynamics, and a human-to-robot morphology gap; simulation suffers from imperfect sensing, actuation, contact, deformable-object coverage, and sim-to-real transfer; and general data lack executable actions and contact grounding. They also state that the optimal mixture of pyramid layers is unknown, that controlled ablations are limited, that failure and tactile data are scarce, and that action-coordinate conventions remain inconsistent. These limitations are confronted directly and form the basis of the future-work section rather than being hidden. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The paper does not establish a reproducible review methodology or explain how the hundreds of included datasets and models were selected, deduplicated, verified, or scored on the six dimensions. The six dimensions remain qualitative: no rating rubric, normalized scale, Pareto analysis, or evidence-weighted comparison lets readers determine whether one category is actually better than another for a given task. The apparent growth trends in Figures 2 and 3 are vulnerable to selection bias, inconsistent units, release-date effects, and inclusion of self-reported or inaccessible resources; the paper does not quantify these uncertainties. It also conflates dataset scale with useful information content and does not systematically account for duplicated trajectories, synthetic generations derived from the same seeds, annotation quality, task difficulty, or embodiment concentration. Most importantly, it catalogs data recipes but does not separate data-source effects from model architecture, training objective, action representation, compute budget, post-training, or private engineering; consequently, the claims connecting composition to capabilities remain largely interpretive. The review gives limited attention to data governance, licensing, privacy, human-subject consent, demographic bias, operator skill, safety, and reproducibility of proprietary datasets. Finally, it does not provide a benchmark or protocol for testing the central practical question: how should a practitioner allocate a fixed budget among real-robot, UMI, human-video, simulation, and general data for a specified embodiment and task family? Bottom Line: This is a useful, well-scoped field map for researchers planning embodied-data collection or foundation-model pretraining, but its novelty is primarily taxonomic and organizational, and practitioners seeking evidence-backed data recipes should wait for or consult controlled scaling and mixture studies.

Scaling Native Multimodal Pre-Training From Scratch (14 ▲ )

Haoyuan Wu, Aoqi Wu, Hai Wang, Jiajia Wu, Jinxiang Ou, Bei Yu · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 27 Jul 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper establishes empirical compute-optimal scaling laws for native multimodal pre-training, including modality-specific allocation exponents and a joint language–multimodal Pareto frontier. - Why it's important: Training multimodal foundation models from scratch requires deciding how to allocate a fixed budget among parameters, text tokens, multimodal tokens, and data mixture, but existing scaling guidance primarily targets text-only models. - How it does it: It trains decoder-only MoE Transformers from 71M to 3B activated parameters at multimodal ratios r ∈ {0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3}, fits IsoFLOP minima and training-curve envelopes, and combines separate language and multimodal loss laws under a shared compute budget. - The good: The two allocation estimators agree, and the paper reports a clear modality-dependent pattern: language allocation is nearly composition-invariant, whereas multimodal parameter/token allocation changes materially with the multimodal ratio. - The missing: The scaling laws are validated only to 3B active parameters on one undisclosed image–text data family using training loss as the primary proxy, without external model baselines, uncertainty estimates, or large-scale validation. - Read it or not: Scaling-law researchers and teams designing native multimodal pre-training should read it for the allocation framework, but practitioners seeking evidence of competitive model quality should treat it as an early preprint rather than a deployment recommendation.

Problem & Motivation Native multimodal pre-training aims to learn language and visual representations jointly from scratch, avoiding the representational and optimization asymmetry of attaching a vision encoder to an already trained language model. The practical problem is how to allocate a fixed compute budget between active model parameters, total training tokens, and the fraction of multimodal data when language and multimodal objectives share parameters. Prior compute-optimal laws for language models do not establish whether the same allocation applies when visual tokens are introduced, nor whether the optimal allocation differs across objectives. The paper targets researchers and infrastructure teams training multimodal foundation models, with the specific goal of closing this resource-allocation gap rather than proposing a new multimodal architecture. Key Idea The core insight is to decouple the shared training problem into language and multimodal objectives, estimate a separate compute-optimal allocation law for each, and then recombine them through a data-mixture-dependent joint Pareto frontier. The reported asymmetry is that language loss can be modeled primarily as a function of isolated text compute, while multimodal loss changes with the multimodal data ratio and therefore requires composition-dependent scaling exponents. This is a methodological extension of established IsoFLOP and envelope analysis rather than a new optimization algorithm or architecture. Methodology The study trains decoder-only Transformer MoE models with a single image patch-embedding layer and no conventional vision encoder. The model family has 71M, 128M, 340M, 590M, 874M, and 3B activated parameters, 128 total experts, 8 activated experts, a 4,096-token context, a 16M-token global batch, Muon optimization, weight decay 0.1, gradient clipping at 1.0, and a warmup-stable learning-rate schedule. The corpus contains 250B text tokens and up to 75B multimodal tokens from web-crawled image–text pairs and interleaved image–text documents; the mixture ratio is r = Dmm/Dtext and is evaluated at 0, 0.1, 0.2, and 0.3. Under the approximation C = 6ND, the paper first constructs IsoFLOP profiles by varying model size and adjusting token count to hold compute fixed, fits a parabola to each loss profile, and obtains Nopt and Dopt from its minimum. It independently extracts the lower envelope of training loss versus compute across model sizes and regresses Nopt and Dopt against C. Both methods fit allocation laws Nopt ∝ C^a and Dopt ∝ C^b with a + b = 1, while the loss frontier uses L(C) = E + (Cc/C)^β. The joint analysis uses the IsoFLOP estimates, treating language scaling as ratio-invariant and multimodal scaling as ratio-dependent, then sweeps r to construct a language–multimodal Pareto frontier. Downstream evaluation uses 16 text benchmarks and 23 multimodal benchmarks in zero-, one-, and three-shot settings. The main design choices—separate objective analysis, dual frontier estimators, and an asymmetric joint model—are plausible and empirically motivated, but the paper does not provide statistical model-selection tests, confidence intervals for exponents, or a direct optimization procedure that validates the predicted joint frontier. Key Results For the language objective, the IsoFLOP estimates give approximately a = 0.697 and b = 0.303 at r = 0, changing to a = 0.663 and b = 0.337 at r = 0.3; the paper argues that this modest drift is fitting noise because the envelope estimator does not show a monotonic trend. For the multimodal objective, the IsoFLOP estimates change from approximately a = 0.709 and b = 0.291 at r = 0.1 to a = 0.643 and b = 0.357 at r = 0.3, with the envelope estimator supporting the same downward parameter exponent and upward token exponent. In the unified-compute analysis, the reported parameter exponent falls from 0.69 at r = 0.1 to 0.66 at r = 0.3, while the token exponent rises from 0.31 to 0.34. With 250B text tokens fixed, aggregate text accuracy differs by less than one percentage point across multimodal ratios at each tested scale; for the 3B model, the aggregate text score is 44.77 for r = 0, 45.50 for 25B multimodal tokens, 45.21 for 50B, and 46.03 for 75B. On the text-only abstract spatial-reasoning subset of SpatialEval, the r = 0.3 models outperform r = 0 models, with the plotted gap increasing toward 3B, although the paper does not give a complete numerical table for this comparison in the main text. Multimodal average accuracy for the 3B model trained with 250B text and 75B multimodal tokens is 31.77 zero-shot, 36.05 one-shot, and 36.56 three-shot, corresponding to a reported three-shot gain of +2.43 points over zero-shot at 3B. Multimodal few-shot gains are concentrated in spatial reasoning and structured tasks; OCR and recognition categories show little improvement or degradation. These are internally consistent scaling and transfer findings, but the experiments compare primarily variants of the authors' own model family rather than strong late-fusion or other native multimodal baselines, so they do not establish competitive downstream quality. Novelty Classification NEW FORMULATION, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, and ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION: the paper applies established IsoFLOP and training-envelope scaling methodology to native multimodal pre-training, but its substantive contribution is the modality-specific formulation and the empirical finding that language allocation is approximately mixture-invariant while multimodal allocation is mixture-dependent, leading to a joint Pareto frontier. The MoE architecture, patch embeddings, auxiliary-loss-free routing, and next-token-style training are standard or previously reported components rather than the primary novelty. Rigor & Reproducibility The study includes a useful cross-check between IsoFLOP profiles and training-curve envelopes, multiple model sizes, multiple token checkpoints, four data ratios, and per-benchmark results in the appendix. However, it reports no error bars, repeated random seeds, confidence intervals, statistical significance tests, or uncertainty on fitted exponents. The authors use smoothed training loss as a proxy for test loss because each token is seen approximately once, but they do not demonstrate that this proxy predicts downstream multimodal quality or remains valid under extrapolation. The analysis also masks vision tokens from loss computation, so the reported multimodal objective appears to measure text-token prediction in multimodal contexts rather than an explicitly supervised visual-token objective; this distinction limits interpretation of the claimed multimodal scaling law. The data are described only at a high level, with no dataset release or composition audit stated, and no code, model weights, or repository URL is mentioned. Baselines are largely internal text-only and ratio variants; the paper does not compare against contemporary late-fusion models, other native multimodal models, dense Transformers, or alternative image tokenizers under matched compute. The use of a single image–text data family and the authors' own benchmark pipeline creates a narrow evaluation setting and potential benchmark-specific optimization risk. Deployability (4-property check) Profile: EMPIRICAL. Practical: The 71M–3B active-parameter MoE models and 4,096-token inference context are compatible with commercially available accelerator hardware, although the paper does not report hardware, wall-clock training time, or an end-to-end deployment artifact. Efficient: The method uses sparse MoE activation, but no measured training or inference throughput, memory footprint, energy cost, or comparison against dense and late-fusion alternatives is provided, so compute efficiency beyond the fitted FLOP allocation is not established. Effective: The evidence shows predictable training-loss frontiers, preservation of aggregate text accuracy, a reported spatial-reasoning transfer effect, and few-shot gains up to +2.43 points at 3B, but it does not show that the system outperforms strong multimodal baselines or reliably solves real applications rather than benchmark proxies. Scalable: The largest tested model has 3B activated parameters, while the paper extrapolates scaling laws to larger budgets; behavior at 10×–100× scale, larger image resolutions, longer contexts, other modalities, and different data mixtures is not evaluated. The work delivers a research model family and scaling analysis in paper form, but no reusable software library, CLI, dataset, or publicly released trained model is stated. Strengths - The paper identifies an actionable allocation distinction between language and multimodal objectives instead of collapsing them into a single aggregate loss. - Agreement between IsoFLOP minima and training-curve envelopes provides a stronger internal check than relying on one fitted scaling form. - The joint Pareto framing connects isolated scaling laws to the actual shared-parameter training problem and reports concrete exponents, including a shift from approximately C^0.69 to C^0.66 in optimal parameter scaling as the multimodal ratio increases from 0.1 to 0.3. - The controlled family of six model sizes, four mixture ratios, and token-budget trajectories supports analysis of both model and data scaling, while the downstream results expose a potentially non-obvious positive transfer effect on text-only spatial reasoning. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors explicitly state that the analysis is limited to models with at most 3B active parameters, one image–text data family, and loss-based scaling proxies. They also call for validation at larger scales and across more diverse modalities and data compositions. They do not substantially discuss the absence of external baselines, lack of uncertainty estimates, the consequences of masking vision tokens from the loss, or the difference between training-loss scaling and downstream task scaling. Analyst-Identified Gaps - The proposed joint Pareto frontier is modeled asymmetrically by assumption: language scaling is forced to be ratio-invariant while multimodal scaling varies with r. The paper does not provide an unconstrained comparison, cross-validation, likelihood test, or held-out mixture ratio showing that this modeling choice is preferable. - The central scaling laws are fit over only six model sizes, with the largest at 3B active parameters, and are then extrapolated beyond the observed range without a held-out large-scale validation point. - No strong matched-compute baselines establish whether native pre-training is preferable to late fusion, a separately pretrained vision encoder, dense Transformer training, or prior native multimodal systems. - The multimodal loss definition is under-specified for interpreting visual learning: vision tokens are masked from loss computation, so the paper may be scaling language modeling conditioned on visual embeddings rather than a symmetric multimodal generative objective. - The claimed cross-modal transfer is demonstrated mainly on SpatialEval and aggregate benchmark averages; it lacks task-level significance analysis, multiple-seed replication, and controls for differences in text data exposure or prompt formatting. - The paper gives no dataset deduplication, contamination, licensing, or train/test overlap analysis, and it does not release the corpus or implementation needed to reproduce the fitted frontiers. Bottom Line This is a useful early empirical framework for researchers planning native multimodal pre-training, but its scaling recommendations should not yet guide major infrastructure decisions because the evidence stops at 3B active parameters, relies on proxy loss and internal comparisons, and omits uncertainty and matched external baselines.

Multi-turn RL with Structural and Performance Aware Rewards for CUDA Kernel Generation

QI Mahmud, NK Ahmed, A Jannesari · arxiv.org · Recommended articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces CUDAPERF, a two-stage multi-turn reinforcement-learning framework that generates CUDA kernels using both execution-based rewards and learned rewards from CUDA code structure. - Why it's important: Correct CUDA translation requires simultaneously satisfying functional correctness and hardware-dependent performance constraints, while compilation and benchmarking feedback are expensive and sparse. - How it does it: It trains an offline MLP ranker on structural features such as coalescing, arithmetic intensity, occupancy, divergence, synchronization, atomics, transfers, and operation counts, then combines its score with correctness, speedup, compilation, and runtime-variance rewards during GRPO training with iterative feedback. - The good: On the reported pass@5 evaluation, CUDAPERF reaches 89% correctness and 11.02× geometric-mean speedup on its C→CUDA benchmark, 94% and 9.02× on BabelTower, and 93% and 6.41× on KernelBench, exceeding the strongest listed baselines on the same tables. - The missing: The paper does not isolate the effects of the offline ranker, individual structural features, prompt few-shot selection, or iterative refinement, and it provides no variance estimates or repeated-seed results for its large performance claims. - Read it or not: CUDA-generation and program-optimization researchers should read it for the reward-design idea and empirical setup, but practitioners should wait for artifact release, cost accounting, and stronger controlled comparisons before treating it as deployment-ready.

Problem & Motivation: The work addresses automatic translation of sequential C or PyTorch programs into functionally correct and high-performance CUDA programs. The users are HPC, GPU-systems, and machine-learning practitioners who otherwise rely on expert knowledge, profiling, and repeated kernel editing. Existing LLM and RLVR approaches generally use compilation success, test correctness, or measured speedup as sparse outcome signals, which do not directly communicate why a kernel is likely to perform well. The claimed gap is the lack of performance-aware structural signals covering memory access patterns, thread/block configuration, arithmetic intensity, divergence, synchronization, atomics, and host-device transfers. The paper is a preprint, dated July 23, 2026 in the supplied text, and its conclusions therefore have not been established through peer review. Key Idea: The central insight is to use a learned structural prior as a dense reward alongside execution feedback: CUDA candidates with performance-relevant static properties receive a score from an offline pairwise ranker trained using measured speedup preferences. This is intended to provide guidance before expensive execution feedback becomes sufficiently informative. The conceptual contribution is the integration of standard pairwise ranking, GRPO, and multi-turn reflection around a CUDA-specific structural reward rather than a new RL algorithm. Methodology: CUDAPERF first extracts an 11-dimensional feature vector from each candidate CUDA program: memory coalescing, arithmetic intensity, occupancy proxy, control divergence, transfer overhead, atomics, synchronization, kernel count, threads per block, global-memory accesses, and operation count. Features are normalized using training-split statistics. For each source task, candidates in the top and bottom speedup quartiles form positive and negative pairs, and a two-hidden-layer MLP with dimensions 64 and 32, ReLU, dropout, AdamW, and pairwise logistic loss learns a scalar score sψ(φ(y)); that score becomes the structural reward. Online training starts from Qwen-3-32B fine-tuned with 4-bit QLoRA on two A100 40 GB GPUs. For each source program, the policy samples 16 CUDA candidates. The execution harness checks compilation, runs at least five test cases, and benchmarks correct candidates five times. The verifiable reward applies a compilation penalty of −3, an incorrect-test penalty of −2(1−pass rate), a clipped log2 speedup reward with coefficient 1 and range [−0.5, 4], and a runtime coefficient-of-variation penalty with coefficient 0.5. The composite reward is Rver + Rstr, normalized within each group, and optimized with GRPO using clipping ε=0.2 and βDKL=0. Up to five refinement turns feed compiler errors, failed cases, speedup, and structural feature values back into the prompt; a second Qwen-3-32B call summarizes prior changes to limit context growth. Prompts also include five randomly selected examples from the top 20 of a pool of 50 samples. Training runs for 60 epochs, uses nucleus sampling with p=0.9 and temperatures from 0.2 to 0.7, limits generation to 1,536 tokens, and computes masked log probabilities over a 1,024-token window. The structural feature definitions are only weakly justified: for example, coalescing uses hand-set stride scores, occupancy is reduced to coarse threads-per-block bins, and arithmetic intensity is approximated by counted operations divided by counted array accesses. The paper does not justify reward weights, the zero KL coefficient, five refinement turns, or the sampling and prompt parameters beyond reporting that they were empirically selected. Key Results: On the authors' 290-example held-out CUDAPERF C→CUDA split, pass@5 correctness is 89% and geometric-mean speedup is 11.02×, compared with Qwen-3-32B at 72% and 6.2×, QiMeng-MuPa at 63% and 5.9×, and Qwen2.5-Coder-32B at 61% and 5.3×. On the 233-example BabelTower evaluation set, CUDAPERF obtains 94% and 9.02×, matching QiMeng-MuPa's 94% correctness while exceeding its 6.01× speedup and Qwen-3-32B's 86% and 4.92×. On the 250-task KernelBench PyTorch→CUDA benchmark, it obtains 93% and 6.41×, compared with CUDA Agent at 86% and 3.09× and Kevin at 82% and 1.10×. Pass@1/pass@3/pass@5 for CUDAPERF are 45%/64%/89% on the authors' C→CUDA set, 76%/91%/94% on BabelTower, and 55%/82%/93% on KernelBench; corresponding speedups are 3.1×/5.7×/11.02×, 2.5×/4.9×/9.02×, and 1.9×/2.8×/6.41×. Model-size ablations show Qwen-3-8B, 14B, and 32B reaching 69%/6.9×, 77%/9.1×, and 89%/11.02× on the authors' set, respectively. Reward ablations show that removing structural rewards reduces correctness and speedup from 89%/11.02× to 81%/9.3× on the authors' set, from 94%/9.02× to 87%/6.1× on BabelTower, and from 93%/6.41× to 84%/4.3× on KernelBench; removing verifiable rewards reduces them further to 75%/6.9×, 81%/4.6×, and 76%/3.7×. The experiments use standard-sized datasets rather than stress-scale workloads. The tables report strong numerical gains, but no confidence intervals, seed variation, task-level distributions, or statistical tests establish whether the differences are robust. The paper also inconsistently describes the maximum C→CUDA speedup claim as up to 5× or 6× in different sections, while the reported geometric means reach 11.02×. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD, NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION; the genuinely new element is the use of a learned, CUDA-structural reward combined with execution rewards in multi-turn GRPO, whereas the ranker, static features, QLoRA, GRPO, execution harness, and reflection loop are largely standard components combined for CUDA generation, and the dataset is primarily a curated and LLM-expanded collection rather than an independently sourced corpus. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper includes model-size and reward-source ablations and reports exact training hardware, major hyperparameters, training duration, candidate count, test-count minimum, benchmark sizes, and baseline source links. It reports 2.9k C→CUDA and 1,013 PyTorch→CUDA source programs, generated from CodeNet, AIZU, AtCoder, BabelTower, and CUDA Agent-related data; the filtering process retains tasks with at least five compiling, fully correct candidates and at least one candidate with at least 1.5× speedup. However, the ablations do not separately evaluate the ranker versus fixed hand-designed rewards, individual structural features, pairwise ranking versus direct regression, iterative refinement, feedback summarization, or prompt retrieval. There are no multiple random seeds, error bars, significance tests, ranker validation metrics, per-task speedup distributions, or independent profiling analyses. The training corpus is selected using correctness and speedup, and many CUDA candidates are generated by Qwen-3-32B, which creates distribution and selection bias; the authors' evaluation set is drawn from the same curated pipeline, so it may be easier or more aligned with the reward than naturally occurring programs. The external BabelTower and KernelBench tests improve credibility, but their preprocessing, hardware configuration, prompt budget, and baseline generation budgets are not described in enough detail to establish strict comparability. No CUDAPERF code, dataset, model weights, or release URL is stated; only baseline repositories and model URLs are provided. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS/EMPIRICAL, because the paper builds a CUDA-generation and training system and evaluates generated programs experimentally. - Practical: The generator can run on commercially available NVIDIA hardware, but training required two A100 40 GB GPUs and repeated compilation and benchmarking, while inference-time cost and required CUDA/toolchain versions are not stated. - Efficient: The structural extractor is lightweight, but the full approach is computationally expensive: offline ranking takes 2 hours 16 minutes and RL training takes 3 days 12 hours 12 minutes for C→CUDA and 3 days 8 hours 44 minutes for PyTorch→CUDA on two A100s; no comparison against the compute cost of CUDA Agent, search-based methods, or direct inference is provided. - Effective: The evidence shows improved test-pass rates and geometric-mean speedups on three benchmarks, but correctness is limited to the supplied test cases and performance is measured on a single pinned GPU, so it establishes benchmark effectiveness rather than broad correctness or production reliability. - Scalable: The paper tests 290 held-out C→CUDA tasks, 233 BabelTower tasks, and 250 KernelBench tasks, but does not test 10×–100× larger workloads, larger kernels, multiple GPUs, newer GPU architectures, longer programs, or production-scale training; scalability is therefore claimed rather than demonstrated. The work delivers a described framework and a curated dataset, but no publicly released software artifact, dataset, trained model, or command-line tool is stated. Strengths: - The reward design targets a real weakness of sparse execution-only supervision by adding dense, interpretable signals tied to CUDA performance factors. - The evaluation spans two translation settings and includes external BabelTower and KernelBench benchmarks, rather than reporting only on the authors' generated data. - The paper reports useful pass@1, pass@3, and pass@5 results, model-size comparisons, reward ablations, hardware, training times, and concrete hyperparameters. - The system combines correctness feedback, profiling-like runtime feedback, compiler diagnostics, and iterative repair in a single training loop, which is a plausible design for difficult kernel-generation tasks. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly acknowledge the high computational overhead caused by repeatedly compiling and benchmarking candidates during RL training. They also state that iterative refinement remains limited by the policy and reward design and may fail to discover optimization strategies beyond observed patterns. They do not discuss the narrowness of static feature proxies, possible reward hacking, test-case coverage, dataset filtering bias, missing uncertainty estimates, or the absence of cross-hardware evaluation. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The structural reward is trained from measured speedup on LLM-generated candidates and then applied to similarly generated candidates, but the paper does not measure whether it generalizes to unseen optimization patterns or prevents reward hacking. The hand-coded feature proxies are particularly questionable: occupancy is inferred only from threads per block, coalescing is assigned fixed stride scores, arithmetic intensity ignores bytes and cache behavior, and no comparison with NVIDIA occupancy calculators, static analyzers, Nsight metrics, or roofline estimates is provided. The dataset filtering requires five valid candidates and a 1.5× candidate, potentially excluding hard or inherently non-speedup tasks and inflating reported performance. The paper does not clarify whether speedup is averaged over only correct candidates, how baseline systems were given equivalent sampling and refinement budgets, or whether external benchmark prompts and test inputs overlap with training examples. It omits ablations for the ranker architecture, feature groups, reward coefficients, KL regularization, refinement, few-shot retrieval, and feedback summarization. Runtime measurements use five executions without reporting warm-up handling, variance distributions, compiler flags, CUDA versions, GPU model details beyond A100 training hardware, or statistical confidence. Finally, the claimed practical impact is not supported by end-to-end latency, energy, training-cost, or deployment-reliability measurements. Bottom Line: This is a worthwhile preprint for researchers designing execution-guided CUDA generation because it presents a plausible structural-reward extension with strong but incompletely controlled benchmark results, while practitioners should prefer it only after reproducibility artifacts, cost comparisons, broader hardware tests, and leakage-resistant ablations are available.

Progress Reward Modeling for Robotic Learning: A Comprehensive Survey (68 ▲ )

Jianshu Zhang, Keliang Wu, Haoran Lu, Anbang Liu, Ce Zhang, Weijie Yin, Chengxuan Qian, Xiyuan Yang, Zhenyu Pan, Guo Ye, Han Liu · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 28 Jul 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces a unified taxonomy of progress reward models for robotic learning organized by model interface, reward-construction mechanism, supervision pipeline, and evaluation protocol. - Why it's important: Progress signals can improve credit assignment and support monitoring, reranking, planning, failure detection, and long-horizon policy learning where terminal success labels are sparse and uninformative. - How it does it: The survey analyzes each method as a task-conditioned interface, then classifies how its signal is constructed—frozen foundation-model scoring, temporal or relative supervision, instruction tuning, or programmatic reward synthesis—and links each class to its data and benchmarks. - The good: Its strongest contribution is separating progress fidelity from downstream policy utility, making clear that a reward can improve task success without accurately measuring progress, and vice versa. - The missing: It provides no standardized quantitative meta-analysis, reproducible cross-method evaluation, or tabulated evidence sufficient to determine which methods outperform others under matched tasks and conditions. - Read it or not: Researchers entering VLM-based robotic reward modeling should read it for its organizing framework; experts seeking new algorithms or validated performance improvements can skip it unless they need a literature map.
Why this rank
Profile: empirical. Novelty (62) and Non-Obviousness (68) reflect a useful interface-based taxonomy and the important distinction between progress fidelity and downstream utility, but this is a conceptual synthesis rather than a new algorithm or validated empirical result. Rigor (45) and Resilience (58) are limited by the absence of a systematic search protocol, quantitative comparison, standardized evidence tables, and independent verification of heterogeneous cited results; Completeness (63) benefits from candid discussion of assumptions and limitations, while Impact (42) is modest because the released index is not a runnable model or benchmark. empirical Novelty 62 Rigor 45 Non-Obv 68 Completeness 63 Resilience 58 Impact 42
Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: Robotic learning must make decisions over long, sequential, high-dimensional executions in which terminal success provides little information about intermediate actions. The central problem is to estimate whether an ongoing execution is advancing toward a task, stagnating, regressing, or undoing earlier progress, while accounting for task goals, alternative valid action sequences, and history-dependent state. Prior work uses incompatible notions of progress, including success probability, goal similarity, temporal position, scalar completion percentage, pairwise preference, transition-level improvement, and executable reward logic. It also varies in observation context, goal representation, supervision source, and evaluation target, making reported results difficult to compare or interpret. Key Idea: The core insight is to treat progress reward modeling as a three-part interface-and-evidence problem: what representation of the current task state the model observes, how the goal is specified, and what output form it produces. This interface view is connected to a second taxonomy of construction mechanisms and a third taxonomy of supervision and evaluation. The paper’s most useful conceptual distinction is that progress-model fidelity and downstream usefulness are different properties and must be evaluated separately. Methodology: This is a literature survey rather than a new algorithmic pipeline. First, it classifies current-state access as single observation, temporal context, relational comparison, or state/API access; goals as language-conditioned, vision-conditioned, or structured/programmatic; and outputs as state-wise scalar scores, progress deltas, rankings, or executable reward functions. Second, it classifies reward construction into frozen foundation-model scoring, temporal or relative supervision, instruction-tuned progress prediction, and programmatic reward construction. These categories cover, respectively, zero-shot semantic scores from CLIP/VLMs; rewards learned from demonstration order, pairwise preferences, or sketches; fine-tuned models that explicitly predict progress, success, preferences, or reasoning-grounded scores; and LLM/VLM-generated reward programs refined through environment or policy feedback. Third, it organizes supervision by human involvement—human-driven, human-in-the-loop, or fully automated—and evaluations by progress fidelity, robustness/generalization, and downstream utility. The paper does not define a common objective function, derive a formal model, or reimplement the surveyed methods. Its major design decisions—separating input/output interfaces, distinguishing construction mechanisms, and separating fidelity from utility—are well motivated conceptually, but the paper does not quantitatively validate whether these categories are mutually exclusive, exhaustive, or predictive of performance. Key Results: The paper reports no new experiments, benchmark scores, accuracy, F1, calibration error, success-rate improvements, latency measurements, parameter counts, or compute comparisons. Its result is a qualitative synthesis of the literature. It argues that single-frame and frozen-foundation-model methods offer low setup cost but often lack history and calibration; temporal and relational methods provide stronger execution evidence but may accumulate local errors; programmatic methods provide interpretability and dense rewards when simulator state or APIs expose relevant variables but transfer poorly to raw real-world settings; and instruction-tuned VLMs make progress prediction an explicit capability but incur data and inference costs. It identifies evaluation families including scalar calibration, temporal consistency, relative ordering, task grounding, uncertainty or abstention, unseen-task generalization, viewpoint and embodiment transfer, non-monotonic execution, online RL, offline relabeling, retrieval/reranking, and planning. No matched baseline study establishes which category is superior, and no stress-scale evaluation is presented. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION; NEW EMPIRICAL SYNTHESIS. The genuinely new contribution is the proposed interface-based and evidence-based organization of a fragmented literature; the underlying reward models, VLM scoring methods, preference learning, instruction tuning, and program synthesis techniques are existing ideas surveyed and recombined conceptually rather than newly invented here. Rigor & Reproducibility: The survey cites a broad set of relevant work spanning 2017–2026 and explicitly discusses assumptions such as temporal monotonicity, clean state access, goal underspecification, synthetic-failure artifacts, and history dependence. It does not report a systematic-review search protocol, inclusion/exclusion criteria, inter-rater agreement, coverage statistics, formal comparison tables, quantitative meta-analysis, ablations, error bars, multiple seeds, or significance tests. Because it does not run models, standard experimental baselines and reproducibility checks are not applicable to the paper’s own results. The paper links a reusable literature index at https://github.com/sterzhang/Awesome-Progress-Models, but no survey dataset, extraction schema, code for analysis, or unified benchmark implementation is stated. The cited literature includes peer-reviewed papers, conference papers, and many arXiv preprints; the paper itself is an arXiv preprint, version 1 dated 22 July 2026. Its claims about individual methods are therefore dependent on the quality and comparability of heterogeneous source evaluations, and the survey does not independently verify those results. Deployability (4-property check): EMPIRICAL profile used for the evidence-synthesis paper, although it contains no primary experiments or deployed system. Practical: The conceptual taxonomy and linked literature index are usable on commercially available hardware, but the survey itself does not deliver a runnable reward model. Efficient: Not evaluated; it compares qualitative trade-offs but provides no normalized inference cost, memory, or throughput analysis. Effective: The paper establishes that progress rewards support several downstream uses in prior studies, but it does not independently demonstrate effectiveness or isolate progress fidelity from policy gains. Scalable: Not evaluated; the survey identifies long-horizon memory, online VLM latency, fine-grained sensing, and non-monotonic execution as unresolved scale barriers rather than testing performance at 10×–100× scale. The work delivers a literature-index artifact through the GitHub repository, but no library, CLI, trained model, dataset, or benchmark implementation is stated. Strengths: - The interface taxonomy—state representation, goal specification, and output type—provides a practical vocabulary for comparing methods that otherwise use incompatible terminology. - The four-way construction taxonomy exposes distinct assumptions: semantic priors from frozen models, temporal monotonicity or preference consistency, instruction-following supervision, and access to structured environment state. - The paper correctly distinguishes progress fidelity from downstream utility and explains why policy improvement, reranking success, or completion detection cannot by themselves establish calibrated progress estimation. - The limitations section identifies deployment-relevant issues—coarse temporal resolution, fixed-rate progress assumptions, VLM inference latency, and insufficient long-horizon memory—instead of treating progress as a simple scalar prediction problem. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state that current methods remain too coarse-grained, often assume progress changes at a fixed rate, suffer from inefficient online inference, and lack reliable long-horizon memory. They also acknowledge limitations of language goals, visual-goal sensitivity to viewpoint and embodiment, state/API dependence in programmatic rewards, temporal-order supervision, model-generated labels, and synthetic failure augmentation. The paper confronts these issues directly and proposes finer multimodal sensing, adaptive temporal modeling, streaming or distilled models, hierarchical querying, and compact task memory as future directions. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The survey does not state a systematic literature-search methodology, so claims of comprehensiveness and category coverage cannot be independently assessed. It lacks a structured table reporting each method’s datasets, task domains, embodiment, supervision cost, context length, output calibration, inference latency, and downstream performance, which limits the framework’s usefulness for evidence-based method selection. The taxonomy may conflate distinct targets such as success probability, value estimation, goal similarity, and semantic alignment under the broad label of progress without defining necessary and sufficient criteria for inclusion. It also does not analyze reward hacking, temporal-difference inconsistency, calibration under distribution shift, annotator disagreement, or the relationship between progress rewards and potential-based shaping or policy invariance in sufficient technical depth. Several cited 2025–2026 works are preprints, and the survey does not distinguish their evidence quality from peer-reviewed results. Finally, it offers no common benchmark design, formal evaluation protocol, or empirical test of whether its proposed categories predict robustness or downstream performance. Bottom Line: This is a useful conceptual map for researchers working on robotic progress and VLM-based reward modeling, but it is not evidence that any particular approach is best and should be supplemented with the primary papers and a standardized cross-method evaluation.

JarvisHub: An Open Harness for Canvas-Native Multimodal Creative Agents (104 ▲ )

Yunlong Lin, Zixu Lin, Zhaohu Xing, Biqiang Li, Chenxin Li, Haonan Wang, Haitao Wu, Hengyu Liu, Jianghai Chen, Kaituo Feng, Kaixin Li, Shawn Chen, Shijue Huang, Sixiang Chen, Tsung-Yi Ho, Wenxuan Huang, Xiangyan Liu, Xiaomeng Hu, Xuanhua He, Yan Sun, Yunqing Zhao, Zhiqin Yang, Zehan Wang, Zhengyang Tang, Tianyu Pang, Xiangyu Yue · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 28 Jul 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces JarvisHub, an open canvas-native harness that represents multimodal creative projects as editable artifact graphs and lets agents inspect, generate, revise, connect, and recover project elements through a protocol-checked runtime. - Why it's important: Long-horizon creative work depends on persistent references, alternatives, dependencies, feedback, and revision history that prompt logs and isolated generation tools generally fail to preserve or expose. - How it does it: It combines a typed canvas state layer, a protocol bridge with capability manifests and execution grants, and an agent runtime that invokes tools and commits validated state transitions back to the canvas. - The good: The system makes intermediate creative state, tool actions, dependencies, feedback, and recovery traces inspectable across narrative media, web development, and presentation-generation workflows. - The missing: The paper provides no quantitative benchmark, controlled comparison, ablation, task count, cost analysis, or objective evidence that the canvas improves output quality, consistency, recovery, or efficiency over chat- or workflow-based alternatives. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on multimodal agents, human-in-the-loop creative systems, or process-level evaluation and want an open orchestration substrate; skip it if you need validated performance gains rather than an architectural demonstration.

Rigor (25), Completeness (45), and Resilience (38) dominate the weakness because the paper offers only three curated demonstrations, no quantitative baselines or ablations, and insufficient implementation and cost detail. Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: The work addresses the problem of maintaining coherent, editable project state during extended multimodal creative production such as storyboarding and video creation, interactive web development, and slide-deck construction. Creators and creative agents must manage references, drafts, rejected candidates, versions, spatial layouts, dependencies, feedback, and local revisions rather than merely map one prompt to one asset. The paper argues that chat histories are linear and opaque, while node-based workflow systems usually encode fixed pipelines and leave project-state management to users. Its target users are researchers and practitioners building agents for creative production who need inspectable context, human steering, controlled tool use, and recovery across multiple steps. Key Idea: Treat the editable canvas as the agent's external memory, action space, and shared project state, rather than as a presentation layer over a hidden conversational or workflow state. Typed, addressable nodes and typed links preserve artifact identity, provenance, versions, dependencies, selections, and runtime status, allowing an agent to continue from specific prior artifacts and perform local updates. The idea is conceptually clear and useful, but it overlaps with established graph-based editors, visual programming environments, workflow managers, and human-in-the-loop agent interfaces; the paper's distinctive claim is generality across multimodal creative domains and integration into a single open harness. Methodology: JarvisHub models a project at turn t as a state C_t=(G_t,X_t,M_t,U_t,L_t), where G_t=(V_t,E_t) is a typed artifact graph, X_t stores editable contents and payloads, M_t stores provenance and execution metadata, U_t records user choices and feedback, and L_t stores spatial layout. Each node has a stable identifier, type, position, editable inputs, outputs or artifact handles, metadata, and runtime status. For each user request, the runtime observes the canvas, receives a capability manifest Γ_t and execution grant Ω_t, selects an action from the permitted action set A(Ω_t,Γ_t,C_t,q_t), invokes a canvas, generation, native-execution, recovery, or MCP-backed tool, and commits the observation through a validation bridge. The state transition is represented as C_{t+1}=F(C_t,a_t,o_t,f_t,r_t), incorporating tool observations, feedback, and repair or follow-up decisions. Skills encode reusable procedures such as storyboarding and design-to-web reconstruction; memory preserves preferences and prior decisions; subagents support bounded parallel subtasks. The trajectory records requests, states, manifests, grants, actions, observations, feedback, repair decisions, and subsequent states. These design choices are well aligned with auditability and human intervention, but the paper does not specify the concrete schemas, validation rules, permission semantics, planning prompts, memory implementation, subagent protocol, or objective criteria used by evaluators in enough detail to independently reconstruct behavior. Key Results: The evaluation runs three qualitative demonstrations in one JarvisHub environment: narrative media generation for a short drama about a “cowboy robot zombie scavenger,” interactive development of an Awwwards-inspired photography website, and generation of a PowerPoint deck on decision trees styled like a Stanford lecture. The reported backends are GPT-5.5 for the main agent, GPT Image 2 for image generation, Seedance 2.0 for video generation, and Gemini 3.1 Pro for multimodal evaluation. Figures show workspace traces containing briefs, references, drafts, dependencies, previews, and progress, alongside final images, website screens, and slides. The paper reports no accuracy, F1, human-preference score, consistency metric, repair-success rate, latency, throughput, token cost, memory use, number of runs, number of turns, failure rate, or statistical uncertainty. It compares no baseline experimentally, so the claim that JarvisHub improves long-horizon creative work remains illustrative rather than measured. The tested scale is three hand-selected demonstrations, not a standard benchmark or stress-scale evaluation. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION, NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, and potentially NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING in the limited sense of demonstrating cross-domain canvas-centered workflows; the genuinely new contribution is the proposed integration of a typed editable project graph, protocol-constrained mutations, multimodal tool orchestration, feedback/recovery, and trajectory logging into an open general-purpose harness, while the individual ingredients are largely standard ideas from visual workflows, graph-based creative tools, agent runtimes, tool-use protocols, and human-in-the-loop systems. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper is an arXiv preprint dated 26 July 2026 and presents qualitative demonstrations rather than a controlled empirical study. It includes no ablations isolating the canvas, protocol bridge, skills, memory, subagents, feedback, or trajectory recording; no multiple seeds, error bars, significance tests, participant study, task-level scoring rubric, or independent evaluation; and no quantitative comparison against chat agents, node-based workflows, or commercial systems. The paper names an open GitHub repository, `https://github.com/LYL1015/JarvisHub`, and a project page, `https://www.jarvishub.site/`, but the parsed paper does not state which code, data, configurations, trajectories, model prompts, or weights are released. The demonstrations depend on proprietary or externally hosted backends, which limits full reproducibility. The evaluation is also vulnerable to selection bias because the authors choose the tasks, prompts, outputs, and visual evidence, and the stated evaluator model is not independently calibrated. The paper appropriately acknowledges that it has not produced a benchmark, but the absence of even process-level metrics prevents validation of its central advantages. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS, because the paper presents a built harness and evaluates it through end-to-end creative workflows rather than only proposing an abstract method. - Practical: The architecture can in principle run on commercially available hardware, but actual hardware requirements, hosting model, browser/runtime dependencies, external API requirements, and operational setup are not stated; the demonstrations rely on proprietary model services. - Efficient: Compute, memory, latency, tool-call count, and cost relative to chat or workflow alternatives are not measured, and persistent graphs, multimodal artifacts, trajectory logs, evaluator calls, and parallel subagents may add substantial overhead. - Effective: The traces demonstrate that the harness can produce inspectable multimodal workflows and artifacts, but they do not establish that it improves creative quality, consistency, user productivity, feedback adherence, or recovery compared with simpler systems. - Scalable: No experiment tests projects with more nodes, longer trajectories, more concurrent subagents, larger media assets, more users, or 10×–100× the demonstrated workload; scalability is an architectural aspiration rather than an evidenced property. The work delivers a software artifact through the cited GitHub repository and project page, but the paper does not document its release completeness or long-term maintainability. Strengths: - It identifies a real systems gap: creative-agent context includes spatial, versioned, multimodal, rejected, and user-selected artifacts that ordinary conversation histories represent poorly. - The canvas/project-graph abstraction gives artifacts stable identities and explicit dependencies, which supports provenance, branching, local revision, inspection, and recovery more directly than a linear chat transcript. - The protocol bridge separates agent decisions from state mutation and introduces manifests, execution grants, validation, and logging, providing a plausible foundation for safer and more auditable tool use. - The same substrate is demonstrated across narrative media, web development, and presentation generation, making the proposed harness broader than a domain-specific storyboard or image-editing system. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state that the evaluation consists of qualitative demonstrations rather than a completed benchmark or leaderboard; final artifact quality depends on external generation models and tools; protocol validation does not guarantee semantically correct creative decisions; and raw trajectory data requires filtering, consent, anonymization, quality control, and copyright review before reuse. They confront these limitations directly in the conclusion, but they do not quantify their impact. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The paper does not define measurable success criteria for its central claims of context preservation, consistency, feedback adherence, repair, inspectability, or human steerability. It lacks controlled baselines and ablations, so the contribution of the canvas versus simply using a capable agent with more context remains unknown. The paper does not report the number or duration of runs, failed tool calls, recovery episodes, user interventions, or artifact revisions, and it provides no evidence that the displayed workflows were not manually curated or substantially edited. The formal state-transition notation describes an interface contract but does not establish correctness, concurrency guarantees, conflict resolution, provenance integrity, or resistance to malformed or adversarial tool outputs. The claimed openness is also unverified in the paper: proprietary backends, unspecified implementation details, and unclear release contents may limit reproducibility. Finally, the work does not evaluate usability, cognitive load, or whether a canvas helps users more than a well-designed task-specific interface. Bottom Line: JarvisHub is a useful open systems concept and potentially valuable research substrate for studying long-horizon creative agents, but in its current preprint form it offers an architectural demonstration rather than evidence that canvas-native state management produces better, cheaper, safer, or more scalable creative-agent behavior.

Efficient Multimodal AI — avg: 72 (Innovative)

These papers collectively address efficient multimodal perception, representation, generation, and action under computational or latency constraints. “TURBOVLA” targets real-time robot control on resource-limited hardware, while “Mage-VL” reduces the cost of continuous video understanding through codec-aware selective streaming. “OmniVAE” and “dRAE” focus on improving the underlying representations—respectively through temporally aligned audio-video latents and hyperspherical discrete visual codes—whereas “Sol-Attn” accelerates video generation at inference through adaptive sparse attention. Together, they suggest a broader trend toward specialized architectures and selective computation that preserve multimodal quality while enabling real-time or scalable deployment.
